title: FINITENESS CONDITIONS. FIBRED TOPOI AND SITES. APPLICATIONS TO QUESTIONS OF PASSAGE TO THE LIMIT

pages.title: FINITENESS CONDITIONS. FIBRED TOPOI AND SITES. APPLICATIONS TO QUESTIONS OF PASSAGE TO THE LIMIT

blocks.html:
EXPOSÉ VI
FINITENESS CONDITIONS. FIBRED TOPOI AND SITES.
APPLICATIONS TO QUESTIONS OF PASSAGE TO THE LIMITby A. Grothendieck and J.L. Verdier
0. Introduction
In the present exposé, we study two kinds of intimately related questions.

First of all, we make a systematic study of the finiteness conditions for topoi, examining in turn the notion of quasi-compactness, of quasi-separation, and of coherence (= quasi-compactness + quasi-separation), inspired by the well-known analogous notions in the theory of schemes, in the case of an object \(X\) of a topos and in that of an arrow \(u : X \to Y\) of a topos (§ 1), then for the topos \(E\) itself (§ 2), and finally for a morphism of topoi \(f : E \to E'\) (§ 3). Section 4 studies these notions in the particular case of a topos obtained by the process of gluing two topoi (IV 9). For the following sections, what it essentially suffices to retain from these somewhat technical developments is the definition of a coherent topos as a topos equivalent to a topos of the form \(\widetilde{C}\), where \(C\) is a small site in which finite projective limits are representable and in which every covering family admits a finite covering subfamily; and that of a coherent morphism \(f : E \to E'\) of coherent topoi as being a morphism which can be described (up to equivalence) as a morphism associated with a morphism of sites \(f : C \to C'\), where \(C\) and \(C'\) are as above, and where the corresponding functor \(f^* : C' \to C\) is left exact.

It is no doubt useful to note that with the finiteness notions used here, and in particular that of a coherent topos, we move resolutely away (and for the first time) from the topological spaces familiar to analysts and to "topologists"(∗). Thus the topos associated (IV 2.1) with a separated topological space \(X\) is coherent only if \(X\) is a finite set! This is to say that the present exposé is entirely oriented towards the types of topos arising from algebraic geometry and algebra. In fact, all the topoi used up to now in these disciplines (except of course those of algebraic geometry by the transcendental route over the field of complex numbers!) happen to be locally coherent.

In the second place, we develop two theorems of passage to the inductive limit for the cohomology of topoi. One (5.2) tells us that the functors \(H^i(E,-)\) on a coherent topos commute with inductive limits of abelian sheaves. The other (8.7) says essentially that if a topos \(X\) is represented as a filtered projective limit of coherent topoi \(X_i\), with coherent transition morphisms \(f_{ij} : X_j \to X_i\), then the cohomology of \(X\) (with coefficients in an arbitrary abelian sheaf) is computed as the inductive limit of the cohomologies of the \(X_i\). To give a precise meaning to this statement, it is above all appropriate to make precise the notion of "projective limit of topoi", which is done in §§ 7.8. This is a very useful geometric notion, including no doubt in contexts other than that of projective limits of schemes (which had served as a model for M. ARTIN in his initial definition of this notion). We show for example (8.4) how one can unify the various notions of "localized at a point" (of a noetherian space, of a scheme for its usual topology, or even for its étale topology), by defining it as the projective limit of the "neighbourhoods" of this point, — in perfect accord with the intuitive idea of the notion of localization at a point.

The two theorems of passage to the limit will be made explicit again in the following exposé in the particular framework of the étale cohomology of schemes (VII 3.3 and 5.7); in this case, they will moreover be constantly used throughout the remainder of this Seminar, and practically everywhere where one has worked up to now with étale cohomology. The reader willing to grant these two theorems, in the particular case where they are stated in Exposé VII, and interested exclusively in the applications of étale cohomology, may therefore omit reading the present exposé. It is true that the notion of a constructible object of a topos (i.e. whose structural morphism \(X \to e\) into the final object \(e\) is coherent) will also play an important role throughout the remainder of the seminar (whereas it plays only a very secondary role in the present exposé, if only because in the case of a coherent topos it coincides with the notion of coherent object, which here takes the leading role). But this notion is developed in Exposé IX, in the particular case of étale sheaves on schemes, in a manner independent of the general study made in the present exposé, and it moreover exhibits in this case some very useful special phenomena, which have served as the basis for the account given of it in IX (beginning with definition IX 2.3). Since the writing of IX predates the present writing of Exposé VI by five years, and is nevertheless very usable for the user, we have limited ourselves at the end of Exposé IX to proving the equivalence of the notion of constructibility used in IX with the one introduced here.

footnotes.html: (∗) The quotation marks indicate that it is a matter of a "..." that ignores the notion of topos (cf. IV 0.4 for the meaning of the word "topology").

pages.title: 1. Finiteness conditions for the objects and arrows of a topos

blocks.html: 1. Finiteness conditions for the objects and arrows of a topos

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1

Let \(C\) be a site. An object \(X\) of \(C\) is said to be quasi-compact if for every covering family \((X_i \to X)_{i \in I}\), there exists a finite subset \(J\) of the index set \(I\) such that the subfamily \((X_i \to X)_{i \in J}\) is still covering.
Since a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(E\) is always regarded as a site (IV 1.1.1), the preceding definition applies in particular to an object of \(E\). One reduces moreover to this case, thanks to the

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(\varepsilon : C \to \widetilde{C}\) the canonical functor, \(X\) an object of \(C\). Then \(X\) is a quasi-compact object of the site \(C\) if and only if \(\varepsilon(X)\) is a quasi-compact object of the topos \(\widetilde{C}\).

Suppose that \(X\) is quasi-compact; let us prove that \(\varepsilon(X)\) is. Let \((F_i \to \varepsilon(X))_{i \in I}\) be an epimorphic family. For each \(i \in I\) take an epimorphic family \(\varepsilon(X_{ij}) \to F_i\), \(j \in J_i\). The composite \(\varepsilon(X_{ij}) \to \varepsilon(X)\) is identified with an element \(\alpha_{ij}\) of \(\varepsilon(X)(X_{ij})\); one cannot assert in general that it comes from a morphism \(X_{ij} \to X\), but by the construction of the associated sheaf, one knows that one can find (for fixed \(i,j\)) a covering family \(Y_k \to X_{ij}\) such that the image elements of \(\alpha_{ij}\) in the \(\varepsilon(X)(Y_k)\) come from elements of \(X(Y_k)\), i.e. from morphisms \(Y_k \to X\). Thus, refining the epimorphic family \(\varepsilon(X_{ij}) \to F_i\) if necessary, one may suppose that the composites \(\varepsilon(X_{ij}) \to \varepsilon(X)\) come from morphisms \(X_{ij} \to X\). For \(i,j\) varying, the family of the \(\varepsilon(X_{ij}) \to \varepsilon(X)\) is epimorphic, hence (II 4.4) the family of the \(X_{ij} \to X\) is covering. By the hypothesis on \(X\), it admits a finite covering subfamily, and it follows again from loc. cit. that the corresponding morphisms \(\varepsilon(X_{ij}) \to \varepsilon(X)\) form an epimorphic family. Since these factor through a finite number of the morphisms \(F_i \to \varepsilon(X)\), this finite family is already epimorphic. This proves that \(\varepsilon(X)\) is quasi-compact.
The fact that \(\varepsilon(X)\) quasi-compact implies \(X\) quasi-compact is on the other hand trivial, thanks to loc. cit.
The preceding result thus shows that the notion of quasi-compactness in sites reduces to the notion in question in topoi.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.3

Let \(C\) be a site, \((X_i \to X)_{i \in I}\) a finite covering family, with the \(X_i\) quasi-compact. Then \(X\) is quasi-compact.

To see this, one may suppose, thanks to 1.2, that \(C\) is a topos. Let \((X'_j \to X)\) be a covering, i.e. epimorphic, family in \(C\); then for each \(i \in I\) the family deduced by the base change \(X'_i \to X\) is epimorphic, hence (since \(X_i\) is quasi-compact) admits a finite epimorphic subfamily, corresponding to a finite subset \(J_i \subset J\) of the index set \(J\). Setting \(J' = \bigcup_{i \in I} J_i\), \(J'\) is a finite subset of \(J\) since \(I\) is finite, and the family \((X'_j \to X)_{j \in J'}\) is already epimorphic since it is so locally, q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.4

Let \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of objects of a topos \(E\), and let \(X\) be the sum. For \(X\) to be quasi-compact, it is necessary and sufficient that all the \(X_i\) be quasi-compact, and that all but a finite number of the \(X_i\) be isomorphic to the "empty object" \(\varnothing_E\) of \(E\).

The sufficiency indeed follows at once from 1.3 (for the sum does not change when one drops the empty summands). For the necessity one notes that a finite subfamily \((X_i)_{i \in J}\) must cover \(X\), which implies that for \(i \in I-J\) one has \(X_i \simeq X_i \times_X \coprod_{j \in J} X_j = \coprod_{j \in J} X_i \times_X X_j = \varnothing\) (II 4.5.1); on the other hand, to show that every \(X_i\) is quasi-compact, one notes that \(X \simeq X_i \amalg X'_i\), and that every covering family \(Y_j \to X_i\) of \(X_i\) defines a covering family \(Y_j \amalg X'_i \to X_i \amalg X'_i = X\) of \(X\), which admits a finite covering subfamily, which evidently implies that the corresponding finite family of the \(Y_j \to X_i\) is also covering, which shows that \(X_i\) is quasi-compact.

The property of an object \(X\) of a topos \(E\) of being quasi-compact depends only on the induced topos \(E_{/X}\), and means that the final object of the latter is quasi-compact. Likewise, an object \(X\) of a site \(C\) is quasi-compact if and only if the final object of the induced site \(C_{/X}\) (III 5.1) is quasi-compact.

Let \(X\) be an object of a topos \(E\). For \(X\) to be quasi-compact, it is necessary and sufficient that every increasing filtered family \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) of subobjects of \(X\) covering \(X\) contain an \(X_i\) equal to \(X\). This condition therefore depends only on the ordered set of subobjects of the object \(X\) (i.e. of the open sets of the induced topos \(E_{/X}\)).

Consider a generating family \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) of \(E\). It then follows from the definitions and from 1.3 that: for an object \(X\) of \(E\) to be quasi-compact, it is necessary that it admit a covering family by a finite number of the \(X_i\), i.e. that \(X\) be isomorphic to a quotient object of a finite sum of objects of \(E\), and this condition is sufficient if the \(X_i\) are quasi-compact. Note on the other hand that, with the hypothesis made on \(E\), one may evidently, upon replacing the generating family under consideration by a subfamily, suppose that \(I \in \mathcal{U}\). Using the fact that the set of quotients of an object of \(E\) is small (I 7.5), one then finds that the full subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{qc}}\) of \(E\) formed by the quasi-compact objects of \(E\) is equivalent to a category \(\in \mathcal{U}\), i.e. that the cardinal of the set of isomorphism classes of objects of \(E_{\mathrm{qc}}\) is \(\in \mathcal{U}\).
Examples 1.6.1

Let \(X\) be a topological space. An open set \(U\) of \(X\) is a quasi-compact object of the site \(\mathrm{Ouv}(X)\) of open sets of \(X\) if and only if \(U\) is a quasi-compact space for the topology induced by \(X\). More generally, a sheaf \(F\) on \(X\) is a quasi-compact object of the topos \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) if and only if the étalé space \(X'\) over \(X\) associated with \(F\) is quasi-compact. (This follows from the preceding assertion, from 1.5, and from the fact that \(\mathrm{Top}(X)_{/F}\) is equivalent to \(\mathrm{Top}(X')\) (IV 5.7)).

Consider on the category (Sch) of schemes (elements of \(\mathcal{U}\)) one of the topologies \(T_i\) of [6] 6.3 (for example the Zariski topology, or the étale topology, or the fppf topology, or the fpqc topology). For a scheme to be quasi-compact in the sense of this topology, it is necessary and sufficient that it be a quasi-compact scheme in the usual sense. (With the notations of loc. cit., one uses only the fact that every family \(\in P'\) is finite.)

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.7

Let \(E\) be a topos, \(f: X \to Y\) an arrow of \(E\). One says that \(f\) is a quasi-compact morphism if for every arrow \(Y' \to Y\), with \(Y'\) quasi-compact, the object \(X' = X \times_Y Y'\) is likewise quasi-compact. One says that \(f\) is quasi-separated if the diagonal morphism \(X \to X \times_Y X\) is quasi-compact. One says that \(f\) is coherent if \(f\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated.

Making explicit the definition of a quasi-separated morphism \(f: X \to Y\), one sees that it also means that for every double arrow \(g_1, g_2 : X' \rightrightarrows X\) "over \(Y\)", i.e. such that \(fg_1 = fg_2\), \(X'\) quasi-compact implies \(\operatorname{Ker}(g_1, g_2)\) quasi-compact.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.8

Let \(E\) be a topos.

  1. (i)

    Every isomorphism in \(E\) is a coherent morphism, i.e. is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. The composite of two quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) morphisms is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent).

  2. (ii)

    Let \(f: X \to Y\) and \(g: Y' \to Y\) be morphisms in \(E\), and \(f' : X' = X \times_Y Y' \to\) deduced from \(f\) by the base change \(g\). If \(f\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent), so is \(f'\).

  3. (iii)

    Let \(f: X \to Y\) and \(g: Y \to Z\) be morphisms in \(E\). If \(gf\) is quasi-separated, \(f\) is quasi-separated.

  4. (iv)

    Let \(f: X \to Y\) and \(g: Y \to Z\) be morphisms in \(E\), with \(g\) quasi-separated. If \(gf\) is quasi-compact (resp. coherent), then \(f\) is quasi-compact (resp. coherent).

The proofs are well known (Cf. EGA IV 1 or EGA I 2nd edition). The statements (i) and (ii) in the "quasi-compact" case follow trivially from the definitions; in the "quasi-separated" case, stability under base change (ii) follows at once from the definition and from the preceding case, as does the fact that every isomorphism is quasi-separated. Stability under composition \(X \to Y \to Z\) is seen with the aid of the diagram
\[ (*) \qquad \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]^-{\Delta_{X/Y}} \ar@/_5pc/[dd]_-{\Delta_{X/Z}} \\ X \times_Y X \ar[r] \ar[d]^-{u} & Y \ar[d]^-{\Delta_{Y/Z}} \\ X \times_Z X \ar[r] & Y \times_Z Y } \]

with cartesian square. By hypothesis \(\Delta_{Y/Z}\) is quasi-compact, hence so is \(u\), which is deduced from it by base change, and \(\Delta_{X/Y}\) is quasi-compact, hence so is the composite \(u \, \Delta_{X/Y} = \Delta_{X/Z}\). This establishes (i) and (ii), the "coherent" case following from the conjunction of the two preceding cases. To prove the first case considered in (iv), one considers the following diagram with cartesian squares

\[ (**) \qquad \xymatrix{ & X \ar[r]^-{gf} & Z \\ X \ar[r]^-{\Gamma_f = (\mathrm{id}_X, f)} \ar[d]_-{v} \ar@/^3pc/[rr]^-{f} & X \times_Z Y \ar[u]_-{\mathrm{pr}_1} \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{pr}_2} \ar[d]^-{f \times_Z \mathrm{id}_Y} & Y \ar[u]_-{g} \\ Y \ar[r]_-{\Delta_{Y/Z}} & Y \times_Z Y } \]

By the hypothesis \(g\) is quasi-separated, \(\Delta_{Y/Z}\) is quasi-compact, hence \(\Gamma_f\) is quasi-compact by base change; likewise by hypothesis \(gf\) is quasi-compact, hence \(\mathrm{pr}_2\) is too by base change; consequently \(f = \mathrm{pr}_2 \, \Gamma_f\) is quasi-compact as the composite of two quasi-compact morphisms. The resp. case of (iv) follows at once from the preceding case and from (iii), which it remains to prove now. For this one takes up again the diagram (*), noting that the hypothesis \(gf\) quasi-separated means that \(\Delta_{X/Z} = u \, \Delta_{X/Y}\) is quasi-compact, and that the conclusion \(f\) quasi-separated means that \(\Delta_{X/Y}\) is quasi-compact, which follows from (iv) once one has proved that \(u\) is quasi-separated. Now \(u\) is manifestly a monomorphism, and one has indeed the trivial result:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.8.1

Every monomorphism is quasi-separated.
Indeed, if \(u: X \to Y\) is a monomorphism, \(\Delta_{X/Y}\) is an isomorphism, hence is quasi-compact, q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.8.2

Let \(f: X \to Y\), \(f' : X' \to Y'\) be two \(S\)-morphisms in \(E\). If \(f, f'\) are quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent), so is \(f \times_S f' : X \times_S X' \to Y \times_S Y'\).
This follows in a well-known manner from the conjunction of (i) and (ii).

Let \(E\) be an arbitrary category, \(Q\) a subset of ob \(E\) stable under isomorphism (the datum of \(Q\) thus amounts to that of a strictly full subcategory of \(E\)), playing the role of "quasi-compact" objects. Suppose that in \(E\) the fibre products are representable. Then one can paraphrase definition 1.7 to define the notion of \(Q\)-quasi-compact, \(Q\)-quasi-separated, and \(Q\)-coherent morphisms. Then 1.8 and 1.8.1 hold, and 1.8.2 as well when in \(E\) the products of two objects are representable.

Let \(S\) be an object of \(E\), and \(f: X \to Y\) a morphism of \(E_{/S}\). It follows at once from remark 1.5 that for \(f\) to be quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) it is necessary and sufficient that the morphism corresponding in \(E\) (deduced from \(f\) by the functor "forgetting \(S\)") be so. In particular, if \(f: X \to Y\) is a morphism in \(E\), taking above \(S=Y\), one sees that \(f\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) if and only if the structural morphism of the object \((X,f)\) of the topos induced \(E_{/Y}\), with target the final object of the said topos, is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent). One also says that (by means of the structural morphism \(f\)) \(X\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) over \(Y\), a locution which one may interpret indifferently as referring to the topos \(E\), or to the induced topos \(E_{/Y}\) (of which \(Y\) is regarded as a final object).

An object \(X\) of a topos \(E\) will be said to be constructible if it is coherent over the final object. Every morphism from one constructible object into another is coherent (1.8 (iv)). The full subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{cons}}\) of \(E\) formed by the constructible objects of \(E\) is stable under finite \(\varprojlim\), as follows at once from 1.8.2 and 1.8 (ii).

The notions 1.7 are of hardly any interest except in topoi \(E\) which admit a generating family formed of quasi-compact objects. In this case, these notions are "of local nature below" (IV 8.5.4), as we shall now see.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.10

Suppose that the topos \(E\) admits a generating subcategory \(C\) formed of quasi-compact objects, and let \(f : X \to Y\) be a morphism in \(E\).

  1. (i)

    For \(f\) to be quasi-compact, it is necessary and sufficient that for every morphism \(S \to Y\), with \(S \in\) Ob \(C\), \(X \times_Y S\) be quasi-compact.

  2. (ii)

    Let \(Y_i \to Y\), \(i \in I\), be a covering family. For \(f\) to be quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) it is necessary and sufficient that for every \(i \in I\), \(f_i : X_i = X \times_Y Y_i \to Y_i\) be so.

Let us prove (i). The necessity is trivial by definition. For the sufficiency, one must prove that for every quasi-compact object \(Y'\) and every morphism \(Y' \to Y\), \(X' = X \times_Y Y'\) is quasi-compact. Now there exists a covering family \(S_i \to Y'\), the \(S_i\) in Ob \(C\), and since \(Y'\) is quasi-compact, one may take the covering family in question to be finite. Then by hypothesis the \(X'_i = X \times_Y S_i \simeq X' \times_{Y'} S_i\) are quasi-compact, and since they cover \(X'\) (the \(S_i\) covering \(Y'\)), \(X'\) is quasi-compact by virtue of 1.3.

Let us prove (ii). It suffices to treat the "quasi-compact" case, for the "quasi-separated" case follows from it by definition 1.7, and the "coherent" case likewise, by the conjunction of the two preceding cases. The "necessity" has already been seen in 1.8 (ii); it remains to see that if the \(f_i\) are quasi-compact, then \(f\) is, i.e. that for every quasi-compact \(Y'\) and every morphism \(Y' \to Y\), the object \(X' = X \times_Y Y'\) is quasi-compact. Now since \((Y_i \to Y)\) is covering, there exist \(S_\alpha\) over \(Y\) covering \(Y'\), such that the composite morphisms \(S_\alpha \to Y' \to Y\) each factor through some \(Y_i\). Since \(C\) is generating, one may take the \(S_\alpha\) in Ob \(C\), and since \(Y'\) is quasi-compact, one may take the covering family finite. Then the \(X' \times_{Y'} S_\alpha\) form a finite covering family of \(X'\), and one is reduced by 1.3 to proving that each \(X' \times_{Y'} S_\alpha = X \times_Y S_\alpha\) is quasi-compact. Now, choosing a factorization of \(S_\alpha \to Y\) through some \(Y_i\), the object under consideration is also isomorphic to \(X_i \times_{Y_i} S_\alpha\), which is indeed quasi-compact since \(X_i\) is quasi-compact over \(Y_i\) and \(S_\alpha\) is quasi-compact.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.11

Let \(g: Y \to Z\) be a morphism in the topos \(E\), \((f_i : X_i \to Y)_{i \in I}\) a covering family of morphisms with target \(Y\). Then:

  1. (i)

    Suppose \(I\) finite. If the \(gf_i\) are quasi-compact, so is \(g\).

  2. (ii)

    Suppose the \(f_i\) quasi-compact. If the \(gf_i\) are quasi-separated, so is \(g\). If \(I\) is finite, and if the \(gf_i\) are coherent, \(g\) is coherent.

Case (i) follows at once from the definitions and from 1.3, (without hypothesis on \(E\)). To prove (ii), it suffices, by virtue of (i), to treat the non-resp. case. Consider the diagram 1.8 (*) with \(X\) replaced by an \(X_i\). Since the family of the \(f_i\) is covering, so is the family of the \(f_i \times_Z \mathrm{id}_Y\) deduced from it by base change, hence by virtue of 1.10 (ii), to prove that \(\Delta_{Y/Z}\) is quasi-compact, it suffices to prove that the \(\Gamma_{f_i}\) are. Now \(gf_i\) being quasi-separated by hypothesis, so is \(\mathrm{pr}_2 : X_i \times_Z Y \to Y\), which is deduced from it by base change; on the other hand \(\mathrm{pr}_2 \, \Gamma_{f_i} = f_i\) is quasi-compact by hypothesis. So is \(\Gamma_{f_i}\) then, by virtue of 1.8 (iv) applied to the composite morphism of \(\mathrm{pr}_2\) and \(\Gamma_{f_i}\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.12

Let \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) be a finite family of objects of \(E\), \(X\) the sum of the \(X_i\), \(f_i : X_i \to Y\) morphisms in \(E\), and \(f: X \to Y\) the corresponding morphism. For \(f\) to be quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) it is necessary and sufficient that the \(f_i\) be so; in the "quasi-separated" case, the hypothesis "\(I\) finite" may be omitted.

The sufficiency of the condition is a particular case of 1.11, taking into account that the canonical morphisms \(X_i \to X\) form a finite covering family, and that these are quasi-compact morphisms, as follows at once from the definition and from 1.4. The necessity follows from transitivity 1.8 (i), taking into account that the \(f_i\) are even coherent (for they are quasi-separated by virtue of 1.8.1).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.13

Let \(X\) be an object of a topos \(E\). One says that \(X\) is a quasi-separated object of the topos \(E\) if for every quasi-compact object \(S\) of \(E\), every morphism from \(S\) into \(X\) is quasi-compact, i.e. (1.7) if for two quasi-compact objects \(S,T\) of \(E\) and morphisms \(S \to X\), \(T \to X\), the fibre product \(S \times_X T\) is always quasi-compact. One says that \(X\) is a coherent object of the topos \(E\) if \(X\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.14

Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a morphism in a topos \(E\).

  1. (i)

    If \(Y\) is quasi-compact, then \(f\) quasi-compact implies \(X\) quasi-compact. If \(Y\) is quasi-separated, then \(X\) quasi-compact implies \(f\) quasi-compact. If \(Y\) is coherent, \(f\) quasi-compact is equivalent to \(X\) quasi-compact.

  2. (ii)

    If \(Y\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) and if \(f\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) then \(X\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent).

The first two assertions of (i) are trivially contained in the definitions of quasi-compact morphism (1.7) resp. of quasi-separated object (1.13), the third follows from the conjunction of the first two. The first case of (ii) is but a repetition, the third follows again from the conjunction of the first two, it remains to treat the quasi-separated case. So let \(S\) be a quasi-compact object of \(E\) and \(g:S \to X\) a morphism; let us prove that \(g\) is quasi-compact. Since \(Y\) is quasi-separated, \(fg\) is quasi-compact, and since \(f\) is quasi-separated, it follows (1.8 (iv)) that \(g\) is quasi-compact, q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.15

Every subobject of a quasi-separated object of \(E\) is quasi-separated. Let \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of objects of \(E\), with \(I \in \mathcal{U}\); then \(X = \coprod_i X_i\) is quasi-separated (resp. coherent) if and only if the \(X_i\) are so.

The first assertion follows from 1.14 (ii) and from 1.8.1, but is likewise trivial from the definition. For the second, non-resp., one, since the \(X_i \to X\) are monomorphisms, it remains to prove the "sufficiency", which follows easily from the definitions and from 1.3; the resp. case follows from the case treated and from 1.4.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.16

Under the conditions of 1.10 (ii), if the \(Y_i\) are coherent, then \(f\) is quasi-compact if and only if the \(X_i = X \times_Y Y_i\) are quasi-compact objects of \(E\).
Indeed, by virtue of the criterion 1.10 (ii), one must express that the \(f_i : X_i \to Y_i\) are quasi-compact, which is equivalent to \(X_i\) quasi-compact by virtue of 1.14 (i).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.17

Let \(E\) be a topos admitting a generating family formed of quasi-compact objects, and \((g_i : Y_i \to Y)_{i \in I}\) a covering (resp. finite covering) family in \(E\), with the \(Y_i\) coherent. For \(Y\) to be quasi-separated (resp. coherent), it is necessary and sufficient that for every \(i \in I\), \(g_i\) be quasi-compact, or again that for every pair of indices \(i,j \in I\), \(Y_i \times_Y Y_j\) be a quasi-compact object of \(E\).

The resp. case follows at once from the non-resp. case and from 1.3. The necessity of the first condition is trivial by definition; let us prove that it is sufficient. So let \(f: X \to Y\) be a morphism, with \(X\) quasi-compact; let us prove that \(f\) is quasi-compact. Now since the \(g_i\) are quasi-compact, it follows that the \(X_i = X \times_Y Y_i\) are quasi-compact, which implies that \(f\) is so by virtue of 1.16. Finally, expressing the quasi-compactness of the \(g_i\) with the aid of the same criterion 1.16, one finds the second criterion of 1.17. In particular:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.17.1

Let \(E\) be as in 1.17, \(X\) a coherent object of \(E\), \(\mathcal{R} \rightrightarrows X\) an equivalence relation in \(X\), \(Y = X/\mathcal{R}\). Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(Y\) is coherent,

  2. (ii)

    \(f: X \to Y\) is quasi-compact,

  3. (iii)

    \(\mathcal{R}\) is quasi-compact.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.18

Let \(E\) be a topos admitting a generating subcategory \(C\) formed of quasi-compact objects, \(Y\) an object of \(E\). For \(Y\) to be quasi-separated, it is necessary and sufficient that every morphism \(X \to Y\), with \(X \in\) ob \(C\), be quasi-compact.

The necessity is trivial by definition, the \(X \in\) ob \(C\) being quasi-compact by hypothesis. To prove the sufficiency, let \(Z\) be a quasi-compact object of \(E\); let us prove that every morphism \(Z' \to Y\) is quasi-compact. For this, it suffices by virtue of 1.10 (i) to verify that for every \(X \to Y\), with \(X \in\) ob \(C\), \(Z \times_Y X\) is quasi-compact, which follows indeed from the fact that the \(X \to Y\) are quasi-compact by hypothesis, and that \(Z\) is quasi-compact.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.19

Let \(E\) be a topos admitting a generating subcategory formed of quasi-compact objects, \((g_i : Y_i \to Y)_{i \in I}\) a covering family in \(E\), with the \(Y_i\) quasi-separated and the \(g_i\) quasi-compact. Then \(Y\) is quasi-separated.

Indeed, let \(X\) be a quasi-compact object of \(E\); let us show that every morphism \(f : X \to Y\) is quasi-compact. By virtue of 1.10 (ii) it suffices to prove that the induced morphisms \(f_i : X_i = X \times_Y Y_i \to Y_i\) are quasi-compact. Now since \(g_i\) is quasi-compact, \(X_i\) is quasi-compact (\(X\) being so), and since \(Y_i\) is quasi-separated, it indeed follows that \(f_i\) is quasi-compact.

The reader accustomed to the use of the terms "quasi-compact" and "quasi-separated" in algebraic geometry will expect certain other relations between the "absolute" notions (concerning the objects of the topos \(E\)) and the "relative" notions (concerning arrows of \(E\)) under consideration, for example: if \(f: X \to Y\) is a morphism in \(E\) such that \(X\) is quasi-separated, then \(f\) is quasi-separated. Such properties are valid only subject to restrictive finiteness conditions on the topos \(E\), stronger than those considered in 1.10, conditions which we shall study in the following section.

It follows again from 1.5 that the property for an object \(X\) of the topos \(E\) of being quasi-separated depends only on the induced topos \(E_{/X}\), and means that the final object of the said topos is quasi-separated, i.e. that in \(E_{/X}\), the product of two quasi-compact objects is quasi-compact.
1.21. The case of sites

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(E\) the topos of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaves on \(C\), \(f\) an arrow of \(C\), \(X\) an object of \(C\). One says that \(f\) is a quasi-compact morphism (resp. quasi-separated) of the site \(C\) if \(\varepsilon(f)\) is a quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated) morphism of the topos \(E\); and likewise that \(X\) is a quasi-separated object of the site \(C\) if \(\varepsilon(X)\) is a quasi-separated object of the topos \(E\) (compare 1.2). When \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos equipped with its canonical topology, then the canonical functor \(\varepsilon : C \to E\) is an equivalence of categories, and consequently the preceding definition is compatible with the earlier definitions 1.7 and 1.13. Note also that the definition under consideration does not change when one replaces the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) by another universe \(\mathcal{V}\) such that \(C\) is also a \(\mathcal{V}\)-site, at least when \(C\) admits a topologically generating family formed of quasi-compact objects. To see this, one is at once reduced to the case where \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{V}\), so that \(E\) is a \(\mathcal{V}\)-site, and to proving that for every arrow \(f\) of the \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(E\), \(f\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated) if and only if it defines a quasi-compact arrow in the topos \(E'\) of \(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaves on \(E\), and likewise that for every object \(X\) of \(E\), \(X\) is quasi-separated if and only if the corresponding object of \(E'\) is quasi-separated. Note that we already know (without hypothesis on \(E\)) the analogous statement for the case of a quasi-compact object (1.2). The case "\(f\) quasi-compact" follows from it, thanks to the criterion 1.10 (i) applied successively in \(E\) and in \(E'\), for the same generating family \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) of \(E\) formed of quasi-compact objects; whence also the case "\(f\) quasi-separated", which means that the corresponding diagonal morphism is quasi-compact. Finally for the case "\(X\) quasi-separated", one is again reduced to the case "\(f\) quasi-compact", thanks to the criterion 1.18.
1.22. Examples

Let us take up again example 1.6.2 of the category (Sch) with a topology \(T_i\), which is a \(\mathcal{V}\)-site for suitable \(\mathcal{V}\), admitting the subcategory of affine schemes as a topological generating category formed of quasi-compact objects. We leave to the reader the task of verifying that an arrow \(f: X \to Y\) of this site is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated) if and only if it is a quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated) morphism of schemes in the usual sense ([3] or [4]); likewise an object of the site is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated) if and only if it is a quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated) scheme in the usual sense of loc. cit. It is moreover fitting to say, as here, coherent morphism of schemes, coherent scheme, instead of "quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphism of schemes", "quasi-compact and quasi-separated scheme", as is moreover done in EGA I 2nd edition.

For a given scheme \(X \in \mathcal{U}\), one may also consider the topos \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) associated with the underlying topological space, or the topos \(\mathrm{Top}(X_{\text{ét}})\) (resp. \(\mathrm{Top}(X_{\mathrm{fppf}})\)), associated with the site of étale \(X\)-schemes (resp. locally of finite presentation) that are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\), with the étale (resp. fppf) topology. It is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos which admits a generating family formed of coherent objects, corresponding to the affine objects of the defining site;

This said, the final object of this topos is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) if and only if the scheme \(X\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent). Likewise, a morphism of the site of étalé spaces over \(X\) (resp. of the site \(X_{\text{ét}}\) of étale schemes over \(X\), resp. of the site \(X_{\mathrm{fppf}}\) of schemes locally of finite presentation over \(X\)) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) if and only if it is a morphism of schemes which is (in the usual sense of loc. cit.) quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.23

Let \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos, \(X\) an object of \(E\).

  1. (i)

    For \(X\) to be quasi-compact, it is necessary and sufficient that for every filtered inductive system \((Y_i)_{i \in I}\) of \(E\), with \(I \in \mathcal{U}\), the natural map \[ \text{(1.23.1)} \qquad \varinjlim \mathrm{Hom}(X, Y_i) \to \mathrm{Hom}(X, \varinjlim Y_i) \] be injective.

  2. (ii)

    Suppose that \(E\) admits a generating subcategory \(C\) formed of quasi-compact objects. For \(X\) to be coherent, it is necessary that for every datum as in (i), the map (1.23.1) be bijective.

(i) Necessity. Suppose \(X\) quasi-compact; one must prove that if \(i \in I\) and \(f_i, g_i : X \rightrightarrows Y_i\) are such that the composites \(f, g\) of \(f_i\), \(g_i\) with \(Y_i \to Y = \varinjlim Y_j\) are equal, then there exists \(j \geq i\) such that the composites \(f_j\), \(g_j\) with \(Y_i \to Y_j\) are already equal. Now since in \(E\) the filtered inductive limits commute with finite projective limits, and in particular with kernels, one has \[ \operatorname{Ker}(f,g) = \varinjlim_{j \geq i} \operatorname{Ker}(f_j, g_j) . \] By hypothesis \(\operatorname{Ker}(f,g) = X\), hence \(X\) is the limit of the increasing filtered family of its subobjects \(\operatorname{Ker}(f_j, g_j)\), hence since \(X\) is quasi-compact, it is equal to one of these subobjects, so there exists \(j \geq i\) such that \(f_j = g_j\).

Sufficiency. To prove that \(X\) is quasi-compact, it amounts to the same (1.5.2) to prove that for every increasing filtered family \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) of subobjects of \(X\) whose \(\varinjlim\) is \(X\), there exists \(i \in I\) such that \(X_i = X\). Now since in \(E\) every monomorphism is effective (II 4.0), it follows that \[ X_i = \operatorname{Ker}(f_i, g_i : X \rightrightarrows X \amalg_{X_i} X) . \] Let \(Y_i = X \amalg_{X_i} X\), and consider the inductive system formed by the \(Y_i\). If \(Y\) is its inductive limit, one has \(Y \simeq X \amalg_{\varinjlim X_i} X = X \amalg_X X = X\). Consequently, for a fixed \(i \in I\), \(f_i\), \(g_i\) give the same element of \(\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)\), hence by hypothesis there exists \(j \geq i\) such that \(f_j = g_j\) i.e. \(X_j = X\), q.e.d.

(ii) It remains to prove that under the indicated conditions, every morphism \(X \to Y\) comes from a morphism \(X \to Y_i\) for a suitable \(i \in I\). Since \(C\) generates \(E\) and the \(Y_i\) cover \(Y\), we can cover \(X\) by objects \(X_\alpha\) of \(C\), in such a way that each of the composites \(X_\alpha \to X \to Y\) factors through one of the \(Y_i\). Since \(X\) is quasi-compact, one may suppose the family of the \(X_\alpha\) finite, hence that the morphisms \(X_\alpha \to Y\) factor through a fixed \(Y_i\) in the form \(g_{\alpha i} : X_\alpha \to Y_i\). Since \(X\) is quasi-separated, the \(X_\alpha \times_X X_\beta\) are quasi-compact. Moreover, for every \((\alpha, \beta)\), the composites of \(\mathrm{pr}_1\) and \(\mathrm{pr}_2\) on \(X_\alpha \times_X X_\beta\) with \(X_\alpha\), \(X_\beta \to Y_i\) are such that their composites with \(Y_i \to Y\) are equal:
\[ \xymatrix{ X_\alpha \times_X X_\beta \ar@<0.6ex>[r] \ar@<-0.6ex>[r] \ar[d] & X_\alpha \ar[r] \ar[dl] & Y_i \ar[d] \\ X \ar[rr] & & Y } \]

By virtue of (i), there therefore exists a \(j \geq i\) such that the composites with \(Y_i \to Y_j\) are already equal. Since the set of pairs \((\alpha, \beta)\) is finite, one may take \(j\) independent of this pair. Consequently the morphisms \(g_{\alpha j}\) come by composition from a morphism \(g_j : X \to Y_j\), whose composite with \(Y_j \to Y\) is moreover the given morphism \(X \to Y\), since this is so after composition with the \(X_\alpha \to X\). This completes the proof.
The hypothesis on \(E\) in (ii) may be replaced by an additional hypothesis on \(X\), namely that \(X\) admits a fundamental system of covering families by quasi-compact objects.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.24

Let \(E\) be a topos, and let \(C\) be a strictly full subcategory of \(E\) formed of coherent objects. Using the fact that in \(E\) the \(\mathcal{U}\)-filtered inductive limits are representable, one finds (I 8.6.1) a canonical functor \[ \text{(1.24.1)} \qquad \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to E . \] This functor is fully faithful. If \(E\) admits a generating subcategory formed of coherent objects, and if \(C\) is stable under direct summands, then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    The functor (1.24.1) is essentially surjective, i.e. it is an equivalence of categories.

  2. (ii)

    \(C\) is a generating subcategory of \(E\), stable under finite inductive limits.

  3. (iii)

    The category \(C\) is equal to the full subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of \(E\) formed of all the coherent objects of \(E\), and the necessary condition 1.23 (ii) of coherence for an object of \(E\) is also sufficient.

Let \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) be the full subcategory of \(E\) defined in I 8.7.6. By virtue of I 8.7.5 a), the statement 1.23 (ii) is equivalent to the second inclusion of \[ C \subset E_{\mathrm{coh}} \subset E_{\mathrm{PF}} , \] and the composite inclusion \(C \subset E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) means that (1.24.1) is fully faithful. Since by hypothesis the subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of \(E\) is generating, so a fortiori is \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\); on the other hand in \(E\) the finite projective limits are representable, so that we can apply I 8.7.7. The condition (iii) of 1.24 is also written \(C = E_{\mathrm{coh}} = E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), and is equivalent to the condition \(C = E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), which is none other than the condition (ii bis) of loc. cit. (taking into account that by hypothesis, \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) hence \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) is a generating subcategory of \(E\)). Likewise the condition (ii) of 1.24 is none other than the condition (iii bis) of loc. cit. Thus the equivalence of the conditions (i), (ii bis) and (iii bis) in loc. cit. gives the equivalence of the conditions (i), (ii) and (iii) of 1.24, q.e.d.
The proof (or more precisely, the invocation of I 8.7.7 (ii bis)) also furnishes part a) of the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.24.2

Let \(E\) be a topos admitting a generating subfamily formed of coherent objects, and let \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) be the strictly full subcategory of the objects \(X\) of \(E\) such that the covariant functor \(\mathrm{Hom}(X,-)\) which it represents commutes with filtered inductive limits. Then:

  1. a)

    The natural functor \[ \mathrm{Ind}(E_{\mathrm{PF}}) \to E \] is an equivalence of categories.

  2. b)

    For an object \(X\) of \(E\) to belong to \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), it is necessary and sufficient that it be isomorphic to a direct summand (= image of a projector (I, 10.6))
of the cokernel of a double arrow \(X_1 \rightrightarrows X_0\), with \(X_1\) and \(X_0\) coherent.
c)The subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) of \(E\) is stable under finite inductive limits, and is equivalent to a small category

It remains to prove b) and c). The first assertion of c) is trivial thanks to I 2.8, and implies the "sufficiency" in b) thanks to 1.23 (ii). For the "necessity", we use 1.23 (i), which shows that \(X\) is quasi-compact, whence the existence of an epimorphism \(X_0 \to X\), with \(X_0\) coherent, taking into account that \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) generates \(E\) and is stable under finite sums. Let \(R = X_0 \times_X X_0\), so that \(X\) is identified with the cokernel of \(R \rightrightarrows X_0\). By a), we have \(R = \varinjlim R_i\), a filtered inductive limit with the \(R_i\) in \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), hence \(X\) is the filtered inductive limit of the \(\operatorname{Coker}(R_i \rightrightarrows X_0) = X'_i\). By the hypothesis \(X \in\) Ob \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), for \(i\) large enough the morphism \(u_i : X'_i \to X\) admits a section \(v: X \to X'_i\). Let \(w = v u_i : X'_i \to X'_i\), so that \(w^2 = w\) and \(X \simeq \operatorname{Coker}(w, \mathrm{id}_{X'_i} : X'_i \rightrightarrows X'_i)\). Since \(R_i\) is again quasi-compact, we cover it by \(X_1 \to R_i\) with \(X_1\) coherent, whence \(X'_i \simeq \operatorname{Coker}(X_1 \rightrightarrows X_0)\), which proves b).
Finally, since \(E_{\mathrm{PF}} \subset E_{\mathrm{qu.cpct}}\), the last assertion of c) follows from 1.5.3.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.25

Let \(E\) be a topos such that the full subcategory \(C\) of \(E\) consisting of the coherent objects is generating. Consider the canonical functor \[ \varphi : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to E . \] The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    The functor \(\varphi\) is essentially surjective, i.e. every object of \(E\) is a filtered inductive limit of coherent objects.

  2. (i bis)

    The functor \(\varphi\) is an equivalence of categories.

  3. (ii)

    Every finite inductive limit in \(E\) of coherent objects is a coherent object.

  4. (ii bis)

    The cokernel in \(E\) of a double arrow of coherent objects is a coherent object.

  5. (iii)

    The converse of 1.23 (ii) holds.
This is a special case of 1.24, taking into account that \(C\) is stable under finite sums (1.4), which implies the equivalence of (ii) and (ii bis), and taking into account the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.25.1

Let \(E\) be a topos. Every direct summand \(X'\) of a coherent object \(X\) of \(E\) is coherent.
Indeed, \(X'\) is quasi-compact as a quotient of \(X\) (1.3), and quasi-separated as a subobject of \(X\) (1.15).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.26

Let \(E\) be a topos satisfying the equivalent conditions 1.25. Then the same holds for every induced topos.

This follows immediately from criterion (ii), taking into account 1.20.2 and the fact that the existence of a generating subcategory of \(E\) consisting of coherent objects manifestly implies the same property for an induced topos.

Among the important examples of topoi satisfying the conditions of 1.25, let us mention the noetherian topoi (2.14), and the Zariski or étale topos (VII 1) of a scheme \(X\) (cf. IX, note p.42). But even when the topos \(E\) is coherent (2.3) (i.e. the full subcategory \(C\) of coherent objects is generating and stable under finite projective limits), it is not always true that \(C\) is perfect (2.9.1), i.e. satisfies the equivalent conditions of 1.25; cf. 1.28 below.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 1.28

Let \(E\) be a topos, \(p_1, p_2 : X_1 \rightrightarrows X_0\) a double arrow in \(E\). Define an increasing sequence of subobjects \(R_n\) (\(n \geq 0\)) of \(X_0 \times X_0\) by the condition \(R_0 = \operatorname{Sup}(\operatorname{Im}(p_1,p_2), \operatorname{Im}(p_2,p_1))\), and \(R_n = \mathrm{pr}_{13}(\mathrm{pr}_{12}^{-1}(R_{n-1}), \mathrm{pr}_{23}^{-1}(R_{n-1}))\) for all \(n \geq 1\), where \(\mathrm{pr}_{ij}\) (\(1 \leq i < j \leq 3\)) denote the evident projections from the triple product of \(X_0\) to the double product.

  1. a)

    Show that one thus obtains an increasing sequence of subobjects of \(X_0 \times X_0\), that \(R = \varinjlim R_n\) is an equivalence graph (I 10.4) in \(X_0\), and that the canonical morphism \[ X = \operatorname{Coker}(p_1,p_2) \to X_0/R \] is an isomorphism.

  2. b)

    Conclude that if \(X_0\) is quasi-compact and \(X = \operatorname{Coker}(p_1,p_2)\) is quasi-separated (hence coherent), then the sequence of the \(R_n\) is stationary. Conversely, if this sequence is stationary, and if one assumes \(X_0\) coherent and \(X_1\) quasi-compact, then \(X\) is coherent. (For this last point, write \(R_n \simeq (R_{n-1}, \mathrm{pr}_2) \times_{X_0} (R_{n-1}, \mathrm{pr}_1)\) and conclude that \(R_n\) is quasi-compact over \(X_0\) for all \(n\), then use 1.19.)

  3. c)

    Construct an example of two maps of sets \(p_1, p_2 : X_1 \rightrightarrows X_0\), such that the sequence of the \((R_n)\) is not stationary.

  4. d)

    Let \(C\) be a small category in which finite inductive limits and finite projective limits are representable, and in which every morphism factors as an effective epimorphism followed by a monomorphism. Repeat, for a double arrow \((p_1, p_2)\) of \(C\), the construction of the \(R_n\). Equipping \(C\) with the canonical topology, show that the canonical functor \(\varepsilon : C \to \widetilde{C}\) is exact, and consequently commutes with the formation of the \(R_n\).

  5. e)

    Take for \(C\) a small full subcategory of (Ens), stable up to isomorphism under finite projective limits and finite inductive limits, and containing the sets \(X_0, X_1\) of c). Conclude that the topos \(\widetilde{C}\) (which is a coherent topos (2.3), i.e. generated by the subcategory of its coherent objects, which is stable under finite projective limits) does not satisfy the equivalent conditions of 1.25.

  6. f)

    Let \(k\) be a field, \(C\) the fppf site of schemes locally of finite presentation over \(k\) (SGA 3 IV 6.3). Show that there exists a reduced affine scheme \(X\) over \(k\) admitting an automorphism \(f\) that is not of finite order (take for example the affine space \(E^2\) equipped with the automorphism \(f(x)=x, f(y)=x+y\)). Show that if \(p_1, p_2 : X_1 \rightrightarrows X_0\) is a double arrow in \(C\), such that the corresponding double arrow in (Ens) \(p_1(\overline{k}), p_2(\overline{k}) : X_1(\overline{k}) \rightrightarrows X_0(\overline{k})\) gives a non-stationary sequence \((R_n)\), then the same holds for the double arrow of \(\widetilde{C}\) defined by \(p_1, p_2\); hence, if \(X_0\) is of finite type over \(k\), then the cokernel in \(\widetilde{C}\) of \((p_1,p_2)\) is not coherent. Conclude that the cokernel in \(\widetilde{C}\) of the pair \((f, \mathrm{id}_X)\) is not coherent, hence that the topos \(\widetilde{C}\) does not satisfy the equivalent conditions of 1.25. Conclude more generally that if \(S\) is a non-empty scheme, \(C\) the fppf site of schemes locally of finite presentation over \(S\), then the topos \(\widetilde{C}\) does not satisfy the conditions of 1.25. (Note that, contrary to appearances, \(\widetilde{C}\) is therefore noetherian (2.11) only if \(S\) is empty, as follows from the foregoing and from 2.14.)

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.30

Let \(E\) be a topos. An object \(X\) of \(E\) is called a prenoetherian(∗) object of the topos \(E\) if it satisfies the two following equivalent conditions:

  1. (i)

    Every subobject of \(X\) is quasi-compact.

  2. (ii)

    Every increasing sequence of subobjects of \(X\) is stationary.

The equivalence of conditions (i) and (ii) is clear. Note that these conditions again depend only on the induced topos \(E_{/X}\), and indeed only on the ordered set of opens of \(E_{/X}\), isomorphic to the ordered set of subobjects of \(X\). They are stable under passage to a subobject of \(X\).

One proves, as for 1.3 and 1.4, the following facts: if \((X_i \to X)\) is a finite covering family, with the \(X_i\) prenoetherian, then \(X\) is prenoetherian; in particular a quotient of a prenoetherian object of \(E\) is prenoetherian. If \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) is a family of objects of \(E\), then their sum \(X\) is a prenoetherian object of \(E\) if and only if all but a finite number of the \(X_i\) are isomorphic to \(\varnothing_E\), and all the \(X_i\) are prenoetherian.

Evidently a prenoetherian object of a topos \(E\) is quasi-compact; when \(E\) admits a generating family consisting of prenoetherian objects, the converse holds (as follows immediately from 1.31): the prenoetherian objects of \(E\) are then its quasi-compact objects.
Suppose that \(E\) admits a generating family \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) consisting of quasi-compact objects; then the three following conditions are equivalent:

1. (i)

    The \(X_i\) are prenoetherian.

  2. (ii)

    Every quasi-compact object of \(E\) is prenoetherian.

  3. (iii)

    Every monomorphism in \(E\) is quasi-compact.
(We have just seen the equivalence of (i) and (ii); (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iii) is trivial from the definitions, and (iii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) from definition 1.30 (i).)

Note that (iii) has as a consequence that every morphism of \(E\) is quasi-separated; hence (1.14 (ii)) every object \(X\) of \(E\) over a quasi-separated object \(Y\) of \(E\) is itself quasi-separated.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 1.33 (Classifying topos of a group)

Let \(G\) be a group \(\in \mathcal{U}\), \(B_G\) its classifying topos (IV 2.4), i.e. the category of sets \(\in \mathcal{U}\) on which \(G\) acts on the left. The connected non-empty objects of \(B_G\) (IV 4.3.5) are the sets with operators that are non-empty and on which \(G\) acts transitively, and every object \(E\) of \(B_G\) is the sum of its connected components, which are the minimal non-empty subobjects of \(E\) (namely the orbits of \(G\) in \(E\)). Consequently \(E\) is a quasi-compact object of \(B_G\) if and only if the set \(\pi_0(E)\) of orbits of \(G\) in \(E\) is finite, and then \(E\) is even a prenoetherian object of \(B_G\). These objects (and even the single object \(G_s\), which is connected non-empty) form a generating subcategory of \(B_G\). For the final object \(e\) of \(B_G\) to be quasi-separated, i.e. for the product of two quasi-compact objects of \(B_G\) to be quasi-compact, it is necessary and sufficient that the product \(G_s \times G_s\) be quasi-compact, which manifestly amounts to the fact that \(G\) is finite. We conclude, more generally, that an object \(E\) of \(B_G\) is quasi-separated if and only if the stabilizers of its points are finite subgroups of \(G\); i.e. if it is isomorphic to a sum of homogeneous spaces \(G/H\), with \(H\) finite.)
Indeed, by 1.15 we may assume in this criterion that \(E\) is connected, but if \(x \in E\) has stability group \(G_x\), we know

(IV 5.8) that \(B_G/E\) is equivalent to the topos \(B_{G_x}\), so its final object is quasi-separated if and only if \(G_x\) is finite. From this criterion we conclude that every object of \(B_G\) that lies over an object quasi-separated is quasi-separated; a fortiori, the product of two objects quasi-separated of \(B_G\) is quasi-separated. We also conclude that the coherent objects of \(B_G\) are the objects isomorphic to finite sums of homogeneous spaces \(G/H\), with \(H\) finite. Since \(G_s\) is coherent, we see that the coherent objects of \(B_G\) already form a generating subcategory of \(B_G\). Moreover, this subcategory is stable under fibre products (as follows from the fact that every object over a quasi-separated object is quasi-separated). (In the terminology of 2.11 below, \(B_G\) is a locally noetherian topos, but it is quasi-separated only if \(G\) is finite, and then \(B_G\) is even noetherian.)

One sees at once that a morphism \(f: E' \to E\) is quasi-compact if and only if the induced map \(\pi_0(f) : \pi_0(E') \to \pi_0(E)\) on the sets of orbits is proper, i.e. has finite fibres; we recover that a monomorphism is quasi-compact (1.32), hence every morphism is quasi-separated. Consequently the coherent morphisms in \(B_G\) are simply the morphisms quasi-compact, which we have just characterized.

Let \(E\) be an object of the topos \(B_G\). One easily verifies that \(E\) is a filtered inductive limit of coherent objects of \(B_G\) if and only if the stabilizers of the points of \(E\) are ind-finite groups (i.e. filtered inductive limits of their finite subgroups). In particular, if \(G\) is not ind-finite (for example if \(G = \mathbf{Z}\)), the final object of the topos \(B_G\) is not an inductive limit of coherent objects; more precisely, for the topos \(B_G\) to satisfy the equivalent conditions of 1.25, it is necessary and sufficient that its final object be a filtered inductive limit of coherent objects, or equivalently that the group \(G\) be ind-finite.

footnotes.html: (∗) By the stronger notion of noetherian object, cf. 2.11 below.

blocks.html: 2. Finiteness conditions for a topos

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.1

Let \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos. The following conditions are equivalent

  1. (i)

    There exists a generating full subcategory \(C\) of \(E\), consisting of quasi-compact objects, and stable under fibre products.

  2. (ii)

    There exists a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site \(C\), such that every object of \(C\) is quasi-compact, that in \(C\) the fibre products are representable, and that \(E\) is equivalent to the category of sheaves \(\widetilde{C}\).

Suppose that these conditions are satisfied. Then one can even choose in (i) (resp. (ii)) the category \(C\) \(\mathcal{U}\)-small. On the other hand, for every \(X \in\) ob \(C\), the object \(X\) (resp. \(\varepsilon(X)\)) of the topos \(E\) is coherent.

The implication (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) follows from IV 1.2.1, and the fact that in (i) (resp. (ii)) one can take \(C\) \(\mathcal{U}\)-small is seen at once by the argument of IV 1.2.3 applied to a small generating full subcategory in the topological sense (II 3.0.1) of \(C\). It remains to prove (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i) and the last assertion of 2.1, which follows at once from the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.1.1

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site in which fibre products are representable and every object of which is quasi-compact, and let \(E : \widetilde{C}\), \(\varepsilon : C \to E\) the canonical functor. Then for every \(X \in\) ob \(C\), \(\varepsilon(X)\) is a coherent object of \(E\). The full subcategory of \(E\) consisting of the coherent objects of \(E\) that lie over some \(\varepsilon(X)\) is stable under fibre products (and is evidently generating in \(E\)).

We already know that \(\varepsilon(X)\) is quasi-compact (1.2); let us prove that it is quasi-separated. So let \(F,G\) be two quasi-compact objects of \(E\) and \(F \to \varepsilon(X)\), \(G \to \varepsilon(X)\) two morphisms; let us prove that the fibre product \(F \times_{\varepsilon(X)} G\) is quasi-compact. Covering \(F\) and \(G\) by a finite number of objects of the form \(\varepsilon(Y_i)\) resp. \(\varepsilon(Z_j)\), and proceeding as in 1.2 to reduce us to the case where the composites \(\varepsilon(Y_i) \to \varepsilon(X)\), \(\varepsilon(Z_j) \to \varepsilon(X)\) come from morphisms \(Y_i \to X\) resp. \(Z_j \to X\), we are reduced by 1.3 to the case where the morphisms \(F \to \varepsilon(X)\) and \(G \to \varepsilon(X)\) are the transforms under \(\varepsilon\) of morphisms \(Y \to X\), \(Z \to X\). But since fibre products are representable in \(C\) and \(\varepsilon\) commutes with them, we are reduced to proving that \(\varepsilon(Y \times_X Z)\) is quasi-compact, which has already been noted above for every object of the form \(\varepsilon(U)\).

Now let \(G \to F\), \(H \to F\) be morphisms of coherent objects of \(E\), such that there exists a morphism \(F \to \varepsilon(X)\), for some \(X \in\) ob \(C\); let us prove that \(G \times_F H\) is coherent. Since \(G\) and \(H\) are quasi-compact and \(F\) quasi-separated, it already follows from the definitions that the fibre product is quasi-compact. It remains to see that it is quasi-separated, or what amounts to the same (1.15), that \(G \times_{\varepsilon(X)} H\) is quasi-separated. This follows from the more general fact:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.1.2

Under the conditions of 2.1.1, for every object quasi-separated \(G\) of \(E\), every morphism \(G \to \varepsilon(X)\) is quasi-separated. If \(H \to \varepsilon(X)\) is a second morphism, with \(H\) quasi-separated, then \(G \times_{\varepsilon(X)} H\) is quasi-separated.

The first assertion implies the second, for it implies by base change that \(G \times_{\varepsilon(X)} H \to H\) is quasi-separated, hence, since \(H\) is quasi-separated, \(G \times_{\varepsilon(X)} H\) is too (1.14 (ii)). To prove that \(G \to \varepsilon(X)\) is quasi-separated, we shall use the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.1.3

Let \(E\) be a topos, \(f: X \to Y\) a morphism in \(E\). Suppose that \(E\) admits a generating family of quasi-compact objects, and that there exists a covering family \((g_i : X_i \to X)_{i \in I}\) of \(X\) such that the \(X_i\) are quasi-compact, and that for every pair of indices \(i,j \in I\), \(X_i \times_Y X_j\) is quasi-separated. Then, if \(X\) is a quasi-separated object of \(E\), \(f\) is a quasi-separated morphism.

Indeed, the family \((g_i \times_Y g_j : X_i \times_Y X_j \to X \times_Y X)_{(i,j) \in I \times I}\) is covering, so to see that the morphism \(\Delta_{X/Y} : X \to X \times_Y X\) is quasi-compact, it suffices to see that for every \((i,j) \in I \times I\), the morphism deduced from it by base change \(g_i \times_Y g_j\) is (1.10 (ii)). But the latter is none other than the canonical morphism \(X_i \times_X X_j \to X_i \times_Y X_j\); since by hypothesis \(X\) is quasi-separated and the \(X_i\) are quasi-compact, \(X_i \times_X X_j\) is quasi-compact, hence, since \(X_i \times_Y X_j\) is quasi-separated by hypothesis, the morphism \(X_i \times_X X_j \to X_i \times_Y X_j\) is indeed quasi-compact, q.e.d.

We can now finish the proof of 2.1.2, by proving that every morphism \(f: G \to \varepsilon(X)\), with \(G\) quasi-separated, is quasi-separated. For this, let us cover \(G\) by objects \(\varepsilon(X_i)\), such that the composite morphisms \(\varepsilon(X_i) \to \varepsilon(X)\) come from morphisms \(X_i \to X\). By 2.1.3, since the \(\varepsilon(X_i)\) are quasi-compact, it suffices to check that the fibre products \(\varepsilon(X_i) \times_{\varepsilon(X)} \varepsilon(X_j) = \varepsilon(X_i \times_X X_j)\) are quasi-separated. But we have already seen that every object of \(E\) of the form \(\varepsilon(U)\) is coherent. This proves 2.1.2 and completes the proof of 2.1.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.2

Let \(E\) be a topos containing a generating full subcategory \(C\) consisting of coherent objects. The following conditions on \(E\) are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    Every quasi-separated object of \(E\) is quasi-separated over the final object.

  2. (i bis)

    For every morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(E\), \(X\) quasi-separated implies \(f\) quasi-separated.

  3. (i ter)

    Every object \(X\) of \(C\) is quasi-separated over the final object of \(E\), i.e. the diagonal morphism \(X \to X \times X\) is quasi-compact.

  4. (ii)

    The product of two quasi-separated objects of \(E\) is quasi-separated.

  5. (ii bis)

    The product in \(E\) of two objects of \(C\) is quasi-separated.

These conditions imply that the full subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of \(E\) consisting of the coherent objects of \(E\) is stable under fibre products (and a fortiori, that \(E\) satisfies the equivalent conditions of 2.1).

Evidently (i bis) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i), and the reverse implication follows from 1.8 (iii). We have (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) by an argument already made: if \(X\) and \(Y\) are quasi-separated, since by hypothesis (i) \(X\) is quasi-separated over \(e\), \(X \times Y\) is quasi-separated over \(Y\) by base change, hence \(X\) is quasi-separated by 1.14 (ii). The same argument shows that (i ter) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii bis), and on the other hand (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i ter) and (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii bis) are trivial, so that it remains to establish (ii bis) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i). But if \(X\) is a quasi-separated object of \(E\), covering \(X\) by objects \(X_i\) of \(C\) (which is possible, \(C\) being generating), since the \(X_i\) are quasi-compact by hypothesis on \(C\), we can apply 2.1.3 to the morphism \(X \to e\), so that to prove that the latter is quasi-separated, we are reduced precisely to seeing that the \(X_i \times X_j\) are quasi-separated, which is hypothesis (ii bis).
Condition (i ter) is also equivalent to the condition

1. (i quater)

    For every double arrow \(g_1, g_2 : Y \rightrightarrows X\) in \(C\), the kernel in \(E\) is quasi-compact (or equivalently (1.15) coherent).
To see this, it suffices to apply criterion 1.10 (i) to the diagonal morphism \(X \to X \times X\) considered in (i ter).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.3

A topos \(E\) satisfying the equivalent conditions of 2.2 (resp. of 2.1) is called an algebraic topos (resp. a locally algebraic topos, or locally coherent). An object \(X\) of a topos \(E\) is called an algebraic object of the topos \(E\) if the induced topos \(E_{/X}\) is algebraic. A topos \(E\) is said to be quasi-separated (resp. coherent) if it is algebraic and if its final object is quasi-separated (resp. coherent).

It is in algebraic topoi that the finiteness notions developed in n° 1 have fully satisfactory properties, analogous to the properties of the notions of the same name in the category of schemes. All the locally algebraic ( = locally coherent) topoi encountered in practice are in fact algebraic, so the practical interest of this notion seems for the moment rather limited. One can nevertheless construct locally algebraic topoi that are not algebraic (2.17 f).
Here are some general remarks concerning the notions introduced in 2.3, which will convince the reader (at least one hopes so) that the terminology introduced is coherent.
Under the conditions of 2.1 (i) resp. (ii), for every \(X \in C\), \(X\) (resp. \(\varepsilon(X)\)) is a (coherent) algebraic object of \(E\) (2.1.2 and 1.19.2),

in other words the induced topos \(E_{/X}\) (resp. \(E_{/\varepsilon(X)} \simeq \widetilde{(C_{/X})}\)) is algebraic, hence coherent. It amounts to the same to say that when \(C\) admits a final object, then \(E\) itself is algebraic, hence coherent.

If \(E\) is an algebraic topos, then every induced topos \(E_{/X}\) is likewise algebraic (2.2 (i bis)); for a topos \(E\) to be locally algebraic = locally coherent, it is necessary and sufficient that there exist a family \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) of objects of \(E\), covering the final object, such that the \(X_i\) are algebraic (resp. coherent), i.e. such that the induced topoi \(E_{/X_i}\) are algebraic (resp. coherent). — The sufficiency follows at once from the definitions, the necessity from the observations 2.4.1. — Of course, an algebraic topos is locally algebraic, and if \(E\) is a locally algebraic topos, every induced topos \(E_{/X}\) is locally algebraic.

If \(X\) is an algebraic object of a topos \(E\), then every object \(X'\) of \(E\) that lies over \(X\) is again algebraic (cf. 2.4.2). In particular, every object of an algebraic topos is algebraic, and conversely of course.

The full subcategory of \(E\) consisting of the quasi-separated objects that are algebraic is stable under fibre products and under subobjects (1.15), hence also under kernels. If \(E\) is algebraic, this category (which is then none other than the category of quasi-separated objects of \(E\) without more) is likewise stable under the product of two objects. If \(E\) is quasi-separated (and only then) this category is stable under arbitrary finite projective limits, or equivalently contains the final object of \(E\).

The full subcategory \(C\) of \(E\) consisting of the coherent objects that are algebraic is stable under fibre products. If \(E\) is locally algebraic, i.e. locally coherent, to say that \(E\) is algebraic amounts to saying that \(C\) is likewise stable under kernels of double arrows (2.2.1); and to say that \(E\) is quasi-separated amounts to saying that moreover \(C\) is stable under the product of two objects (cf. 1.17). Finally, to say that \(E\) is coherent amounts to saying that \(C\) is stable under arbitrary finite projective limits, or equivalently that it contains the final object of \(E\).

Let \(E\) be a topos. For \(E\) to be locally coherent (resp. algebraic, resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent), it is necessary and sufficient that it admit a generating full subcategory \(C\) consisting of objects quasi-compact (which will automatically be coherent (2.1)), and which is stable under fibre products (resp. under fibre products and kernels, resp. under fibre products and products of two objects, resp. under arbitrary finite projective limits); or equivalently that \(E\) be equivalent to a topos \(\widetilde{C}\), where \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site every object of which is quasi-compact, and in which the fibre products and products of two objects (resp. all finite projective limits) are representable. (For the necessity, one takes for \(C\) the category of objects of \(E\) that are coherent and algebraic, and applies 2.4; for the sufficiency, one applies 2.2 (i ter)). In this statement, one can evidently again assume \(C\) \(\mathcal{U}\)-small.

Let \(E\) be a topos. If \(E\) is algebraic, an object \(X\) of \(E\) is quasi-separated (resp. coherent) if and only if the induced topos \(E_{/X}\) is. When \(E\) is no longer assumed algebraic, one can say only that \(E_{/X}\) is quasi-separated (resp. coherent) if and only if \(X\) is quasi-separated (resp. coherent) and algebraic. This is not serious, since one will doubtless not have to use these notions outside the case where \(E\) is algebraic.

For the notion of coherent (resp. quasi-separated) object of a topos \(E\) to have satisfactory properties, one must restrict to the objects that are moreover algebraic, a condition automatically satisfied if \(E\) is algebraic. Since we will doubtless never have to work with locally algebraic \(E\) that are not algebraic, the question of revising the terminology introduced in 1.13, possibly reserving it for algebraic objects alone, does not therefore arise in very sharp terms!

On the other hand, we have refrained from defining the notion of quasi-compact topos. In the spirit of the present section, it would be natural to call thus the algebraic topoi whose final object is quasi-compact. We hesitated to introduce such a usage, because if \(X\) is a topological space, it would not be true that \(X\) is quasi-compact if and only if the associated topos \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) is. Note in this connection that \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) is locally coherent if and only if \(X\) admits a base of open sets consisting of quasi-compact open sets \(U\) such that for \(U_j, U_k \subset U_i\), \(U_j \cap U_k\) is again quasi-compact (and then \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) is even algebraic). This condition is satisfied for the topological spaces underlying schemes, but rarely for the spaces encountered by analysts, even if they (the spaces) are compact. Let us make explicit once more, for convenience of reference:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.5

Let \(E\) be an algebraic topos, \(f: X \to Y\) a morphism in \(E\). If \(Y\) is a quasi-separated (resp. coherent) object of \(E\), then, for \(X\) to be a quasi-separated (resp. coherent) object of \(E\), it is necessary and sufficient that the morphism \(f\) be quasi-separated (resp. coherent).

The sufficiency has already been seen in 1.14 (ii), and is true without any hypothesis on \(E\). The necessity in the non-parenthetical case is true without even assuming \(Y\) quasi-separated, and is none other than definition 2.3 via 2.2 (i bis). It remains to prove that if \(Y\) is coherent and \(X\) coherent, then \(f\) is coherent. Since we already know that \(f\) is quasi-separated, it suffices to see that \(f\) is quasi-compact, which follows from the fact that \(X\) is quasi-compact and \(Y\) quasi-separated (1.13).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.6

Let \(E\) be an algebraic topos, \(f: X \to Y\) a morphism in \(E\), \((Y_i \to Y)_{i \in I}\) a covering family, with the \(Y_i\) quasi-separated (resp. coherent). For \(f\) to be quasi-separated (resp. quasi-compact, resp. coherent), it is necessary and sufficient that for every \(i \in I\), \(X_i = X \times_Y Y_i\) be a quasi-separated (resp. quasi-compact, resp. coherent) object of \(E\).

It suffices to combine 1.10 (ii) and 2.5 in the case "quasi-separated" or "coherent"; the case "quasi-compact" has already been seen in 1.16. Note that the necessity of the condition stated in 2.6 is likewise valid without any hypothesis on the topos \(E\).
As a special case of 2.6 we find:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.7

Let \(E\) be a coherent topos, \(X\) an object of \(E\). For \(X\) to be a quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) object of \(E\), it is necessary and sufficient that it be quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) over the final object (1.9.2).
In particular, \(X\) is constructible (1.9.2) if and only if it is coherent.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.8

Let \(E\) be a locally coherent topos, \(f: X \to Y\) a morphism in \(E\). For \(f\) to be quasi-separated, it is necessary and sufficient that for every quasi-separated object \(Y'\) of \(E_{/Y}\), \(f^*(Y')=X \times_Y Y'\) be a quasi-separated object of \(E_{/X}\) (or of \(E\), which amounts to the same (1.20.2)).

The "necessity" is valid without any condition on \(E\), for if \(Y'\) is quasi-separated, since \(f' : X'=X \times_Y Y' \to Y'\) is quasi-separated by base change, \(X'\) is quasi-separated (1.14 (ii)). For the converse, note that there exists a covering family \(Y_i \to Y\) of \(Y\) by objects quasi-separated and algebraic. By 1.10 (ii), to check that \(f\) is quasi-separated, it suffices to check that the \(f_i : X_i = X \times_Y Y_i \to Y_i\) are. But the hypothesis on \(f^*\) implies that the \(X_i\) are quasi-separated, hence the \(f_i\) are, since \(E_{/Y_i}\) is an algebraic topos.

Statements 2.5 and 2.6 remain valid if one replaces in them the hypothesis "\(E\) algebraic" by the more general hypothesis "\(Y\) is algebraic", as one sees trivially by applying the original statement to the topos induced \(E_{/Y}\), which is algebraic. Likewise, in 2.8 it suffices to assume that \(E_{/Y}\) (instead of \(E\)) is locally coherent.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.9

Let \(E\) be a topos, \(C\) a subcategory of \(E\). The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(E\) is locally coherent (resp. coherent), satisfies the equivalent conditions of 1.25, and \(C\) is the full subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of \(E\) consisting of the coherent objects.

  2. (ii)

    \(C\) is a strictly full generating subcategory of \(E\), stable under finite inductive limits and under fibre products (resp. and under finite projective limits), and consists of objects quasi-compact.

The implication (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) follows trivially from the definitions and from the form 1.25 (ii) of the conditions considered in 1.25; let us prove the reverse implication. The fact that \(C\) is a generating full subcategory, consisting of quasi-compact objects, and stable under fibre products (resp. under finite projective limits) implies, by definition, that \(E\) is locally coherent (resp. coherent). The fact that moreover \(C\) is strictly full and stable under finite inductive limits then implies that \(C = E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) (by 1.24 (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iii)), and that condition 1.25 (ii) is satisfied, q.e.d.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.9.1

A \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(E\) is said to be perfect if it is coherent (2.3) and if it satisfies the equivalent conditions of 1.25, i.e. if the subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of \(E\) consisting of the coherent objects of \(E\) is stable under finite inductive limits. We say that \(E\) is locally perfect if there exists a family \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) of objects of \(E\) covering the final object, such that for every \(i \in I\), the induced topos \(E_{/X_i}\) is perfect.

It follows at once from this definition that a perfect topos (resp. locally perfect) is coherent (resp. locally coherent). As examples of perfect (resp. locally perfect) topoi, let us mention the noetherian (resp. locally noetherian) topoi introduced in 2.11 below (cf. 2.14), the Zariski topos and the étale topos of a coherent scheme (resp. of an arbitrary scheme) (IX, note page 42). As

a counterexample, let us mention the fppf topos of a scheme \(S\), which is locally coherent (and even coherent if \(S\) is a coherent scheme, i.e. quasi-compact and quasi-separated) (VII 5.6), but which is not locally perfect if \(S \neq \varnothing\) (1.28 f).

In a locally perfect topos, the notion of constructible object is particularly stable (2.9.3 below), which is one reason why the notion seems interesting. Another reason lies in the fact that, like that of coherent or locally coherent topos, the notion of perfect or locally perfect topos is stable with respect to the formation of the closed subtopos complementary to an open one (4.6), and that it behaves in a particularly simple way for the operation of gluing of topoi (4.11, 4.14).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.9.3

Let \(E\) be a locally perfect topos (2.9.1). Then the full subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{cons}}\) of \(E\) consisting of the constructible objects of \(E\) (1.9.3) is stable under finite inductive limits (and also under finite projective limits of course, by (1.9.3)).

Since the property for an object of \(E\) of being constructible is local on \(E\) (1.10 (ii)), we are reduced to the case where \(E\) is a topos perfect. But then \(E_{\mathrm{cons}} = E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) (2.7), and the conclusion follows from definition 2.9.1.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.9.4

Let \(E\) be a locally perfect topos. Then \(E\) is perfect if and only if \(E\) is coherent. For every object \(X\) of \(E\), the induced topos \(E_{/X}\) is locally perfect.

blocks.title: Problem
blocks.html:
Problem 2.9.5

It is conceivable that the perfect topoi are special enough to lend themselves to a rather explicit structure theory (following a model proposed by M. ARTIN at the time of the oral seminar). Let us call finite topos a topos equivalent to a topos of the form \(\widehat{C}\), where \(C\) is a finite category (cf. exercise 3.11), and profinite topos a topos which is a filtered projective limit of finite topoi (in the sense of 6. below, which applies thanks to 3.12 c)). Since a finite topos is noetherian (2.17 g)) hence perfect, and since a filtered projective limit of perfect topoi is perfect (6. ), we see that a profinite topos is perfect. The question that arises would be to know whether conversely every perfect topos is profinite. This is equivalent to the question whether every finite subcategory of \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) is contained in a full subcategory \(F_0\) of \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) which is equivalent to a category \(F_{\mathrm{coh}}\), where \(F\) is a finite topos (cf. 3.11). (If the answer were negative, it would be appropriate to find additional manageable intrinsic conditions for a perfect topos ensuring that it is profinite.) It would finally remain to study the structure of profinite topoi in terms of a suitable notion of "profinite Karoubian category", inspired by IV 7.6 h). This study has not yet been carried out even in the particular case where \(E\) is the Zariski, or étale, topos of a nice coherent scheme \(X\), and should then yield profinite invariants finer than the compact space \(X_{\mathrm{cons}}\) (EGA IV 1. ) associated to \(X\).

In the same vein, let us point out the following question: Let \(E\) be a perfect topos, \(E'\) the topos induced on an open of \(E\), and \(E''\) the corresponding closed subtopos (IV 9.9). If \(E'\) and \(E''\) are finite topoi, is the same true of \(E\)?

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.10

Let \(E\) be a topos. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(E\) admits a generating full subcategory stable under fibre products, consisting of prenoetherian objects of \(E\).

  2. (ii)

    \(E\) admits a generating full subcategory consisting of quasi-separated prenoetherian objects (i.e. coherent prenoetherian objects).

  3. (iii)

    \(E\) is locally coherent (2.3) and every quasi-compact object of \(E\) is prenoetherian.

  4. (iii bis)

    \(E\) is locally coherent and admits a generating family consisting of prenoetherian objects of \(E\).

The equivalence of (iii) and (iii bis) follows from 1.32, and it is trivial that (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iii bis) and (iii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i), so (i) is equivalent to (iii) and (iii bis). Finally (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) follows from the last assertion of 2.1, and it remains to prove (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i). This implication follows from the fact that the full subcategory of \(E\) consisting of the prenoetherian quasi-separated objects, if it is generating, is stable under fibre products, since such a fibre product is quasi-compact by the definitions, hence prenoetherian by the first assertion of 1.32; and it is quasi-separated by the last assertion of 1.32.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.11
