A topos \(E\) is called a locally noetherian topos if it satisfies the equivalent conditions of 2.10, noetherian if moreover its final object is coherent (or what amounts to the same (1.32) prenoetherian and quasi-separated). An object \(X\) of a topos \(E\) is called a noetherian object of \(E\) if the induced topos \(E_{/X}\) is a noetherian topos.

If \(E\) is a locally noetherian topos, then the same holds of every induced topos \(E_{/X}\); conversely, if one can find a family \((X_i)\) covering the final object such that the \(E_{/X_i}\) are locally noetherian, the same holds of \(E\). If \(C\) is a generating full subcategory of \(E\) consisting of prenoetherian objects and stable under fibre products (2.11 (i)), then for every \(X \in C\), \(E_{/X}\) is a noetherian topos, i.e. the objects of \(C\) are even noetherian, (for if \(E\) is locally noetherian and \(X \in\) Ob \(E\), then \(E_{/X}\) is noetherian if and only if \(X\) is coherent). It follows that a topos \(E\) is locally noetherian if and only if one can cover the final object of \(E\) by noetherian objects \(X_i\).

In a locally noetherian topos \(E\), every monomorphism is quasi-compact, and every morphism is quasi-separated (1.32). A fortiori, \(E\) is an algebraic topos (2.3) and not only locally coherent, i.e. locally algebraic. Hence a topos \(E\) is noetherian if and only if it is locally noetherian and coherent (2.3). In other words, if \(E\) is a locally noetherian topos, then the noetherian objects of \(E\) are none other than the coherent objects of \(E\).

Let \(E\) be a locally noetherian topos. If \(E\) is quasi-separated, i.e. if its final object is quasi-separated, then every object of \(E\) is quasi-separated (1.32), hence the prenoetherian objects are identical to the objects noetherian (i.e. coherent) of \(E\). Since a quotient object of an object prenoetherian is prenoetherian, it follows that \(E\) satisfies the conditions equivalent of 1.25 (since it satisfies condition 1.25 (ii bis)). In particular, if \(C\) is the full subcategory of \(E\) consisting of the objects noetherian (= coherent) of \(E\), then the natural functor \[ \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to E \] is an equivalence of categories. From this we conclude that a topos noetherian is perfect (2.9.1), hence that a locally noetherian topos is locally perfect.

If one only assumes \(E\) locally noetherian, it will still be true that every object of \(E\) is an inductive limit of its subobjects prenoetherian (for in a topos admitting a generating subcategory consisting of quasi-compact objects, every object is a filtered inductive limit of its quasi-compact subobjects). But since a prenoetherian object of \(E\) is no longer necessarily coherent, this statement then has only a very limited usefulness, and one knows (1.33) that the conditions of 1.25 are no longer necessarily satisfied.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 2.15 (Topological spaces)

Let \(X\) be a topological space. Then the following conditions are equivalent: (i) the topological space \(X\) is noetherian (i.e. every open set of \(X\) is quasi-compact, i.e. every increasing sequence of open sets of \(X\) is stationary); (ii) the topos \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) is noetherian; (iii) the final object \(X\) of \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) is noetherian; (iv) the final object \(X\) of \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) is prenoetherian.

Indeed, one has trivially (ii) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) (iii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iv) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) (i), and on the other hand (i) implies that the generating subcategory \(\mathrm{Ouv}(X)\) of \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\), which is stable under finite projective limits, consists of prenoetherian objects, whence (ii).
One sees likewise that the topological space \(X\) is locally noetherian (i.e. is a union of noetherian open sets) if and only if the topos \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) is locally noetherian.

Thus, our definitions 1.30, 2.11 are compatible with the received terminology for topological spaces. On the other hand, we have been careful in the general case to give the term "noetherian object" a stronger meaning than that of the more naive notion of 1.30, so that the collection of properties attached to this notion (rather than the mere grammatical structure of the definition) should be in good agreement with the intuition attached to noetherian topological spaces and schemes.
The reader will find further examples in the following exercises.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 2.16 (Spaces with operators and classifying topoi)

Let \(X\) be a topological space on which a discrete group \(G\) operates, whence (IV 2.3) a topos \(E = \mathrm{Top}(X,G)\). One interprets the objects \(X'\) of this topos as spaces étalé over \(X\) with group of operators \(G\), and one notes that the induced topos \(E_{/X'}\) is canonically equivalent to \(\mathrm{Top}(X',G)\).

  1. a)

    For the final object of the topos \(E\) to be quasi-compact, it is necessary and sufficient that the quotient topological space \(X/G\) be quasi-compact (Use IV 8.4.1).

  2. b)

    Let \(P\) be the object of \(E\) defined by the trivial space étalé \(X \times G\) with the diagonal operation of \(G\). Show that the induced topos \(E_{/P}\) is equivalent to the topos \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) (compare IV 5.8.3). Conclude that \(E\) is locally coherent (resp. locally noetherian) if and only if \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) is locally coherent (cf. 2.4.7) (resp. locally noetherian (cf. 2.15)). Show that if \(E\) is locally coherent, i.e. locally algebraic, it is even algebraic, using the generating family formed by the objects \(T_U\), where \(U\) is a coherent open set of \(X\), \(T_U = G \times U\) with operation \(g.(u,g') = (u,gg')\) of \(G\), and the structural morphism \(p_U : T_U \to X\) defined by \(p_U(u,g) = g.u\).

  3. c)

    Suppose \(E\) algebraic, i.e. \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) algebraic (2.4.7). Show that the structural morphism \(P \to e\) is quasi-separated. Show that \(E\) is quasi-separated if and only if \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) is quasi-separated (or again the topological space \(X\) is quasi-separated, i.e. the intersection of two quasi-compact open sets of \(X\) is a quasi-compact open set), and \(G\) is finite or \(X\) empty. (Compare 1.33.)

  4. d)

    Show that the structural morphism \(P \to e\) is quasi-compact if and only if \(G\) is finite. Show that \(E\) is coherent (resp. noetherian) if and only if \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) is, and \(G\) is finite or \(X\) empty.

  5. e)

    Let \(E\) be a topos, \(G\) a Group of \(E\), whence a classifying topos \(B_G\) (IV 2.4). Carry out the study of the finiteness conditions in \(B_G\), taking inspiration from what precedes. Same question when one starts from a strict pro-group \(\underline{G} = (G_i)_{i \in I}\) of \(E\). In particular, one will see that if \(E\) is coherent (resp. noetherian) and the \(G_i\) are coherent, then \(B_{\underline{G}}\) is coherent (resp. noetherian).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 2.17 (Topoi of the form \(\widehat{C}\))

Let \(C\) be a category equivalent to a category \(\in \mathcal{U}\), and \(E = \widehat{C}\) the category of presheaves on \(C\). By the canonical functor \(\varepsilon : C \to \widehat{C}\), one identifies \(C\) with a full subcategory of \(E\).

  1. a)

    \(C\) is a generating subcategory of \(E\) consisting of quasi-compact objects. For these to be prenoetherian (cf. 1.32), it is necessary and sufficient that for every object \(X\) of \(C\), every sieve of \(X\) be generated by a finite family of morphisms \(X_i \to X\) of \(C\). For the final object of \(E\) to be quasi-compact (resp. prenoetherian), it is necessary and sufficient that there exist a final subcategory of \(C\) whose set of objects is finite (resp. that every sieve of \(C\) be generated by a subcategory of \(C\) whose set of objects is finite).

  2. b)

    For \(E\) to admit a generating subcategory formed of coherent objects (or again, quasi-separated), it is necessary and sufficient that the objects of \(C\) be coherent in \(E\), or again that for two arrows \(Y \xrightarrow{f} X\), \(Z \xrightarrow{g} X\) in \(C\), the object \(Y \times_X Z\) of \(E\) be quasi-compact, i.e. one can find a finite family of commutative squares in \(C\) \[ \xymatrix{ & T_i \ar[dl] \ar[dr] & \\ Y \ar[dr]_-{f} & & Z \ar[dl]^-{g} \\ & X & } \] such that every other commutative square in \(C\) \[ \xymatrix{ & T \ar[dl] \ar[dr] & \\ Y \ar[dr]_-{f} & & Z \ar[dl]^-{g} \\ & X & } \] arises from a morphism \(T \to T_i\). (Note that if \((F_i)_{i \in I}\) is a generating family of \(E\), every \(X \in\) ob \(C\) is isomorphic to a direct summand of one of the \(F_i\).)

  3. c)

    For \(E\) to be locally coherent, i.e. to be generated by a family of coherent and algebraic objects, it is necessary and sufficient that the objects \(X\) of \(C\) be coherent and algebraic objects of \(E\), i.e. that the condition of b) be satisfied, together with the following condition: for every double arrow \(f,g: Y \rightrightarrows Z\) of \(C\) over an object \(X\) of \(C\), the kernel of this double arrow in \(E\) is a quasi-compact object of \(E\), i.e. there exists a finite family of commutative diagrams in \(C\) \[ \xymatrix{ T_i \ar[r] & Y \ar@<0.6ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.6ex>[r]_-{g} & Z } \] such that every other commutative diagram in \(C\) \[ \xymatrix{ T \ar[r] & Y \ar@<0.6ex>[r]^-{f} \ar@<-0.6ex>[r]_-{g} & Z } \] arises from a morphism \(T \to T_i\). For \(E\) to be algebraic, it is necessary and sufficient that it satisfy the condition of b) and the preceding condition, but where one takes an arbitrary double arrow \((f,g)\) of \(C\) (not necessarily over an object \(X\) of \(C\)). For \(E\) to be quasi-separated, it is necessary and sufficient that it satisfy the conditions of b), and that moreover for two objects \(X,Y \in\) ob \(C\), the product \(X \times Y\) in \(E\) be quasi-compact. For \(E\) to be coherent, it is necessary and sufficient that it satisfy the two preceding conditions, and that there exist a final subcategory of \(C\) whose underlying set is finite.

  4. d)

    Give an example where the objects of the generating subcategory \(C\) of \(E\) are prenoetherian, but where \(E\) does not admit a generating family formed of coherent objects (i.e. (b) where the objects of \(C\) are not all coherent). For this take for \(C\) the category having objects \(X, T_i\) (\(i = 0,1, \ldots\)) and \(e\) (the final object), the only morphisms between these objects, besides the structural morphisms into \(e\) and the identities, being morphisms \(u_i : T_i \to X\), \(v_i : X \to T_i\) subject to the conditions \(u_i v_i = \mathrm{id}_X\), and finally \(p_i = v_i u_i\) (necessarily satisfying \(p_i^2 = \mathrm{id}_{T_i}\)). One verifies that the only sieves of \(X\) or of a \(T_i\) are the two trivial sieves, and that \(e\) admits exactly one non-trivial sieve, so that by virtue of a), the objects of \(C\) are prenoetherian objects of \(E\). However, the product \(X \times_e X\) in \(E\) is not quasi-compact, for it does not satisfy the criterion of b).

  5. e)

    Give an example where the generating subcategory \(C\) of \(E\) is formed of coherent objects of \(E\), but where \(E\) is not locally coherent. For this take for \(C\) the category whose set of objects is formed of distinct objects \(e\) (the final object), \(Y,Z\) and \(T_i\) (\(i=0,1,\ldots\)), with as only morphisms between these objects, besides the morphisms into the final object \(e\) and the identity morphisms, morphisms \(f,g: Y \rightrightarrows Z\), subject to the conditions \(fu_i = gu_i\). One will verify that \(C\) satisfies the condition of b) (with a little patience; one finds that all the fibre products of objects of \(C\) are isomorphic to \(\varnothing_E\) or lie in \(C\), with the exception of \(Z \times_e Z\) and \(Y \times_e Z\) which are covered by two elements of \(C\)), but evidently \(\operatorname{Ker}(f,g)\) does not satisfy the condition of c).

  6. f)

    Give an example where \(C\) is stable under fibre products (a fortiori, \(E\) is a locally coherent topos, i.e. locally algebraic) but where \(E\) is not an algebraic topos. (Take the example given in d), and the full subcategory \(C'\) of \(E\) formed of the objects \(Y,Z\), \(T_i\) (\(i>0\)) and \(\varnothing_E\)).

  7. g)

    Suppose the category \(C\) finite. Prove that the topos \(E\) is noetherian, that its noetherian (i.e. quasi-compact) objects are the contrafunctors \(F: C^\circ \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) such that for every object \(X\) of \(C\), \(F(X)\) is a finite set, and that the fibre functors on \(E\) transform noetherian objects into finite sets (cf. IV 7.6. h)).

  8. h)

    Suppose that every morphism \(f: X \to X\) of \(C\) factors as a composite \(ip\), where \(i\) is a monomorphism and where \(p\) admits a right inverse. Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\), \(I(X)\) the set of its subobjects in the sense of \(C\), regarded as an ordered set, \(S(I(X))\) the set of subsets \(U\) of \(I(X)\) such that for two elements \(X',X'' \in I(X)\), \(X' \in U\) and \(X'' \leq X'\) imply \(X'' \in U\). Show that the ordered set of subobjects in \(E\) of \(X\) is isomorphic to the set \(S(I(X))\) (ordered by inclusion). Conclude that if \(I(X)\) is finite, then \(X\) is a prenoetherian object of \(E\). In particular, if (in addition to the factorization condition above) \(C\) is stable under fibre products (resp. under finite projective limits) and if for every \(X \in\) ob \(C\), the set \(I(X)\) of subobjects of \(X\) in \(C\) is finite, then the topos \(E\) is locally noetherian (resp. noetherian).

  9. i)

    Let \(C\) be the category of finite sets (or, at will, of non-empty finite sets) \(\in \mathcal{U}\), so that \(E = \widehat{C}\) is the category of augmented simplicial sets (resp. of simplicial sets tout court). Show that \(E\) is a noetherian topos. (Use h).) Taking a non essentially constant pro-object \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) of \(C\), show that \(E\) admits fibre functors that do not transform noetherian objects into noetherian objects (i.e. into finite sets).

  10. j)

    One considers the following diagram of implications of properties for a topos \(E\): \[ \xymatrix@C=1.4em@R=2.2em{ E\ \text{is noetherian} \ar@{=>}[r] \ar@{=>}[d] & E\ \text{is locally noetherian} \ar@{=>}[d] \ar@{=>}[ddr] & \\ E\ \text{is coherent} \ar@{=>}[r] & E\ \text{is algebraic} \ar@{=>}[d] & \\ & \substack{E\ \text{is loc. coherent, i.e.} \\ E_{\mathrm{cohalg}}\ \text{generates}\ E} \ar@{=>}[d] & E_{\text{prénoeth}}\ \text{generates}\ E \ar@{=>}[ddl] \\ & E_{\mathrm{coh}}\ \text{generates}\ E \ar@{=>}[d] & \\ & E_{\mathrm{qucpct}}\ \text{generates}\ E & } \] Show that all the implications of this diagram are strict, and that there are among the notions considered no other implications than the composite implications of the preceding diagram. Here \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\), \(E_{\mathrm{qucpct}}\), \(E_{\text{prénoeth}}\), \(E_{\mathrm{cohalg}}\) denote respectively the full subcategories of \(E\) formed of the coherent, resp. quasi-compact, resp. prenoetherian, resp. coherent and algebraic objects of \(E\). (One will restrict to topoi of the form \(\widehat{C}\), using the results stated in d), e), f).)

  11. k)

    Solve the following question (whose answer the writer of these lines does not know): can \(E = \widehat{C}\) be locally noetherian without the \(\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)\) (for \(X,Y \in\) ob \(C\)) being finite?

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 2.18

Let \(E\) be a topos.

  1. a)

    Let \(X\) be a prenoetherian object of \(E\). Show that \(X\) is isomorphic to a finite sum of connected objects (IV 4.3.5) of \(E\). (Show by contradiction that an increasing sequence of partitions of \(X\) (IV 8.7) is stationary.)

  2. b)

    Let \(X\) be an object of \(E\), \((f_i : X_i \to X)_{i \in I}\) a covering family of \(X\). Show that if each of the \(X_i\) is isomorphic to a sum of connected objects of \(E\), so is \(X\). (Reduce to the case where the \(X_i\) are connected, then to the case where they are subobjects of \(X\), and then consider on the index set \(I\) the equivalence relation \(R\) generated by the relation \(X_i \cap X_j \neq \varnothing_E\), and show that if \(J=I/R\), \(X\) is the sum of the \(X(j) = \operatorname{Sup}_{i \in j} X_i\).)

  3. c)

    Conclude from b) that if one denotes by \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) a generating family of \(E\), then \(E\) is locally connected (IV 8.7, l)) if and only if each of the \(X_i\) (\(i \in I\)) is isomorphic to a sum of connected objects of \(E\).

  4. d)

    Conclude from a) and c) that if \(E\) admits a generating subcategory formed of prenoetherian objects, in particular if \(E\) is locally noetherian, then \(E\) is locally connected, and a fortiori is isomorphic to the sum topos (IV 8.7 b)) of a family of connected topoi (IV 8.7 e)) i.e. whose final object is connected. (In particular, one can associate to \(E\), for every morphism \(f: P \to E\), where \(P\) is a topos "connected non-empty and simply connected" (IV 2.7.5) a fundamental pro-group \(\pi_1(E,f)\); one will note that if \(E\) is locally noetherian "non-empty" one can always find such an \(f\), with \(P\) the punctual topos, thanks to DELIGNE ([9] ).

pages.title: 3. Finiteness conditions for a morphism of topoi

blocks.html: 3. Finiteness conditions for a morphism of topoi

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.1

Let \(f : E' \to E\) be a morphism of topoi. One says that \(f\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated) if for every quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated) object \(X\) of \(E\), \(f^*(X)\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated). One says that \(f\) is coherent if \(f\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated.

One will note that if \(f\) possesses one of the preceding properties, then every morphism of topoi isomorphic to \(f\) possesses the same property. It is also trivial that the composite of two quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) morphisms of topoi is again quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2

With the notations of 3.1, let \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) be a generating family of quasi-compact (resp. coherent) objects of \(E\). Suppose, in the "resp." case, that \(E'\) admits a generating family formed of quasi-compact objects. For \(f\) to be quasi-compact (resp. coherent), it is necessary and sufficient that for every \(i \in I\), \(f^*(X_i)\) be quasi-compact (resp. coherent).

The necessity of the condition is trivial. For sufficiency in the first case, one notes that for every quasi-compact object \(X\) of \(E\), there is a finite epimorphic family of morphisms \(X_i \to X\), so there is a finite epimorphic family \(f^*(X_i) \to f^*(X)\), with the \(f^*(X_i)\) quasi-compact by hypothesis, so \(f^*(X)\) is quasi-compact (1.3). In the second case, it remains to see that if \(X\) is a quasi-separated object of \(E\), then \(f^*(X)\) is quasi-separated. The hypothesis on \(X\) can be expressed (1.17) by the existence of an epimorphic family of morphisms \(X_i \to X\) such that the \(X_i \times_X X_j\) are quasi-compact. This being so, one will have a covering family \(f^*(X_i) \to f^*(X)\), such that the fibre products \(f^*(X_i) \times_{f^*(X)} f^*(X_j)\) are quasi-compact (since by virtue of a), \(f^*\) transforms quasi-compact objects into quasi-compact objects). Since the \(f^*(X_i)\) are coherent, one concludes again with the help of 1.17.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.3

Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites where the fibre products are representable and where every covering family admits a finite covering subfamily, \(g : C \to C'\) a morphism of sites (IV 4.9.1). Then the morphism of topoi \(f: \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C'}\) defined by \(g\) is coherent.
Indeed, \(\varepsilon_C(C)\) (resp. \(\varepsilon_{C'}(C')\)) is a generating family of \(\widetilde{C}\) (resp. of \(\widetilde{C'}\)) satisfying the "resp." conditions of 3.2 (2.1.1).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.4

Let \(E\) be a locally coherent topos (2.3), \(f : X \to Y\) an arrow of \(E\), whence a morphism of induced topoi (IV (5.5.2)) \(E_{/X} \to E_{/Y}\). For the latter to be a quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) morphism of topoi, it is necessary and sufficient that \(f\) be a quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) morphism.

The "quasi-compact" case is trivial by virtue of the definitions (without condition on \(E\)), the "quasi-separated" case is none other than 2.8, finally the "coherent" case results from the conjunction of the two preceding cases.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.5

Let \(f: E' \to E\) be a morphism of locally coherent topoi. Let \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) be a generating family in \(E\) formed of coherent algebraic objects. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    For every quasi-compact arrow \(u\) of \(E\), \(f^*(u)\) is quasi-compact.

  2. (i bis)

    For every arrow \(u: X_i \to X_j\), \(f^*(u)\) is quasi-compact.

  3. (ii)

    For every coherent object \(Y'\) of \(E'\), every coherent algebraic object \(Y\) of \(E\), and every arrow \(v : Y' \to f^*(Y)\), the corresponding morphism of topoi \[ f_v : E'_{/Y'} \to E_{/Y} \] composite of the localization morphism \(E'_{/Y'} \to E'_{/f^*(Y)}\) deduced from \(v\) (IV (5.5.2)) and of the morphism \(E'_{/f^*(Y)} \to E_{/Y}\) induced by \(f\) (IV (5.10.1)) is coherent.

  4. (ii bis)

    Same condition as in (ii), but restricting to a set of data \(v_\alpha : Y'_\alpha \to f^*(Y_\alpha)\) such that the \(Y'_\alpha\) are algebraic and cover the final object of \(E'\).

  5. (ii ter)

    (When one is given a generating family \((X'_{i'})_{i' \in I'}\) in \(E'\) formed of coherent objects, and for every \(i' \in I'\), an \(i \in I\) and an arrow \(v_{i'} : X'_{i'} \to f^*(X_i)\).) For every \(i' \in I'\), the morphism of topoi \(E'_{/X'_{i'}} \to E_{/X_i}\) defined by \(v_{i'}\) is coherent.

Since every arrow \(X_i \to X_j\) is quasi-compact, it is obvious that (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i bis). Conversely, suppose (i bis) satisfied and let us prove (i). Let \(u: X \to Y\) be a quasi-compact arrow of \(E\). In terms of an epimorphic family \(X_i \to Y\), the hypothesis on \(u\) is thus expressed by the fact that the \(X \times_Y X_i\) are quasi-compact (1.16), i.e. that there exists for each \(i\) a finite epimorphic family of morphisms \(X_j \to X \times_Y X_i\) (1.3). Then one has a corresponding epimorphic family \(f^*(X_i) \to f^*(Y)\), such that for every \(i\) one has a finite epimorphic family \(f^*(X_j) \to f^*(X \times_Y X_i) \simeq f^*(X) \times_{f^*(Y)} f^*(X_i)\), whose composite with the projection \(\mathrm{pr}_2\) into \(f^*(X_i)\) is a quasi-compact morphism \(f^*(X_j) \to f^*(X_i)\), thanks to the hypothesis (i bis). It follows (1.11 (i)) that for every \(i\), \(\mathrm{pr}_2 : f^*(X) \times_{f^*(Y)} f^*(X_i)\) is quasi-compact, hence (1.10 (ii)) \(f^*(u) : f^*(X) \to f^*(Y)\) is quasi-compact.

It remains to prove the implications (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) and (ii bis) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i), the implication (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii bis) being trivial, and (ii ter) being a particular case of (ii bis). The implication (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) is immediate: indeed, an object \(X\) of \(E_{/Y}\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated) if and only if the structural morphism \(X \to Y\) (resp. the diagonal morphism \(X \to X \times_Y X\)) is quasi-compact (2.7), and one has the same criterion of quasi-compactness and of quasi-separation for \(f^*(X')\). Let us prove finally (ii bis) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i). So let \(u: X \to Y\) be a quasi-compact arrow in \(E\); let us prove that \(f^*(u)\) is quasi-compact. Since the \(Y'_\alpha\) cover the final object of \(E'\), it suffices to prove that the \(f^*(u)|Y'_\alpha\) are quasi-compact (1.10 (ii)). Now, these morphisms are none other than the \(f^*_{v_\alpha}(u|Y_\alpha)\), and one is thus reduced to proving this:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.6

Let \(f: E' \to E\) be a coherent morphism of locally coherent topoi. Then for every quasi-compact arrow \(u\) of \(E\), \(f^*(u)\) is quasi-compact.

Thanks to the implication (i bis) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i) of 3.5 already proved, it suffices to prove that if \(u: X \to Y\) is an arrow of \(E\), with \(X, Y\) coherent, then \(f^*(u)\) is a quasi-compact morphism, which follows at once from the hypothesis on \(f\), implying that \(f^*(X)\) and \(f^*(Y)\) are likewise coherent.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.7

Let \(f : E' \to E\) be a morphism of locally coherent topoi. One says that \(f\) is locally coherent if it satisfies the equivalent conditions of 3.5.
Let us remark that "locally" means local on top.

This notion again depends only on the isomorphism class of the morphism of topoi \(f\), and it is manifestly stable under composition of morphisms of topoi. Moreover, by virtue of 3.5, if \(f\) is coherent it is locally coherent, the converse being true if \(E'\) and \(E\) are coherent (by virtue of 3.5 (ii bis)). From the criterion 3.5 (ii bis) there follows at once the following criterion:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.7

Let \(f: E' \to E\) be a morphism of locally coherent topoi, \((Y_i)_{i \in I}\), \((Y'_i)_{i \in I}\) two families of objects of \(E\) and of \(E'\), and for every \(i \in I\) \(v_i : Y'_i \to f^*(Y_i)\) a morphism, whence a morphism of topoi \[ f_{v_i} : E'_{/Y'_i} \to E_{/Y_i} . \] Suppose that the \(Y'_i\) cover the final object of \(E'\). Then \(f\) is locally coherent if and only if for every \(i \in I\), \(f_{v_i}\) is.
In particular, applying this to the identity morphism of an induced topos, one finds:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.8

Let \(E\) be a locally coherent topos, \(v: X \to Y\) an arrow of \(E\). Then the morphism of induced topoi \(E_{/X} \to E_{/Y}\) defined by \(v\) is locally coherent.
Remark 3.9

It seems that all the morphisms of algebraic topoi that one has encountered in practice are locally coherent (that is why the term "locally coherent" is doubtless not destined for very great use). It amounts to the same to assert that the coherent morphisms of topoi that one has encountered in practice are coherent. One can however construct non-coherent morphisms of coherent topoi, and more particularly, a non-coherent morphism of the punctual topos (IV 2.2) into a noetherian topos \(E\), cf. 2.17 i).

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.html:
Examples 3.10 (Topoi associated with schemes)

Let us take up again the example 1.22 of the category (Sch) with topologies \(T_i\) of SGA IV 6.3. Let, for every scheme \(X\), \(X_{T_i}\) be the \(\mathcal{V}\)-topos defined by the induced site \((\mathrm{Sch})_{/X}\). Then the morphism of schemes \(f: X \to Y\) defines a morphism of topoi \(f_{T_i} : X_{T_i} \to Y_{T_i}\), and it results from 3.4 and from 1.22 that this latter morphism of topoi is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) if and only if the morphism of schemes \(f\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) in the usual sense of EGA IV 1. In any case, \(f_{T_i}\) is locally coherent by virtue of 3.8.

One can also associate with a scheme \(X\) the \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) and \(\mathrm{Top}(X_{\text{ét}})\) as in 1.22.1, and with every morphism of schemes \(f : X \to Y\) are then associated morphisms \(\mathrm{Top}(f)\) and \(\mathrm{Top}(f_{\text{ét}})\) of the corresponding topoi. Let \(T(f)\) be one of these two

morphisms of topoi. One verifies immediately via 3.2 that this morphism of topoi is always locally coherent, and that it is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) if and only if the morphism of schemes \(f\) is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-separated, resp. coherent) in the usual sense.

These observations thus show once more that the terminology introduced in the present section is compatible with the terminology received in the theory of schemes, and hence deserves to be accepted by the most recalcitrant reader.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 3.11 (Coherent topoi and pretopoi)
  1. a)

    One calls a \(\mathcal{U}\)-pretopos (or simply pretopos), a category \(C\) satisfying the following conditions:

    1. 1)

      The finite projective limits in \(C\) are representable.

    2. 2)

      The finite sums in \(C\) are representable, they are disjoint and universal.

    3. 3)

      The equivalence relations in \(C\) are effective, and every epimorphism in \(C\) is universal effective.

    4. 4)

      \(C\) is equivalent to a category \(\in \mathcal{U}\).

    Show that if \(E\) is a coherent \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos, then the full subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of \(E\) formed of the coherent objects of \(E\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-pretopos, and that the inclusion functor \(E_{\mathrm{coh}} \to E\) is left exact, commutes with finite sums and with passage to the quotient by equivalence relations. (Use 1.5.3, 1.15 and 1.17.1.) Show that the topology induced by \(E\) on \(C\) is the "precanonical" topology, i.e. the topology whose covering families \(X_i \to X\) are those which admit a finite covering subfamily for the canonical topology of \(C\). Consequently \(E\) is reconstituted up to equivalence by the knowledge of the pretopos \(C = E_{\mathrm{coh}}\), as the topos \(\widetilde{C}\) (\(C\) being equipped with its precanonical topology).

  2. b)

    Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-pretopos. Let us equip \(C\) with the precanonical topology. Let us show that every morphism \(f\) of \(C\) factors as \(f'' f'\), with \(f'\) an epimorphism and \(f''\) a monomorphism. Show that the topos \(E = \widetilde{C}\) is coherent, and that the canonical functor \(\varepsilon : C \to E\) induces an equivalence of \(C\) with the subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of \(E\). (Show first that \(\varepsilon\) is a fully faithful functor, left exact, commuting with finite sums and with passage to the quotient by an equivalence relation, then that a coherent subobject in \(E\) of an object of \(C\) is in the essential image of \(C\).) Consequently, the \(\mathcal{U}\)-pretopos \(C\) is reconstituted up to equivalence of categories when one knows the associated \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(E = \widetilde{C}\).

  3. c)

    Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-pretopoi. Show that for a functor \(\varphi : C' \to C\) to be a morphism of sites from \(C\) to \(C'\) (for the precanonical topologies), it is necessary and sufficient that \(\varphi\) be left exact, and commute with finite sums and with passage to the quotient by an equivalence relation.

  4. d)

    With the notations of c), suppose that \(C\) and \(C'\) are associated with two coherent \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi \(E\), \(E'\) as in a). Show that the canonical functor (IV 4.9.3) \[ \mathrm{Morsite}(C,C') \to \mathrm{Homtop}(E,E') \] induces an equivalence of the first member (made explicit in c)) with the full subcategory of the second formed of the morphisms of topoi \(E \to E'\) which are coherent, a quasi-inverse functor being obtained by associating with every coherent morphism of topoi \(f: E \to E'\) the functor \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}} = C' \to E_{\mathrm{coh}} = C\) induced by \(f^*\).

  5. e)

    Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-pretopos and \(E = \widetilde{C}\). Express directly in terms of exactness properties of \(C\) the equivalent conditions of 1.25. (Consult 1.28 b.) Show that an object \(X\) of \(C\) is noetherian in \(E\) if and only if every increasing sequence of subobjects of \(X\) in \(C\) is stationary, hence that \(E\) is noetherian if and only if every object of \(C\) satisfies the preceding condition.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 3.12

A topos \(E\) is called a finite topos if there exists a finite category \(C\) such that \(E\) is equivalent to \(\widehat{C}\).

  1. a)

    For \(E\) to be a finite topos, it is necessary and sufficient that \(E\) admit enough essential points (IV 7.6 b)), and that the category Pointess\((E)\) of essential points of \(E\) be equivalent to a finite category. (Use IV 7.6 d) and h).)

  2. b)

    Suppose \(E\) finite. Prove that every point of \(E\) is essential. Prove that the 2-functors \(E \mapsto \mathrm{Point}(E)\) and \(C \mapsto \widehat{C}\) establish 2-equivalences between the 2-category of finite topoi \(E\), and the 2-category of Karoubian categories (IV 7.5 s)) \(C\) which are equivalent to finite categories, and that every morphism of finite topoi is essential (IV 7.6 a)). (Use a) and IV 7.6 h).)

  3. c)

    Suppose \(E = \widehat{C}\), with \(C\) equivalent to a finite category, and let \(F\) be a coherent topos. Recall (IV (4.6.3.1)) that the morphisms of topoi \(f : E \to F\) correspond to the functors \(u : C \to \mathrm{Point}(F)\). Show that for \(f\) to be coherent, it is necessary and sufficient that \(f\) transform a coherent point of \(E\) (3.1) into a coherent point of \(F\), or again that for every \(X \in\) ob \(C\), \(u(X)\) be a coherent point of \(F\). (Use 3.2 and 2.17 g).) Conclude that every morphism \(f: E \to F\) from a finite topos into a finite topos is coherent.

  4. d)

    Let \(X\) be a sober topological space (IV 4.2.1). For the topos \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) (IV 2.1) to be finite, it is necessary and sufficient that \(X\) be a finite set. (Use IV 7.1.6.)

pages.title: 4. Finiteness conditions in a topos obtained by gluing

blocks.html: 4. Finiteness conditions in a topos obtained by gluing
The present paragraph will no longer be used in the sequel of the Seminar.

Let \(E\) be a topos, \(U\) an open set of \(E\) (i.e. a subobject of the final object of \(E\)), and let us consider the corresponding open and closed subtopoi of \(E\) (IV 9) \[ E' = E_{/U} , \quad E'' = E_{\complement U} . \] We shall denote by \[ j : E' \to E , \quad i : E'' \to E \] the canonical morphisms of topoi. Recall (3.4) that for \(j\) to be a quasi-compact (resp. coherent) morphism of topoi, it is necessary and sufficient that the inclusion \[ j : U \to e \] of \(U\) into the final object of \(E\) (an inclusion that we shall also denote by \(j\)) be a quasi-compact (resp. coherent) morphism in \(E\); on the other hand, \(j : E' \to E\) is always quasi-separated (for \(j : U \to e\) is (1.8.1)). We propose to give criteria for the topos \(E''\) to be coherent, and for the morphism of topoi \(i: E'' \to E\) to be coherent. Let us note first:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2

The notations being those of 4.1, the inclusion morphism \(i: E'' \to E\) is quasi-compact, i.e. for every quasi-compact object \(X\) of \(E\), the object \(i^*(X)\) of \(E''\) is quasi-compact; moreover, if \(X\) is prenoetherian (1.30), \(i^*(X)\) is prenoetherian.
This results from definition 1.1 and from the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.2.1

The map \(Y \mapsto i^*(Y)\) induces an isomorphism of ordered sets between the set of subobjects of \(X\) which contain the subobject \(X_U = X \times U\) of \(X\), and the set of subobjects of \(i^*(X)\).

Let us note that, \(i_*\) being conservative (since fully faithful) and left exact (in particular, commuting with fibre products), it follows at once that a morphism \(u: Y \to Z\) in \(E''\) is a monomorphism if and only if \(i_*(u) : i_*(Y) \to i_*(Z)\) is. It follows at once, identifying (by \(i_*\)) \(E''\) with the full subcategory of \(E\) formed of the objects \(Z\) satisfying the equivalent conditions of IV 9.7 1), that the subobjects in \(E''\) of the object \(Z\) of \(E''\) are identified with the subobjects \(Y\) of \(Z\) in \(E\) which are willing to belong to \(E''\), or, what amounts to the same, which contain \(Z_U \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } U\). Now for \(Z\) of the form \(i_* i^*(X) = X_{\complement U}\) given by the amalgamated sum IV (9.5.1), \[ i_* i^* X = X_{\complement U} = X \amalg_{X_U} U , \] the datum of a subobject \(Y\) of this latter in \(E\) is equivalent to the datum of a pair formed of a subobject \(Y_1\) of \(X\) and a subobject \(Y_2\) of \(U\), with the condition that the inverse images of these subobjects in \(X_U\) coincide. The condition that \(Y\) contain \(U\) then means that \(Y_2=U\), and the remaining condition on \(Y_1\) is that \(Y_1\) contain \(X_U\). This thus establishes a bijection between the set of subobjects of \(i^*(X)\) in \(E''\), and the set of subobjects of \(X\) which contain \(X_U\). It is clear that this is an isomorphism of ordered sets, and that the inverse map is indeed the one announced in 3.14.1.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.3
  1. a)

    Let \(X\) be an object of \(E\). For \(X\) to be quasi-compact, it suffices that \(i^*(X)\) and \(j^*(X)\) be so, and this condition is also necessary if \(j: U \to e\) is quasi-compact.

  2. b)

    Let \(Y\) be an object of \(E''\). For \(Y\) to be quasi-compact, it suffices that \(i_*(Y)\) be so, and this condition is also necessary if \(U\) is quasi-compact.

Proof. a) Sufficiency results from definition 1.1 and from the fact that the pair \((i^*,j^*)\) is conservative (IV 9.11 3)). Necessity results from the fact that \(i\) and \(j\) are quasi-compact (by virtue of 3.14 and of the hypothesis that \(j\) is quasi-compact).
b) Since \(Y \simeq i^* i_*(Y)\), sufficiency results from 4.2. Necessity results from sufficiency in a), taking into account that \(i^* i_*(Y) \simeq Y\) and \(j^* i_*(Y) \simeq U\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.4

Let \(Y\) be an object of \(E''\). If \(U\) is quasi-compact or if \(E\) admits a generating family formed of quasi-compact objects, then for \(Y\) to be quasi-separated (resp. coherent), it suffices that it be so of \(i_*(Y)\). If \(U\) is quasi-separated (resp. coherent) and if \(j: U \to e\) is a quasi-compact morphism, then for \(Y\) to be quasi-separated (resp. coherent), it is necessary that \(i_*(Y)\) be so.

The "resp." case results from the non-"resp." case, taking into account 4.3 b). Suppose \(i_*(Y)\) quasi-separated, and let us prove that so is \(Y\), under one of the two hypotheses made. It is thus necessary to prove that for two quasi-compact objects \(Y'\) and \(Y''\) over \(Y\), the fibre product \(Y' \times_Y Y''\) is quasi-compact. When one supposes \(Y\) quasi-compact, one notes that it suffices to prove that \(i_*(Y' \times_Y Y'')\) is quasi-compact (4.3 b)), which results from the fact that \(i_*(Y')\) and \(i_*(Y'')\) are (4.3 b)), using here the quasi-compactness of \(U\)), that \(i_*\) commutes with fibre products, and the hypothesis \(i_*(Y)\) quasi-separated. When one supposes that \(E\) admits a generating family formed of quasi-compact objects, then \(i_*(Y')\) is a filtered inductive limit of its quasi-compact subobjects \(X'_\alpha\), so \(Y' \simeq i^* i_*(Y')\) is a filtered inductive limit of the subobjects \(i^*(X'_\alpha)\), and since \(Y'\) is quasi-compact, it is equal to one of the \(i^*(X'_\alpha)\). Likewise \(Y''\) is of the form \(i^*(X''_\beta)\), where \(X''_\beta\) is a quasi-compact subobject of \(i_*(Y'')\). But then \(Y' \times_Y Y'' = i^*(X'_\alpha \times_{i_*(Y)} X''_\beta)\), and since \(X'_\alpha \times_{i_*(Y)} X''_\beta\) is quasi-compact by virtue of the hypothesis \(i_*(Y)\) quasi-separated, it follows that \(Y' \times_Y Y''\) is so as well by virtue of 4.2.

Conversely, supposing \(U\) quasi-separated and \(j: U \to e\) quasi-compact, let us show that if \(Y\) is quasi-separated, so is \(i_*(Y)\), i.e. that for two quasi-compact objects \(X',X''\) over \(i_*(Y)\), the fibre product \(X' \times_{i_*(Y)} X''\) is quasi-compact. For this, applying 4.3 a), it suffices to prove that its image under \(i^*\) is quasi-compact (which results from 4.2 and from the hypothesis that \(Y\) is quasi-separated) and that its image under \(j^*\) is quasi-compact; now this latter is \(j^*(X') \times j^*(X'')\), and is indeed quasi-compact since \(j^*(X')\) and \(j^*(X'')\) are (\(j\) being quasi-compact) and \(U\) is quasi-separated.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.5

Suppose that \(E\) admits a generating subcategory formed of quasi-compact (resp. prenoetherian) objects; then so does \(E''\).
This results from 4.2 and from the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.5.1

If \((X_\alpha)_\alpha\) is a generating family in \(E\), then \((i^*(X_\alpha))_\alpha\) is a generating family in \(E''\).

This means indeed that the family of functors \[ Y \to \mathrm{Hom}(i^*(X_\alpha),Y) \] on \(E''\) is conservative; now one has \(\mathrm{Hom}(i^*(X_\alpha),Y) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(X_\alpha, i_*(Y))\), and it suffices to use the fact that the functor \(i_*\) is conservative.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.6

The notations are those of 4.1.

  1. a)

    If \(E\) admits a generating family formed of coherent objects, so does the closed subtopos \(E''\), and the inclusion morphism \(i: E'' \to E\) is coherent.

  2. b)

    Suppose that the morphism \(j: U \to e\) in \(E\) is quasi-compact. If \(E\) is locally coherent (resp. coherent, resp. quasi-separated, resp. locally noetherian, resp. noetherian, resp. locally perfect, resp. perfect) so is \(E''\), and the inclusion morphism \(i : E'' \to E\) is coherent.

a) The first assertion will result from the second and from 4.5.1. In any case, 4.5 implies that \(E''\) admits a generating family formed of quasi-compact objects, so 3.2 applies and shows us that it suffices to verify that for every coherent object \(X\) of \(E\), the object \(i^*(X)\) of \(E''\) is coherent. Using the compatibility of the formation of the topos complementary to an open set with localization (IV 9.13 b)), one is reduced to the case where \(X\) is the final object of \(E\), hence to proving that the final object of \(E''\) is coherent. Now, 4.4 applies, so it suffices to prove that \(i_*(e_{E''}) = e_E\) is coherent, which is indeed the case.

b) Since under each of the hypotheses made in b), \(E\) admits a generating family formed of coherent objects, it already results from a) that \(i: E'' \to E\) is coherent. Moreover, 4.5.1 then implies that \(E''\) admits the full subcategory \(E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\) formed of its coherent objects as a generating subcategory. Suppose \(E\) coherent, and let us show that \(E''\) is so as well, i.e. (2.4.5) let us show that the subcategory \(E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of \(E''\) is stable under finite projective limits, knowing that this holds for the subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of \(E\); now this results at once from the criterion 4.4 "resp." (which applies, since \(U\) is now coherent, \(e\) being so and \(j: U \to e\) being quasi-compact), taking into account that \(i_*\) is left exact. By localization, again using IV 9.13 b), one concludes that if \(E\) is locally coherent, so is \(E''\). If \(E\) is quasi-separated, then \(E''\) is so as well: indeed its final object is quasi-separated by virtue of 4.4, that of \(E\) being so, and it remains to prove that the product of two quasi-separated objects of \(E''\) is quasi-separated (knowing that this holds in \(E''\)), which again results from the criterion 4.4 and from the fact that \(i_*\) commutes with products (taking into account that the subobject \(U\) of \(e\) is quasi-separated, \(e\) being so, so that 4.4 applies).

Since a topos is locally noetherian (resp. noetherian) if and only if it is locally coherent (resp. coherent) and admits a generating family formed of prenoetherian objects (2.10 (iii bis)), it results from what precedes and from 4.5 that if \(E\) is locally noetherian (resp. noetherian), so is \(E''\). Suppose now \(E\) perfect, and let us prove that \(E''\) is. Since one already knows that it is coherent, it remains to verify that it satisfies the criterion 1.25 (i), i.e. that every object \(Y\) of \(E''\) is a filtered inductive limit of coherent objects, knowing that the analogous statement is true in \(E\); \(i_*(Y)\) being a filtered inductive limit of coherent objects \(X_\alpha\), \(Y \simeq i^* i_*(Y)\) is a filtered inductive limit of the coherent objects \(i^*(X_\alpha)\). By localization (IV 9.13 b)) one concludes that if \(E\) is locally perfect, so is \(E''\). This completes the proof of 4.6.

In fact, in 4.6 b) the hypothesis that \(j: U \to e\) be quasi-compact is useless, except perhaps in the case "\(E\) quasi-separated". It suffices indeed, by virtue of the preceding proof, to see that \(E\) coherent implies \(E''\) coherent. Now \(U\) is a filtered inductive limit of its quasi-compact subobjects \(U_\alpha\), and one will then verify in 7. that then \(E''\) is identified with the projective limit topos (in the sense of 7. ) of the closed subtopoi \(E''_i\) complementary to the \(E_{/U_i}\), which by virtue of 4.6 b) are coherent topoi with coherent transition morphisms. It then follows that \(E''\) is a coherent topos (7. ).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.7

Suppose that the subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of \(E\) formed of the coherent objects is generating, and let \(X\) be an object of \(E\).

  1. a)

    For \(X\) to be quasi-separated, it is necessary that \(i^*(X)\) and \(j^*(X)\) be, and this condition is also sufficient if \(j: U \to e\) is quasi-compact.

  2. b)

    Suppose that \(j: U \to e\) is quasi-compact. Then \(X\) is coherent if and only if \(i^*(X)\) and \(j^*(X)\) are.

  3. c)

    Suppose \(E\) coherent and \(j: U \to e\) quasi-compact. Then \(E\) is perfect (2.9.1) if and only if \(E'\) and \(E''\) are.

a) It was pointed out in 4.1 that \(j: E' \to E\) is quasi-separated, and on the other hand one knows by 4.6 a) that so is \(i\), whence necessity. For sufficiency, let \(X'\) and \(X''\) be quasi-compact objects over \(X\); it is necessary to prove that \(X' \times_X X''\) is quasi-compact, and for this it suffices to prove that its images under \(i^*\) and \(j^*\) are (4.3 a)). Since \(i\) and \(j\) are quasi-compact, by virtue of 4.2 and of the hypothesis \(j: U \to e\) quasi-compact, the conclusion then results from the fact that \(i^*\) and \(j^*\) commute with fibre products, and from the hypothesis that \(i^*(X)\) and \(j^*(X)\) are quasi-separated.
b) Results from the conjunction of a) and of 4.3 a).

c) Necessity has already been seen (4.6 b)). Sufficiency results from the fact that, \(E\) being coherent, \(E'\) and \(E''\) are (4.6 b)), so that for one of the topoi considered, the fact that it is perfect means that the category of its coherent objects is stable under finite \(\varinjlim\). One concludes therefore by b).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 4.8
  1. a)

    Solve the following question (whose answer the writer confesses to his embarrassment not to know): with the notations of 4.1, if \(E\) is quasi-separated (resp. algebraic) is the same true of \(E''\)?

  2. b)

    Suppose that \(E\) is equivalent to a topos of the form \(\widehat{C}\), where \(C\) is a category equivalent to a category \(\in \mathcal{U}\). Prove directly, using 2.17 c) and IV 9.24, that if \(E\) is locally coherent (resp. coherent, resp. algebraic, resp. quasi-separated, resp. locally noetherian, resp. noetherian) so is \(E''\).

Let us keep the notations of 4.1, and recall (IV 9.16) that the datum of a situation \((E,U)\), formed by a topos \(E\) and an open set \(U\) of \(E\), is essentially equivalent to that of a triple \((E', E'', f)\), where \(E'\) and \(E''\) are topoi and where \[ \text{(4.9.1)} \qquad f: E' \to E'' \] is a "gluing functor", i.e. a functor which is left exact and accessible; starting from \((E,U)\) as in 4.1, the associated gluing functor is given by \[ \text{(4.9.2)} \qquad f = i^* j_* . \] We propose to express, in terms of the data \(E'\), \(E''\), \(f\), the fact that \(E\) be a coherent (resp. perfect) topos and that \(U\) be a quasi-compact object, or what amounts to the same, that \(E\) and \(E'\) be coherent. We already know that this entails that \(E''\) is likewise coherent (4.6 b)), so that the question amounts to the following: given two coherent topoi \(E'\) and \(E''\) and a gluing functor \(f\) (4.9.1), under what conditions on \(f\) is the glued topos \(E\) coherent (resp. perfect)? We know moreover (4.7 c)) that \(E\) is perfect if and only if \(E\) is coherent, and \(E'\) and \(E''\) are perfect; hence the "resp." case of the problem posed reduces to the non-"resp." case. Let us point out however that the solution (4.10) of the latter is prettier if one already supposes \(E'\) perfect.

Let us note first that if \(E\) is coherent, then one reconstructs the full subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of \(E\) formed of the objects \(X = (X',X'', u: X'' \to f(X'))\) of \(E\) which are coherent, as being the subcategory \(E_0\) of \(E\) formed

of the \(X\) for which \(X' = j^*(X)\) and \(X'' = i^*(X)\) are coherent (4.7 b)). A necessary condition for \(E\) to be coherent is thus that the preceding subcategory \(E_0\) be generating. This condition is also sufficient, for by virtue of 4.3 a) \(E_0\) is formed of quasi-compact objects, and on the other hand it is clear that \(E_0\) is stable under finite projective limits, and one concludes by 3.4.5.

Let us now recall (IV 9.18) that the datum of a gluing functor (4.9.1) is equivalent to that of a sheaf on \(E''\), with values in \(\mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ\): \[ \text{(4.9.4)} \qquad G \in \mathrm{Faisc}(E'', \mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ) , \quad G: (E'')^\circ \to \mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ , \] or what amounts to the same, to that of a functor \(g = G^\circ\), \[ \text{(4.9.5)} \qquad g: E'' \to \mathrm{Pro}(E') \] which commutes with inductive limits. If \(C\) is a generating subcategory of \(E''\), which one equips with the induced topology, one knows (II 6.10) that the datum of \(G\) is also equivalent (up to unique isomorphism) to that of a sheaf on \(C\) with values in \(\mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ\) \[ \text{(4.9.6)} \qquad G_C \in \mathrm{Faisc}(C,\mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ) , \quad G_C : C^\circ \to \mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ , \] or, what amounts to the same, to that of a functor \(g_C = G_C^\circ\), \[ \text{(4.9.7)} \qquad g_C : C \to \mathrm{Pro}(E') , \] satisfying the left exactness conditions that one knows (II 6.2 1)). Of course, \(g_C\) is none other than the restriction of \(g\) (4.9.5) to \(C\). The most interesting case for us is that where one takes \(C = E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\), whence objects \[ \text{(4.9.8)} \qquad G_0 \in \mathrm{Faisc}(E''_{\mathrm{coh}} , \mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ), \quad G_0: (E''_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ \to \mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ, \] \[ \text{(4.9.9)} \qquad g_0 = G_0^\circ : E''_{\mathrm{coh}} \to \mathrm{Pro}(E') , \] each of which again amounts to the datum of \(f\).

Suppose the generating full subcategory \(C\) of \(E''\) formed of quasi-compact objects and stable in \(E''\) under finite sums, under passage to the quotient by equivalence relations, and under fibre products: this is the case for example for \(C = E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\) (1.15 and 1.17.1). It is then immediate, if \(P\) is a category where the finite projective limits are representable (for example \(P = \mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ\)), that a functor \(G_C : C^\circ \to P\) is a sheaf with values in \(P\) if and only if the functor \(g_C = G_C^\circ : C \to P^\circ\) commutes with finite sums and with passage to the quotient by an equivalence relation. This makes precise in particular which are the sheaves (4.9.6) (thus expressing the gluing functors \(f: E' \to E''\)).
These reminders being laid down, we can give the solution to the problem posed in 4.9:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.10

Let \(E'\), \(E''\) be two coherent topoi, and \(f: E' \to E''\) a gluing functor (IV 9.10), i.e. a functor left exact and accessible. Let \(E\) be the topos that one deduces from it by gluing (IV 9.16), and denote by \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}}\) (resp. \(E'_{\mathrm{PF}}\)) the strictly full subcategory of \(E'\) formed of the coherent objects (resp. of the objects \(X\) such that the covariant functor \(\mathrm{Hom}(X,-)\) represented by \(X\) commutes with small filtered inductive limits). Let us consider the following conditions:

  1. (i)

    \(E\) is coherent.

  2. (ii)

    For every object \(X'\) of \(E'\), there exists a family of morphisms \[ v_\alpha : Y'_\alpha \to X' \] with target \(X'\), with sources the coherent objects of \(E'\), such that the family of the \[ f(v_\alpha) : f(Y'_\alpha) \to f(X') \] in \(E''\) is covering.

  3. (ii bis)

    \(f\) commutes with (small) filtered inductive limits, and (ii) is true for every \(X' \in\) Ob \(E'_{\mathrm{PF}}\).

  4. (ii ter)

    The canonical functor (IV 9.20.1) \[ \text{(4.10.1)} \qquad \pi : \mathrm{Point}(E'') \to \mathrm{Pro}(E') \] defined by the gluing functor \(f\) factors (up to isomorphism) through \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})\) (via the fully faithful functor \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}}) \to \mathrm{Pro}(E')\) arising from the inclusion \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}} \to E'\)): \[ \text{(4.10.2)} \qquad \pi_0 : \mathrm{Point}(E'') \to \mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}}) . \]

  5. (iii)

    The functor \(f\) commutes with (small) filtered inductive limits.

  6. (iii bis)

    The functor \(g_0\) (4.9.9) factors (up to isomorphism) through a functor \[ \text{(4.10.3)} \qquad E''_{\mathrm{coh}} \to \mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{PF}}) , \] via the fully faithful functor \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{PF}}) \to \mathrm{Pro}(E')\) deduced from the inclusion \(E'_{\mathrm{PF}} \to E'\).

  7. (iii ter)

    The canonical functor \(\pi\) (4.10.1) factors (up to isomorphism) as \[ \text{(4.10.4)} \qquad \pi_1 : \mathrm{Point}(E'') \to \mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{PF}}) . \]

  8. (iv)

    The functor \(g_0\) (4.9.9) factors (up to isomorphism) through a functor \[ \text{(4.10.5)} \qquad E''_{\mathrm{coh}} \to \mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}}) . \]

One then has the diagram of implications:

(4.10.6) (iv) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii bis) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) (ii ter) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iii) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) (iii bis) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) (iii ter)
Let us point out at once the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.11
  1. a)

    Suppose that \(E'\) is perfect. Then all the conditions considered in 4.10 are equivalent, in particular \(E\) is coherent if and only if \(f\) commutes with filtered inductive limits, or again if and only if the functor \(g_0\) (4.9.9) factors (up to isomorphism) through \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})\).

  2. b)

    For \(E\) to be perfect, it is necessary and sufficient that \(E'\) and \(E''\) be, and that \(f\) (resp. \(g_0\)) satisfy the condition stated in a).

Indeed, a) results from the fact that \(E'\) perfect means \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}} = E'_{\mathrm{PF}}\), so that (iii bis) implies (iv). Assertion b) follows, as it results from the preliminary remarks of 4.9.

a) Let us make explicit the condition equivalent to (i) obtained in 4.9.3, namely that the full subcategory \(E_0\) of \(E\) is generating, i.e. that for every object \(X = (X',X'',u:X'' \to f(X'))\) of \(E\), the family of all the morphisms \[ v = (v',v'') : Y = (Y',Y'',v:Y'' \to f(Y')) \to X , \] with \(Y \in\) Ob \(E_0\) i.e. \(Y'\), \(Y''\) coherent, is epimorphic. Since the pair of functors \((i^*,j^*)\) is conservative, this also means that the family of the corresponding morphisms \(Y' \to X'\) is epimorphic in \(E'\), and that the family of the corresponding morphisms \(Y'' \to X''\) is epimorphic in \(E''\). Now this is clear for the first, as one sees by taking \(Y \in\) Ob \(E_0\) over \(U\) i.e. such that \(Y'' = \varnothing_{E''}\): one finds the family of all the arrows in \(E'\) with target \(X'\), with coherent source, which is indeed epimorphic since \(E'\) is coherent hence the subcategory \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}}\) is generating. It thus remains to express that the family of the \(Y'' \to X''\) is epimorphic, whatever the given object \(X\) of \(E\).

b) Now suppose satisfied the condition (ii) for the object \(X'\) considered here. It results that one can find an epimorphic family of morphisms \(Y''_\beta \to X''\), whose composites with \(u: X'' \to f(X')\) each lift to a morphism \(Y''_\beta \to f(Y'_\alpha)\) for a suitable \(\alpha = \varphi(\beta)\); since \(E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\) is a generating subcategory of \(E''\), one can even suppose the \(Y''_\beta\) coherent. But then the commutative diagrams \[ \xymatrix{ Y''_\beta \ar[r] \ar[d] & f(Y'_{\varphi(\beta)}) \ar[d] \\ X'' \ar[r] & f(X') } \] furnish the sought family of morphisms in \(E\), giving an epimorphic family \(Y''_\beta \to X''\). Hence (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i).

Conversely, suppose (i) and let us prove (ii). One applies the condition made explicit in a) to the case of the object \[ X = j_*(X') = (X',f(X'), \mathrm{id}= f(X') \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } f(X')) ; \] since the \(Y'' \to X'' \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } f(X')\) form an epimorphic family, so does a fortiori the family of the \(f(v'): f(Y') \to f(X')\), whence the conclusion, since the \(Y'\) are coherent by hypothesis. Hence \[ \text{(i)} \Longleftrightarrow \text{(ii)} . \]

c) Let us note now that the condition (iv) also means that for every object \(X''\) of \(E''\), the pro-representable functor \[ g(X'') : X' \to \mathrm{Hom}(X'',f(X')) \] on \(E'\) is pro-representable by a pro-object whose components are in \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}}\), or what amounts to the same, that there exists in the category \(E'_{/g(X'')}\), formed of the pairs of an object \(X'\) of \(E'\) and an element \(u \in g(X'')(X') = \mathrm{Hom}(X'',f(X'))\), \(u: X'' \to f(X')\), a cofinal set of objects \((X'_\alpha , u_\alpha)\), \(u_\alpha: X'' \to f(X'_\alpha)\), with \(X'_\alpha \in\) Ob \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}}\). The cofinality condition, since the category \(E'_{/g(X'')}\) is filtered, means simply that for every object \((X',u)\), \(u: X'' \to f(X')\) of \(E'_{/g(X'')}\) there exists a morphism from an \((X'_i,u_i)\) into the preceding object, i.e. a morphism \(v'_\alpha : X'_\alpha \to X'\) making commutative the triangle \[ (*) \qquad \xymatrix@R=1.5em{ & f(X'_\alpha) \ar[dd]^-{f'(v'_\alpha)} \\ X'' \ar[ur]^-{u_\alpha} \ar[dr]_-{u} & \\ & f(X') } \] Hence the condition (iv) is equivalent to this:

(iv bis) For every arrow \(u: X'' \to f(X')\), with \(X' \in\) Ob \(E'\) and \(X'' \in\) Ob \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}}\), there exists an arrow \(v: Y' \to X'\) in \(E'\) such that \(u\) factors through \(f(v) : f(Y') \to f(X')\). Now it is clear that the condition (iv bis) implies (ii), since for \(X'\) fixed, the family of the

\(u: X'' \to f(X')\) with source a coherent object is epimorphic, so that so is a fortiori the family of all the \(f(v'_\alpha)\) in the corresponding diagrams (*). Hence \[ \text{(iv)} \Longrightarrow \text{(i)} . \]

d) Let us make explicit the condition (ii ter). Let \(p\) be a point of \(E''\), then by definition \(\pi(p)\) is the pro-object of \(E'\) which pro-represents the functor \(h: X' \to f(X')_p\), or again the pro-object defined by the canonical functor \(E'_{/h} \to E'\), where \(E'_{/h}\) denotes the category of pairs \((X',u)\), with \(X' \in\) Ob \(E'\) and \(u \in h(X')\) i.e. \(u \in f(X')_p\). To say that this pro-object is isomorphic to a pro-object arising from \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})\) means that the subcategory of \(E'_{/h}\) formed of the \((X',u)\) with \(X' \in\) Ob \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}}\) is cofinal therein, i.e. that for every object \((X',u)\), \(u \in f(X')_p\), of \(E'_{/h}\), there exists an object \((X'_0,u_0)\) which majorizes it, with \(X'_0\) coherent, i.e. that there exists a morphism \(X'_0 \to X'\) (\(X'_0\) coherent) such that \(u\) be in \(\operatorname{Im}(f(X'_0) \to f(X'))\). To say that this is true for every point \(p\) means that for every object \(X'\) of \(E'\), the family of the \(f(X'_0) \to f(X')\), with \(X'_0 \in\) Ob \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}/X'}\), is such that for every point \(p\) of \(X''\), the family of the \(f(X'_0)_p \to f(X')_p\) is surjective. Since one will see in the appendix (10. ) that a coherent topos \(E''\) has enough points, one sees that the condition obtained also means that for every \(X' \in\) Ob \(E\), the family of the \(f(X'_0) \to f(X')\) is epimorphic. But this is none other than the condition (ii), hence \[ \text{(ii)} \Longleftrightarrow \text{(ii ter)} . \]

e) The condition that \(f\) commute with filtered inductive limits (condition (iii)) is equivalent, since the family of the fibre functors of \(E''\) is conservative, to the condition that the composite functors \(h: X' \to f(X')_p\) do so. Let us prove that this means that the pro-object \(\pi(p)\) which pro-represents this functor is in the essential image of \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{PF}})\): this will then prove the implications \[ \text{(iii)} \Longleftrightarrow \text{(iii ter)} \Longleftarrow \text{(ii ter)} \Longrightarrow \text{(ii bis)} . \] We are thus led to prove the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.12.1

Let \(E'\) be a topos such that the subcategory \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}}\) is generating therein, and \(X' \in\) Ob \(\mathrm{Pro}(E')\). For \(X'\) to belong to the essential image of \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{PF}})\), it is necessary and sufficient that the functor \(h: E' \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) which it pro-represents commute with filtered inductive limits.

Since a filtered inductive limit of functors commuting with filtered inductive limits possesses the same property, the sufficiency results from the definition of \(E'_{\mathrm{PF}}\). For necessity, it is necessary to prove that if the functor \(h\) commutes with filtered inductive limits, then in the filtered category \(E'_{/h}\) of pairs \((X',u)\) with \(u \in h(X')\), the subcategory formed of the pairs \((X',u)\) with \(X' \in\) Ob \(E'_{\mathrm{PF}}\) is cofinal, i.e. that for every \((X',u)\) in \(E'_{/h}\), there exists a morphism \(X'_0 \to X'\), with \(X'_0 \in\) Ob \(E'_{\mathrm{PF}}\), such that \(u \in \operatorname{Im}(h(X'_0) \to h(X'))\). Now one knows that \(X'\) is a filtered inductive limit of objects \(X'_i\) of \(E'_{\mathrm{PF}}\) (1.24.2 a)), so \(h(X')\) is a filtered inductive limit of the \(h(X'_i)\), whence the conclusion.

e) It remains only to prove the implications \[ \text{(ii bis)} \Longrightarrow \text{(ii)} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{(iii)} \Longleftrightarrow \text{(iii bis)} . \] The first implication results trivially from the fact that every object \(X'\) of \(E'\) is a filtered inductive limit of objects \(X'_i\) of \(E'_{\mathrm{PF}}\). For the second, it suffices to note that the family of the functors \[ Y'' \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}(X'',Y'') , \] for \(X'' \in\) Ob \(E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\), is conservative and formed of functors commuting with filtered inductive limits (1.23 (ii)), hence the functor \(f: E' \to E''\) commutes with filtered inductive limits if and only if so do the composite functors \(X' \to \mathrm{Hom}(X'',f(X')) = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Pro}(E')}(g_0(X''),X')\), which is equivalent to the fact that the \(g_0(X'')\) are in the essential image of \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{PF}})\), by virtue of 4.12.1. Q.E.D.
Remarks 4.13

It is fitting to make precise, in sheaf-theoretic language, the meaning of the condition 4.10 (iv). Let us consider the commutative diagram of functors \[ \text{(4.13.1)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ \ar[r]^-{\alpha} \ar[d]_-{\beta_0} & \mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ \ar[d]^-{\beta} \\ \check{E}'_{\mathrm{coh}} & \check{E}' \ar[l]^-{\gamma} } \] where the signs \(\vee\) denote the categories of functors with values in (Ens), and the second horizontal arrow \(\gamma\) is the arrow of restriction of functors, all the other arrows denoting the well-known fully faithful functors. Let us note that the inclusion arrow \(\alpha\) does not commute in general with projective limits, even finite ones, so that in general a sheaf \(F\) on a site \(C\) (such as \(E''\)) defines a presheaf \(\alpha \circ F\) on this same site, with values in \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'')^\circ\), which is not necessarily a sheaf. Nevertheless, if a presheaf \(F\) on \(C\) with values in \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ\) is such that the corresponding presheaf \(\alpha F\) with values in \(\mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ\) is a sheaf, then \(F\) is itself a sheaf. This comes indeed from the fact that the condition of being a sheaf is a left exactness property (II 6.2 1)), and that the functors \(\beta\), \(\beta_0\) and \(\gamma\) commute with small projective limits.

On the other hand, it results from the characterization 4.9.10 of the sheaves on \(E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\) with values in an arbitrary category \(P\), that for every functor \(\alpha : P \to Q\) such that \(\alpha^\circ : P^\circ \to Q^\circ\) commutes with finite sums and with passage to the quotient by equivalence relations, the functor \(g \mapsto \alpha \circ g\) from \(\mathrm{Hom}((E''_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ,P)\) to \(\mathrm{Hom}((E''_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ,Q)\) transforms sheaves into sheaves. On the other hand, we know that in \(E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\) and in \(E'\) the finite sums and the quotients by equivalence relations are representable, and that the inclusion functor \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}} \to E'\) commutes with them (1.15 and 1.17.1). It is therefore the same for the categories \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})\) and \(\mathrm{Pro}(E')\) and the inclusion functor between these categories (I 8.9.5 b) and 8.9.7), which is none other than \(\alpha^\circ\), where \(\alpha\) is the functor intervening in (4.13.1). From this one concludes that if \[ \text{(4.13.2)} \qquad \varphi : (E''_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ \to \mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ \] is a functor, then \(\varphi\) is a sheaf on \(E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\) with values in \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ\) if and only if \(\alpha \circ \varphi\) is a sheaf on \(E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\) with values in \(\mathrm{Pro}(E')^\circ\). Hence the category of gluing functors \(f: E' \to E''\) which satisfy the condition 4.10 (iv) is canonically equivalent to the category of sheaves \(\varphi\) on \(E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\) with values in \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ\). One concludes from this, taking into account 4.10, that such a sheaf \(\varphi\) canonically defines a gluing functor (up to unique isomorphism), and that the topos \(E\) deduced from the latter is coherent; moreover (4.11) if \(E'\) is perfect, one obtains in this way all the coherent topoi that one can deduce from the topoi \(E'\), \(E''\) by gluing.

Let us note on the other hand that \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}}\) is equivalent to a small category and is stable under finite projective limits, so that (I 8.10.14) \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ\) is equivalent, by the fully faithful functor \(\beta_0\) of (4.13.1), to the full subcategory of \(\check{E}'_{\mathrm{coh}} = \mathrm{Hom}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}},(\mathrm{Ens}))\) formed of the functors which are left exact. Hence the datum of a sheaf (4.13.2) is equivalent to that of a functor \[ \text{(4.13.3)} \qquad F: (E''_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ \times E'_{\mathrm{coh}} \to (\mathrm{Ens}) \] which is a sheaf with respect to the first argument and which is left exact in the second argument; or again, to that of a functor \[ \text{(4.13.4)} \qquad f_0 : E'_{\mathrm{coh}} \to E'' \] which is left exact. If \(f\) is the gluing functor satisfying the condition 4.10 (iv) associated with \(\varphi\), one verifies immediately that \(f_0\) is canonically isomorphic to the restriction of the functor \(f: E' \to E''\). One sees therefore that under the conditions considered \(f_0\) determines \(f\) (up to canonical isomorphism). Let us point out finally, to summarize the content of 4.11:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.14

When \(E'\) is a perfect topos, then the category of gluing functors \(f: E' \to E''\) which give by gluing a coherent topos \(E\) is equivalent by \(f \mapsto f_0 = f|E'_{\mathrm{coh}}\) to the category of functors \(f_0 : E'_{\mathrm{coh}} \to E''\) which are left exact, or again to the category of sheaves \(\varphi\) on the site \(E''_{\mathrm{coh}}\) (or, what amounts to the same, on the topos \(E''\)) with values in the category \(\mathrm{Pro}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})^\circ\) (cf. 4.9.10).

One will observe that the first assertion also results from 4.10 by noting that \(E' \simeq \mathrm{Ind}(E'_{\mathrm{coh}})\) (1.25), so that the category of functors \(f : E' \to P\) commuting with filtered inductive limits (where \(P\) is a category where the small filtered inductive limits are representable) is equivalent, by the restriction functor, to the category of arbitrary functors \(f : E'_{\mathrm{coh}} \to P\); it is immediate that under these conditions, if in \(P\) the finite \(\varinjlim\) are representable, that \(f\) is left exact if and only if \(f_0\) is.
Remarks 4.15

a) The proof given of 4.10 shows that one obtains conditions equivalent to (ii ter) resp. (iii ter) by replacing the category \(\mathrm{Point}(E'')\) by a subcategory which defines a conservative family of fibre functors.

b) Taking for \(E''\) the punctual topos (IV 2.2), one sees at once that the conditions (ii ter) and (iii ter) are equivalent only if \(E'_{\mathrm{coh}} = E'_{\mathrm{PF}}\), i.e. if \(E'\) is perfect. Hence the condition "\(E\) coherent" is equivalent to the condition "\(f\) commutes with filtered inductive limits" only if \(E'\) is perfect. On the other hand, taking more generally for \(E''\) a coherent topos of the form \(\widehat{C}\), one sees that in this case the condition (i) is equivalent to (iv) for every \(E'\). In fact, the writer has not managed to construct in the general case an example where \(E\) is coherent, without the condition (iv) being satisfied. It's shameful!

pages.title: 5. Commutation of the functors \(H^i(X,-)\) with filtered inductive limits

blocks.html: 5. Commutation of the functors \(H^i(X,-)\) with filtered inductive limits

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.1

Let \(E'\) be an algebraic topos (2.3), \(E\) a locally coherent topos (2.3), \(f : E' \to E\) a coherent morphism of topoi (3.1). Then, for every integer \(q\), the functors \(R^q f_*\) (V 5.0) commute with filtered inductive limits of abelian sheaves.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.2

Let \(E'\) be a coherent topos (2.3). For every integer \(q\), the functor \(H^q(E',-)\) commutes with filtered inductive limits of abelian sheaves.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3

Let \(E\) be a topos (resp. an algebraic topos) (2.3), \(X\) an object of \(E\) algebraic and coherent (resp. coherent) (2.3). For every integer \(q\), the functor \(H^q(X,-)\) commutes with filtered inductive limits of abelian sheaves.

Corollary 5.2 is deduced from 5.1 by taking for \(E\) the punctual topos and for \(f : E' \to E\) the unique morphism (IV 2.2). Let us show that 5.2 entails 5.3. Let \(j_X : E_{/X} \to E\) be the localization morphism. One has a canonical isomorphism, functorial in the abelian sheaf (V 2.2.1) \(H^q(X,F) \simeq H^q(E_{/X}, j_X^* F)\). The functor \(j_X^*\) commutes with inductive limits and the topos \(E_{/X}\) is coherent (2.4.6) whence 5.3. Let us show that 5.3 entails 5.1. Let \(E_{\mathrm{cohalg}}\) be the full subcategory of \(E\) defined by the algebraic and coherent objects of \(E\). It is a generating category (2.4.5). For every abelian sheaf \(F\), \(R^q f_* F\) is the sheaf associated with the presheaf \(X \mapsto H^q(f^*X,F)\) (\(X \in\) ob \(C\)) (V 5.1). Since \(f\) is coherent, \(f^*X\) is coherent for every object \(X\) of \(C\) (3.1). By 5.3 the presheaf \(X \mapsto H^q(f^*X,F)\) commutes with filtered inductive limits of the argument \(F\) whence 5.1, using the fact that the associated-sheaf functor commutes with inductive limits. (One will remark that one uses only the following property of the morphism \(f\): There exists a generating family \(S\) of \(E\) such that for every \(X\) of \(S\), \(f^*(X)\) is algebraic and coherent). It thus remains to prove 5.2. One already knows that the functor \(H^0(E',-)\) commutes with filtered inductive limits of abelian sheaves (1.2.3). By a classical result of [7], it suffices, in order to prove 5.2, to show that a filtered inductive limit of sheaves acyclic for the functor \(H^0(E',-)\) is acyclic for \(H^0(E',-)\). This results from the following lemma applied to the case where \(C = E'_{\mathrm{coh}}\):

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.4

Let \(E\) be a locally coherent topos (2.3), \(C\) a full subcategory of \(E\), generating and stable under fibre product such that every object of \(C\) be quasi-compact (1.1). A filtered inductive limit of \(C\)-acyclic sheaves (V 4.2) is a \(C\)-acyclic sheaf.

Let \((F_i)_{i \in I}\) be a filtered inductive system of \(C\)-acyclic sheaves and let us denote by \(F\) its inductive limit. Every object \(Y\) of \(C\) is coherent (2.1) and consequently \(F(Y) = \varinjlim_i F_i(Y)\) (1.2.3). To show that \(F\) is \(C\)-acyclic, it suffices to show that \(\check{H}^q(Y,F) = 0\) for every \(q > 0\) and every \(Y\) of \(C\) (V 4.3). Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\), \(\mathfrak{X} = (X_\alpha \to X)_{\alpha \in \Lambda}\) a finite covering family by objects of \(C\). One has \(H^q(\mathfrak{X},F) = H^q(C^\bullet(\mathfrak{X},F))\) (V 2.4.3). By what precedes, and using the fact that \(C^\bullet(\mathfrak{X},F)\) involves only finite products of groups (V 2.3.3), one has \(C^\bullet(\mathfrak{X},F) = \varinjlim_i C^\bullet(\mathfrak{X},F_i)\). Hence \(H^q(\mathfrak{X},F) = H^q(C^\bullet(\mathfrak{X},F)) = H^q(\varinjlim_i C^\bullet(\mathfrak{X},F_i)) = \varinjlim_i H^q(C^\bullet(\mathfrak{X},F_i)) = 0\) for \(q > 0\) (V 4.3). Consequently \(\check{H}^q(X,F) = \varinjlim_{\mathfrak{X}} H^q(\mathfrak{X},F) = 0\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.5

Let \(E\) be a coherent topos (2.3), \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) a filtered decreasing family of coherent subobjects of the final object. Let us denote by \(\Phi\) the family of the closed sets of \(E\) (IV 9) contained in the closed complement of one of the \(X_i\). The family \(\Phi\) is a family of supports of \(E\) (V 6.12) and for every integer \(q\), the functors \(H^q_\Phi(E,-)\) and \(\underline{H}^q_\Phi\) (V 6.13) commute with filtered inductive limits.

Let \(Z_i\) be the closed complement of \(X_i\). For every abelian sheaf \(F\) one has an exact sequence (V 6.5): \[ 0 \to H^0_{Z_i}(E,F) \to H^0(E,F) \to H^0(X_i,F) \to H^1_{Z_i}(E,F) \to \dots . \] The functors \(H^q(E,F)\) and \(H^q(X_i,F)\) commute with inductive limits of the argument \(F\) (5.2, 5.3). Consequently \(H^q_{Z_i}(E,F)\) commutes with filtered inductive limits of the argument \(F\), whence the analogous property for the functors \(H^q_\Phi(E,F)\), by passing to the inductive limit over the \(Z_i\) (V 6.13). The assertion concerning the functors \(\underline{H}^q_\Phi\) is deduced from this by localizing and passing to the associated sheaf.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.6

Let \(E\) be a topos ringed by a ring \(A\) and \(q\) an integer. An \(A\)-Module \(G\) is said to be of finite \(q\)-presentation if there exists a family \(X_i\) of objects of \(E\) covering the final object of \(E\), such that for every \(i\) one has an exact sequence of Modules on \(E_{/X_i}\): \[ \text{(5.5.1)} \qquad L_q \to L_{q-1} \to \dots \to L_1 \to L_0 \to G_{/X_i} \to 0 \] where for every \(p\), \(L_p = A^{n_p}_{/X_i}\), \(n_p\) an integer.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.7

Let \(G\) be a sheaf of finite \(q\)-presentation. For every \(i \leqslant q-1\), the functor \(\mathscr{E}xt^i_A(G,-)\) commutes with filtered inductive limits of \(A\)-Modules.

The problem is local on \(E\) (V 6.1). One can therefore suppose, upon localizing to the \(E_{/X_i}\), that one has an exact sequence of type (5.5.1). Let us set \(L_\bullet = L_q \to \dots L_1 \to L_0\). One has \(\mathscr{E}xt^i_A(G,F) \simeq \mathscr{H}^i(\mathscr{H}om_A(L_\bullet,F))\) and the functor \(F \mapsto \mathscr{H}om_A(L_\bullet,F)\) commutes with inductive limits, whence the proposition.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.8

Let \((E,A)\) be a ringed topos, \(G\) a sheaf of \(A\)-Modules of finite \(q\)-presentation, \(X\) an algebraic and coherent object of \(E\). The functors \(F \mapsto \operatorname{Ext}^i_A(X;G,F)\), such that \(\frac{i(i-1)}{2} \leqslant q-1\), commute with filtered inductive limits of the argument \(F\).
Deduced from 5.7 and from 5.3 by the spectral sequence (V 6.1.3).

Let \((E,A)\) be a ringed topos, \(\Phi\) a family of supports of \(E\) (V 6.12), \(G\) an \(A\)-module of finite \(r\)-presentation (5.6), \(X\) an object of \(E\) algebraic and coherent (2.3). By passing to the inductive limit over the closed sets of \(\Phi\) in the last spectral sequences of V 6.9.1 and V 6.9.2 respectively, one obtains two spectral sequences (V 6.13) \[ \text{5.9.1} \qquad \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {}'E_2^{pq} = \varinjlim_{Z \in \Phi} \operatorname{Ext}^p_A(X;G,\underline{H}^q_Z F) \Longrightarrow \operatorname{Ext}^{p+q}_{A,\Phi}(X;G,F) , \\[1.2ex] {}''E_2^{pq} = \varinjlim_{Z \in \Phi} \mathscr{E}xt^p_A(G,\underline{H}^q_Z F) \Longrightarrow \mathscr{E}xt^{p+q}_{A,\Phi}(G,F) . \end{array} \right. \] It results from 5.7 and from 5.8 that one has canonical isomorphisms \[ \text{5.9.2} \qquad \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {}'E_2^{pq} \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^p_A(X;G,\underline{H}^q_\Phi F) , & \frac{p(p-1)}{2} \leqslant r-1 , \\[1.2ex] {}''E_2^{pq} \simeq \mathscr{E}xt^p_A(G,\underline{H}^q_\Phi F) , & p \leqslant r-1 . \end{array} \right. \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.10

One uses the hypotheses and the notations of 5.5. Let \(A\) be a Ring of \(E\) and \(G\) an \(A\)-Module of finite \(q\)-presentation. For every integer \(i\) such that \(\frac{i(i-1)}{2} \leqslant r-1\), the functors \(F \mapsto \operatorname{Ext}^i_{A,\Phi}(E;G,F)\) and \(F \mapsto \mathscr{E}xt^i_{A,\Phi}(G,F)\) (V 6.13) commute with filtered inductive limits.
Deduced from 5.5 and 5.7 by the first spectral sequences of V 6.9.1 and V 6.9.2 respectively.

pages.title: 6. Inductive and projective limits of a fibred category

blocks.html: 6. Inductive and projective limits of a fibred category

We suppose that the reader is familiar with the theory of fibred categories [3]. This section has essentially the aim of fixing the terminology and the notations concerning fibred categories. All the categories considered in this section will belong, unless mention to the contrary, to a fixed universe \(\mathcal{U}\).

Let \(\mathscr{F}\), \(\mathscr{G}\), \(\mathscr{E}\) be three categories, \(\pi : \mathscr{F} \to \mathscr{E}\) and \(\pi': \mathscr{G} \to \mathscr{E}\) two functors. One denotes by \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathscr{E}}(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G})\) the category whose objects are the functors \(u : \mathscr{F} \to \mathscr{G}\) such that the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \mathscr{F} \ar[rr]^-{u} \ar[dr]_-{\pi} & & \mathscr{G} \ar[dl]^-{\pi'} \\ & \mathscr{E} & } \] is commutative, and whose morphisms are the \(\mathscr{E}\)-morphisms of functors, i.e. the morphisms of functors transformed by \(\pi'\) into identity morphisms.

Let \(\xi\) be an object of \(\mathscr{E}\). The objects \(X\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) such that \(\pi(X) = \xi\) are called the objects of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(\xi\). Let \(f : \xi \to \eta\) be a morphism of \(\mathscr{E}\). The morphisms \(m\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) such that \(\pi(m) = f\) are called the morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(f\).
