Let \(f : \xi \to \eta\) be a morphism of \(\mathscr{E}\) and \(X\) an object of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(\xi\), \(Y\) an object of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(\eta\); one denotes by \(\mathrm{Hom}_f(X,Y)\) the set of morphisms from \(X\) to \(Y\) over \(f\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.1
  1. 1)

    A morphism \(m : X \to Y\) of \(\mathscr{F}\) is said to be cartesian if for every morphism \(p : Z \to Y\) over \(\pi(m)\), there exists a unique morphism \(q : Z \to X\) over the identity of \(\pi(X)\) such that \(mq = p\).

  2. 2)

    The category \(\mathscr{F}\) is said to be prefibred by \(\pi\) over \(\mathscr{E}\) if for every morphism \(f : \xi \to \eta\) of \(\mathscr{E}\) every object of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(\eta\) is the target of a cartesian morphism over \(f\).

  3. 3)

    The category \(\mathscr{F}\) is said to be fibred by \(\pi\) over \(\mathscr{E}\) if it is prefibred and if the composite of two composable cartesian morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}\) is a cartesian morphism.

Let \(\xi\) be an object of \(\mathscr{E}\). One calls fibre category of \(\mathscr{F}\) at \(\xi\), and one denotes by \(\mathscr{F}_\xi\), the subcategory of \(\mathscr{F}\) whose objects are the objects of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(\xi\) and whose morphisms are the morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(\mathrm{id}_\xi\). Given two objects \(X\) and \(Y\) of \(\mathscr{F}_\xi\), one denotes by \(\mathrm{Hom}_\xi(X,Y)\) the set of morphisms from \(X\) to \(Y\) in \(\mathscr{F}_\xi\).

Let \(f : \xi \to \eta\) be a morphism of \(\mathscr{E}\). An object \(Y\) over \(\eta\) is the target of a cartesian morphism over \(f\), if and only if the functor defined on the fibre \(\mathscr{F}_\xi\) with values in the sets \[ Z \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_f(Z,Y) \qquad Z \in \mathrm{ob}(\mathscr{F}_\xi) , \] is representable. When the category \(\mathscr{F}\) is prefibred, the functor \[ Y \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_f(\,\cdot\,,Y) \qquad Y \in \mathrm{ob}(\mathscr{F}_\eta) , \] with values in the category of presheaves of sets on \(\mathscr{F}_\xi\), is in fact with values in the category of representable functors on \(\mathscr{F}_\xi\), and thus defines, up to unique isomorphism, a functor \(f^* : \mathscr{F}_\eta \to \mathscr{F}_\xi\), which is called the inverse image functor for \(f\). Suppose that the category \(\mathscr{F}\) is prefibred and let us choose for every morphism \(f\) of \(\mathscr{E}\) a base change functor \(f^*\). The category \(\mathscr{F}\) is then fibred over \(\mathscr{E}\) if and only if for every pair \(f\) and \(g\) of composable morphisms of \(\mathscr{E}\) the composite functor \(f^* g^*\) is an inverse image functor. Let then \[ \text{(6.1.2.1)} \qquad C_{f,g} : f^* g^* \to (gf)^* \] be the canonical isomorphism. The isomorphisms \(C_{f,g}\) satisfy a cocycle condition, arising from the associativity of the composition of morphisms in \(\mathscr{E}\): \[ \text{(6.1.2.2)} \qquad C_{f,hg}(f^* \circ C_{g,h}) = C_{gh,f}(C_{f,g} \circ h^*) \]

Conversely when one is given for every object \(\xi\) of \(\mathscr{E}\) a category \(\mathscr{F}_\xi\), for every morphism \(f : \xi \to \eta\) a functor \(f^* : \mathscr{F}_\eta \to \mathscr{F}_\xi\), and for every pair \((f,g)\) of morphisms of \(\mathscr{E}\) an isomorphism of functors \(C_{f,g} : f^* g^* \to (fg)^*\), such that the \(C_{f,g}\) satisfy the condition (6.1.2.1), one can construct in an essentially unique manner a category \(\mathscr{F}\) fibred over \(\mathscr{E}\) whose fibres "are" the categories \(\mathscr{F}_\xi\) and whose base change functors can be chosen "equal" to the functors given in advance [5].

Let \(\mathscr{F}\) and \(\mathscr{G}\) be two categories over \(\mathscr{E}\). One denotes by \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/\mathscr{E}}(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G}) \] the full subcategory of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathscr{E}}(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G})\) defined by the functors which transform the cartesian morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}\) into cartesian morphisms of \(\mathscr{G}\). The objects of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/\mathscr{E}}(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G})\) are called cartesian functors.

Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two categories and \(S\) a set of morphisms of the category \(C\). One denotes by \(\mathrm{Hom}_{S^{-1}}(C,C')\) the set of functors from \(C\) to \(C'\) which transform the morphisms of \(S\) into isomorphisms.

Let us denote by \((\mathrm{Cat})\) the category whose objects are the categories belonging to the universe and whose morphisms are the functors between these categories (the category \((\mathrm{Cat})\) does not belong to the universe).

Let \(\mathscr{F}\) be a category over \(\mathscr{E}\) and \(S\) the set of cartesian morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}\). The category \(\mathscr{F}\) defines two functors on \((\mathrm{Cat})\) with values in the category of sets belonging to the universe: \[ C \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_{S^{-1}}(\mathscr{F},C) \qquad C \in \mathrm{ob}(\mathrm{Cat}) \] \[ C \mapsto \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/\mathscr{E}}(\mathscr{F},C \times \mathscr{E}) = \{\text{Cartesian functors from } \mathscr{F} \text{ into } C \times \mathscr{E} \} \] (the category \(C \times \mathscr{E}\) is regarded as a category over \(\mathscr{E}\) by the second-projection functor).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.2

The functors \((\mathrm{Cat}) \to (\mathrm{Ens})\): \[ C \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_{S^{-1}}(\mathscr{F},C) \] \[ C \mapsto \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/\mathscr{E}}(\mathscr{F},C \times \mathscr{E}) \] are canonically isomorphic. They are representable.

Proof: To prove the first assertion, it suffices to remark that the cartesian morphisms of \(C \times \mathscr{E}\) are the morphisms of the form \(m \times f\), where \(m\) is an isomorphism of \(C\). To prove the second assertion, it suffices to prove that the functor \(\mathrm{Hom}_{S^{-1}}(\mathscr{F}, \,\cdot\,)\) is representable. This results from [1]. Let us simply indicate the idea of the proof. One formally adjoins to the morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}\) the inverses of the morphisms of \(S\). One considers the free category generated by the objects of \(\mathscr{F}\), the morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}\) and the formal inverses of the morphisms of \(S\) (category of paths). One passes to the quotient by the relations arising from the relations between morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}\) and the relations of the type \[ s^{-1}s = \mathrm{id} , \qquad ss^{-1} = \mathrm{id} \qquad s \in S . \] The category thus obtained is denoted \(\mathscr{F}(S^{-1})\). The category \(\mathscr{F}(S^{-1})\) equipped with the canonical functor \(Q : \mathscr{F} \to \mathscr{F}(S^{-1})\) represents the functor \(\mathrm{Hom}_{S^{-1}}(\mathscr{F}, \,\cdot\,)\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.3

When \(\mathscr{F}\) is fibred over \(\mathscr{E}\) the functor \(\mathrm{Hom}_{S^{-1}}(\mathscr{F}, \,\cdot\,)\) is denoted \(\varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F}\) and is called the inductive limit functor of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(\mathscr{E}^\circ\). The category which represents it is again denoted \(\varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F}\) and is called the inductive limit category of \(\mathscr{F}\) over \(\mathscr{E}^\circ\).
Suppose \(\mathscr{F}\) fibred over \(\mathscr{E}\); let us choose for every morphism \(f\) of \(\mathscr{E}\) a base change functor over \(f\) and let
\[ Q : \mathscr{F} \to \varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F} \]

be the canonical functor. The inclusion functors of the fibres of \(\mathscr{F}\) into \(\mathscr{F}\) composed with the functor \(Q\) furnish, for every object \(\xi\) of \(\mathscr{E}\), a functor \[ u_\xi : \mathscr{F}_\xi \to \varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F} \] and for every morphism \(f : \xi \to \eta\) of \(\mathscr{E}\) a commutative diagram up to canonical isomorphism: \[ \xymatrix{ \mathscr{F}_\eta \ar[dr]^-{u_\eta} \ar[d]_-{f^*} & \\ \mathscr{F}_\xi \ar[r]_-{u_\xi} & \varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F} } \] The category \(\varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F}\) then appears as the inductive limit in the sense of pseudo-functors [5] of the pseudo-functor \(\mathscr{E}^\circ \to \mathrm{Cat}\) which associates with every \(\xi \in\) ob, \(\mathscr{F}_\xi\) and with every \(f : \xi \to \eta\), the functor \(f^* : \mathscr{F}_\eta \to \mathscr{F}_\xi\). One will note however that even when \(\xi \mapsto \mathscr{F}_\xi\) is a genuine functor, the category \(\varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F}\) is not in general the inductive limit in the sense of I 2 of the functor \(\xi \mapsto \mathscr{F}_\xi\) (cf. 6.8).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.4

Let \(\mathscr{F}\) be a fibred category over \(\mathscr{E}\). Suppose that the category \(\mathscr{E}\) has the following properties:

L1) Every diagram \[ \xymatrix@R=1em{ \bullet \ar[dr] & \\ & \bullet \\ \bullet \ar[ur] & } \] fits into a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ & \bullet \ar[dr] & \\ \bullet \ar[ur] \ar[dr] & & \bullet \\ & \bullet \ar[ur] & } \]

L2) For every pair of morphisms \(u,v : \bullet \rightrightarrows \bullet\) such that there exists a morphism \(t\) satisfying the relation \(tu = tv\), there exists a morphism \(w\) satisfying the relation \(uw = vw\).

(Note that if the category \(\mathscr{E}^\circ\) is pseudo-filtered (I 2.7), it has the properties L1) and L2)). The set \(S\) of cartesian morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}\) then has the properties:

Fr1) The set \(S\) is stable under composition. The isomorphisms belong to \(S\).

Fr2) Every diagram \[ \xymatrix@R=1em{ \bullet \ar[dr]^-{s} & \\ & \bullet \\ \bullet \ar[ur] & } \] where \(s\) belongs to \(S\), can be completed into a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ & \bullet \ar[dr]^-{s} & \\ \bullet \ar[ur]^-{t} \ar[dr] & & \bullet \\ & \bullet \ar[ur] & } \] where \(t\) belongs to \(S\).

Fr3) For every pair of morphisms \(u,v : \bullet \rightrightarrows \bullet\) such that there exists a morphism \(s \in S\) satisfying the relation \(su = sv\), there exists a morphism \(t \in S\) such that \(ut = vt\).
Proof. Left to the reader as an exercise.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.5

Let \(\mathscr{F}\) be a category and \(S\) a set of morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}\) having the properties Fr1), Fr2) and Fr3) (6.4). For every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{F}\), denote by \(S(X)\) the category of morphisms of \(S\) with target \(X\). The category \(S(X)\) is cofiltered (I 2.7). The category \(\mathscr{F}(S^{-1})\) (which represents the functor \(\mathrm{Hom}_{S^{-1}}(\mathscr{F}, \,\cdot\,)\)) can then be described as follows:

  1. a)

    The objects of \(\mathscr{F}(S^{-1})\) are the objects of \(\mathscr{F}\).

  2. b)

    Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two objects of \(\mathscr{F}(S^{-1})\). One has \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathscr{F}(S^{-1})}(X,Y) = \varinjlim_{S(X)} \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathscr{F}}(\,\cdot\,,Y) . \]

  3. c)

    Let \(f : X \to Y\) and \(g : Y \to Z\) be two morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}(S^{-1})\). Let \[ \xymatrix{ & \bullet \ar[dl]_-{t} \ar[dr]^-{f'} & \\ X & & Y } \qquad t \in S \] (resp. \[ \xymatrix{ & \bullet \ar[dl]_-{t'} \ar[dr]^-{g'} & \\ Y & & Z } \qquad t' \in S \;) \] be a diagram in \(\mathscr{F}\) whose image is \(f\) (resp. \(g\)). Let \[ \xymatrix{ \bullet \ar[r]^-{f''} \ar[d]_-{t''} & \bullet \ar[d]^-{t'} \\ \bullet \ar[r]_-{f'} & Y } \qquad t'' \in S \] be a commutative diagram whose existence is ensured by Fr2). The image in \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathscr{F}(S^{-1})}(X,Z)\) of the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ & \bullet \ar[dl]_-{tt''} \ar[dr]^-{g'f''} & \\ X & & Z } \] is the composite morphism \(gf\).

Let \[ Q : \mathscr{F} \to \mathscr{F}(S^{-1}) \] be the canonical functor.

  1. d)

    The functor \(Q^* : \widehat{\mathscr{F}(S^{-1})} \to \widehat{\mathscr{F}}\) (\(F \mapsto F \circ Q\) I 5.0) is fully faithful and injective on objects.

  2. e)

    The functor \(Q_! : \widehat{\mathscr{F}} \to \widehat{\mathscr{F}(S^{-1})}\) (left adjoint to the functor \(Q^*\) (I 5.1) is left exact. (The same therefore holds for the functor \(Q\) when in \(\mathscr{F}\) finite projective limits are representable).
Proof. For the proof we refer to [1].

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 6.6

Let \(\mathscr{F}\) be a category and \(S\) a set of morphisms of \(\mathscr{F}\) having the properties Fr1), Fr2) and Fr3). For every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{F}\), one writes \(S(X)\) for the category of morphisms with target \(X\).

  1. a)

    The category \(S(X)\) is cofiltered (I 2)

  2. b)

    For every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{F}\), denote by \(J_S(X)\) the set of sieves of \(X\) that contain a sieve generated by a morphism of \(S\). The \(J_S(X)\) define on \(\mathscr{F}\) a topology \(T\).

  3. c)

    For the topology \(T\), the morphisms of \(S\) are bicovering (II 5.2).

  4. d)

    For every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{F}\), denote by \(J^2(X)\) the category of bicovering morphisms with target \(X\). The category \(S(X)\) is cofinal in \(J^2(X)\) (I 8).

  5. e)

    Let \(G\) be a presheaf of sets on \(\mathscr{F}\). Let \(\underline{a}\) be the associated functor for the topology \(T\). For every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{F}\), one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \underline{a}G(X) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_{S(X)} G(\,\cdot\,) \] A presheaf is a sheaf if and only if it transforms every morphism of \(S\) into an isomorphism.

  6. f)

    One chooses the associated-sheaf functor so that its restriction to \(\mathscr{F}\) is injective on objects. Denote by \(\mathscr{F}_{\to}\) the full subcategory of the category of sheaves of sets on \(\mathscr{F}\) defined by the sheaves associated to the represented presheaves. The category \(\mathscr{F}_{\to}\) is isomorphic to the category \(\mathscr{F}(S^{-1})\) described in 6.5. The objects of \(\mathscr{F}_{\to}\) form a generating family of the topos \(\widetilde{\mathscr{F}}\) of sheaves of sets on \(\mathscr{F}\). The topology induced on \(\mathscr{F}_{\to}\) by the canonical topology of \(\widetilde{\mathscr{F}}\) is the coarse topology (II 1.1.4).

  7. g)

    Let \(Q : \mathscr{F} \to \mathscr{F}_{\to}\) be the canonical functor. The functor \(Q\) is a morphism of the site \(\mathscr{F}_{\to}\) (coarse topology) into the site \(\mathscr{F}\) (topology \(T\) of b)) (IV 5.9) and induces an isomorphism on the corresponding topoi.

  8. h)

    Let \(u : \mathscr{F} \to C\) be a functor. The functor \(u\) is continuous if and only if it transforms the morphisms of \(S\) into isomorphisms (III 1.1)

  9. i)

    Let \(u : \mathscr{F} \to C\) be a functor transforming the morphisms of \(S\) into isomorphisms. The functor \(u\) factors in a unique way as \[ \xymatrix{ \mathscr{F} \ar[rr]^-{u} \ar[dr]_-{Q} & & C \\ & \mathscr{F}_{\to} \ar[ur]_-{v} & } \] (One will use III 1.4).

  10. j)

    Let \(\mathrm{Pro}_S \mathscr{F}\) be the full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Pro}\, \mathscr{F}\) (I 8) defined by the pro-objects whose transition morphisms lie in \(S\). Show that the functor \(Q\) factors as \[ \mathscr{F} \xrightarrow{\ i\ } \mathrm{Pro}_S \mathscr{F} \xrightarrow{\ j\ } \mathscr{F}_{S^{-1}} \] where \(j\) is the restriction to \(\mathrm{Pro}_S \mathscr{F}\) of \(\mathrm{Pro}\, Q\). Show that the functor \(j\) admits a fully faithful left adjoint \[ A : \mathscr{F}_{S^{-1}} \to \mathrm{Pro}_S \mathscr{F} \] Show that for every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{F}\), \(AQ(X)\) is the pro-object \[ Y \to X \in S(X) \mapsto Y . \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.7

Let \(\mathscr{E}\) be a cofiltered category (I 8.7) and \(\mathscr{F} \to \mathscr{E}\) a fibred category (6.1.3).

  1. 1)

    Let \(\xi\) be an object of \(\mathscr{E}\) and \(\mathscr{F}/\xi\) the fibred category over \(\mathscr{E}/\xi\) obtained by the base change \(\mathscr{E}/\xi \to \mathscr{E}\). The canonical functor \(\varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}/\xi} \mathscr{F}/\xi \to \varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F}\) is an equivalence of categories.

  2. 2)

    More generally, let \(\mathscr{E}' \to \mathscr{E}\) be a cofinal functor (I 8). Let \(\mathscr{F}' \to \mathscr{E}'\) be the fibred category deduced from \(\mathscr{F} \to \mathscr{E}\) by the base change \(\mathscr{E}' \to \mathscr{E}\). The canonical functor: \[ \varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}'} \mathscr{F}' \to \varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F} \] is an equivalence of categories.
Proof. Exercise.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 6.8
  1. 1)

    Let \(g : \mathscr{E}^\circ \to \mathrm{Cat}\) be a functor and \(\mathscr{G} \to \mathscr{E}\) the fibred category corresponding to it [5]. Show that there exists a canonical functor \(\varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{G} \to \varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}} g\). Show that this functor is not necessarily an equivalence of categories. (One may take for \(g\) the constant functor whose value is the final object of \(\mathrm{Cat}\) and for \(\mathscr{E}\) the category associated to a group).

  2. 2)

    Suppose that the category \(\mathscr{E}^\circ\) is pseudo-filtered. Show that then the canonical functor \(\varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{G} \to \varinjlim_{\mathscr{E}} g\) is an equivalence of categories.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.9

Let \(\mathscr{F} \to \mathscr{E}\) be a fibred category (6.1). The functor \((\mathrm{Cat}) \to (\mathrm{Ens})\): \[ C \mapsto \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/\mathscr{E}}(C \times \mathscr{E}, \mathscr{F}) \] is representable by the category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/\mathscr{E}}(\mathscr{E}, \mathscr{F})\).

Let \(C\) be a category, \(F : C \times \mathscr{E} \to \mathscr{F}\) a cartesian \(\mathscr{E}\)-functor (6.1.4), \(X\) an object of \(C\). The functor \(\xi \mapsto F((X,\xi))\) is a cartesian functor, denoted \(F'(X)\), from \(\mathscr{E}\) into \(\mathscr{F}\), which depends functorially on \(X\). Whence a map \(F \mapsto F'\) from \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/\mathscr{E}}(C \times \mathscr{E},\mathscr{F})\) into \(\mathrm{Hom}(C,\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/\mathscr{E}}(\mathscr{E},\mathscr{F}))\), functorial in \(C\), which one immediately verifies to be a bijection.

The category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/\mathscr{E}}(\mathscr{E},\mathscr{F})\) is called the category of cartesian sections of the fibred category \(\mathscr{F}\). It is also sometimes called the category projective limit of \(\mathscr{F}\) along \(\mathscr{E}^\circ\). It is then denoted \(\varprojlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F}\) [2].

Let us choose a splitting of the fibred category \(\mathscr{F} \to \mathscr{E}\), i.e. let us choose for every arrow \(f : \xi \to \eta\) of \(\mathscr{E}\) a base-change functor \(f^* : \mathscr{F}_\eta \to \mathscr{F}_\xi\). For every object \(\xi\) of \(\mathscr{E}\), denote by \[ v_\xi : \varprojlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F} \to \mathscr{F}_\xi \] the evaluation functor at \(\xi\). For every morphism \(f : \xi \to \eta\), one has a diagram of functors commutative up to canonical isomorphism: \[ \xymatrix{ \varprojlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F} \ar[r]^-{v_\xi} \ar[dr]_-{v_\eta} & \mathscr{F}_\xi \ar[d]^-{f^*} \\ & \mathscr{F}_\eta } \] The category \(\varprojlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F}\) thus appears as the projective limit in the sense of pseudo-functors of \(\xi \mapsto \mathscr{F}_\xi\). Even when \(\xi \mapsto \mathscr{F}_\xi\) is a genuine functor (i.e. even when the chosen splitting is a cleavage [5]) the categories \(\varprojlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F}\) (6.10) and \(\varprojlim_{\mathscr{E}^*} \mathscr{F}_\xi\) (I 2) are not, in general, equivalent.
7. Fibred topoi and sites
7.1. Fibred topoi

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.1.1

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe. A \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over a category \(I\) is a fibred category over \(I\) (6.1) \[ p : F \to I \] whose fibres are \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi, and whose inverse-image functors(∗) relative to the morphisms \(f : i \to j\) of \(I\) are functors \(f^* : F_j \to F_i\) that are inverse images of morphisms of topoi \(f_\cdot : F_i \to F_j\) (IV 3.1.2).
It amounts to the same to say that a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over a category \(I\) is a fibred category \(p : F \to I\) whose fibres are \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi and whose inverse-image func-
tors are exact and commute with inductive limits (IV 1.6).

Let us choose for every morphism \(f : i \to j\) of \(I\) an inverse-image functor \(f^* : F_j \to F_i\). One then has, for every pair \(i \xrightarrow{f} j \xrightarrow{g} k\) of composable morphisms of \(I\), a canonical isomorphism \(c_{f,g} : f^* g^* \to (gf)^*\) (6.1.2.1), and the \(c_{f,g}\) have the cocycle property 6.1.2.2. Let us choose moreover, for every \(f : i \to j\), a right adjoint functor \(f_* : F_i \to F_j\) to the functor \(f^* : F_j \to F_i\). The functor \(f_* : F_i \to F_j\) is defined up to canonical isomorphism by its property of being right adjoint to \(f^*\). One deduces from this, by the general results on adjoint functors, canonical isomorphisms; \[ \text{(7.1.3.1)} \qquad c'_{g,f} : g_* f_* \to (gf)_* , \] which have a cocycle property analogous to property 6.2.2.2 and which one leaves to the reader to make explicit. Then applying the results of 6.1.3, one obtains a fibred category over \(I^\circ\): \[ \text{(7.1.3.2)} \qquad p' : F' \to I^\circ . \] One easily verifies that the fibred category \(p' : F' \to I^\circ\) does not depend, up to unique \(I^\circ\)-isomorphism, on the various choices used to construct it(∗). The fibre at any object \(i\) of \(I^\circ\) of the fibred category \(p' : F' \to I^\circ\) is canonically isomorphic to the \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(F_i\) and is identified with the latter. The inverse-image functors of the fibred category \(p' : F' \to I^\circ\) are direct-image functors by morphisms of topoi.

Let \(p : F \to I\) be a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos. Let us choose for each \(f : i \to j\) a morphism of topoi (IV 3.1.2) \(f_\cdot : F_i \to F_j\) such that the inverse-image functor \(f^*\) (by \(f_\cdot\)) is the inverse image for the fibred structure (6.1). One then obtains cocycles \(c_{f,g}\) relating these morphisms of topoi (7.1.3.1 and 7.1.3.2). The collection of the morphisms \(f_\cdot\), \(f \in \mathrm{Fl}(I)\), and of the cocycles \(c_{f,g}\) is called a bisplitting of the fibred topos \(F \to I\). The choice of a bisplitting makes it possible to associate to the fibred topos \(F \to I\) a pseudo-functor \(i \mapsto F_i\) from the category \(I\) into the 2-category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi. One can then associate to it, in an essentially unique manner (cf. [5]), a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(F \to I\) equipped with a bisplitting such that the corresponding pseudo-functor is canonically isomorphic to \(i \mapsto F_i\). In practice one will most often denote a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(F \to I\) by the notation \((F_i)_{i \in I}\), implicitly assuming that a bisplitting has been chosen. One will note, however, that the constructions one carries out on fibred topoi (such as the associated total topos (7.4), the projective limit (8.1)) depend only on the fibred topoi and not on the bisplittings that may have been chosen.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.1.5

Let \(p : F \to I\) and \(q : G \to I\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi fibred over \(I\). A morphism \(m\) of fibred topoi from \((F,p)\) to \((G,q)\) consists of the datum of an \(I\)-functor \(m^* : G \to F\) (6.1.4) together with the datum, for every object \(i\) of \(I\), of a right adjoint \(m_{i*} : F_i \to G_i\) to the functor \(m_i^* : G_i \to F_i\) obtained by restricting to the fibres at \(i\) the functor \(m^*\). This datum must moreover be subject to the following condition: For every object \(i\) of \(I\) the pair of adjoint functors \((m_i^*, m_{i*})\) is a morphism of the topos \(F_i\) into the topos \(G_i\).

Let \(m : (F,p) \to (G,q)\) be a morphism of \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi fibred over \(I\) and \(p' : F' \to I^\circ\), \(q' : G' \to I^\circ\) the fibred categories associated by the procedure 7.1.3 to the fibred topoi \((F,p)\) and \((G,q)\) respectively. Let us choose bisplittings of \(F\) and \(G\) (7.1.4), denoted in both cases \((f:i \to j) \mapsto f_\cdot : (f^*,f_*)\), from \(F_i\) into \(F_j\) and from \(G_i\) into \(G_j\) respectively. Since \(f^* : G \to F\) is an \(I\)-functor, one has, for every morphism \(f : i \to j\), a morphism of functors (transition morphism) \[ \text{(7.1.6.1)} \qquad b_f : f^* m_j^* \to m_i^* f^* , \] and for every pair \(i \xrightarrow{f} j \xrightarrow{g} k\) of composable morphisms, one has \[ \text{(7.1.6.2)} \qquad m_i^*(c_{f,g})\, b_f\, f^*(b_g) = b_{gf}\, c_{f,g} . \] Passing to the adjoint functors, one obtains morphisms \[ \text{(7.1.6.3)} \qquad b'_f : f_* m_{i*} \to m_{j*} f_* , \] which satisfy relations analogous to the relations (7.1.6.2). Since the functors \(f_*\) are inverse-image functors of the fibred categories \((F',p')\) and \((G',q')\) (7.1.3), one can construct an \(I^\circ\)-functor: \[ \text{(7.1.6.4)} \qquad m_* : F' \to G' , \] whose restrictions to the fibres are the functors \(m_{i*}\) and whose transition isomorphisms are the \(b'_f\). One verifies with a little patience that the functor \(m_*\) thus constructed does not depend on the choice of the morphisms of topoi \(f_\cdot\).(∗)

One denotes by \(\mathrm{Homtop}_I(F,G)\) the set of morphisms of fibred topoi between the fibred topos \((F,p)\) and the fibred topos \((G,q)\). The set \(\mathrm{Homtop}_I(F,G)\) is the set of objects of a category denoted \(\underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(F,G)\): If \(m\) and \(n\) are two morphisms of fibred topoi, a morphism from \(m\) to \(n\) is an \(I\)-morphism from the functor \(n^*\) into the functor \(m^*\). One moreover deduces from this, by adjunction, an \(I^\circ\)-morphism from the functor \(m_*\) into the functor \(n_*\) (7.1.6). One thus has, in the end, two functors: \[ \text{(7.1.7.1)} \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(F,G) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_I(G,F)^\circ \] \[ \text{(7.1.7.2)} \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(F,G) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(F',G') \] which associate to every morphism \((m^*, (m_{i*})_{i \in \mathrm{Ob}\,I})\), on the one hand the functor \(m^* \in\) \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_I(G,F)\), and on the other hand the functor \(m_* \in \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(F',G')\) obtained by gluing the \(m_{i*}\) as in (7.1.6). The functor \(m^* : G \to F\) (7.1.7.1) is called the inverse-image functor by the morphism of fibred topoi \(m : F \to G\); the functor \(m_* : F' \to G'\) (7.1.7.2) is called the direct-image functor by the morphism of fibred topoi \(m : F \to G\). It follows immediately from the definitions that the functors \(m \mapsto m^*\) and \(m \mapsto m_*\) are fully faithful and that their essential images are, on the one hand, the set of \(I\)-functors from \(G\) into \(F\) which, fibre by fibre, are exact and commute with inductive limits and, on the other hand, the set of \(I^\circ\)-functors from \(F'\) into \(G'\) which, fibre by fibre, admit an exact left adjoint functor. This justifies the abuses of language consisting in defining a morphism of fibred topoi by its direct image or its inverse image. In fact such a morphism of fibred topoi is then defined only up to unique isomorphism.

One denotes by \(\underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/I}(F,G)\) the full subcategory of \(\underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(F,G)\) generated by the morphisms \(m\) such that \(m_*\) (or, what is equivalent, \(m^*\)) is a cartesian functor (6.1.4). Such morphisms are called cartesian morphisms. One thus has fully faithful functors, induced by 7.1.7.1 and 7.1.7.2 \[ \text{(7.1.7.3)} \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/I}(F,G) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(G,F)^\circ \] \[ \text{(7.1.7.4)} \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/I}(F,G) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I^\circ}(F',G') . \]

Let \(p : F \to I\), \(q : G \to I\), \(r : H \to I\) be three \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi fibred over \(I\) and \(m : F \to G\), \(n : G \to H\) two morphisms of fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi. One defines as in IV 3.3 the composite of the two morphisms \(m\) and \(n\), which one denotes \(nm : F \to H\), and if \(\mathcal{V}\) is a universe such that \(\mathcal{U} \in \mathcal{V}\), one defines a category \((\mathcal{V}\text{-}\mathcal{U}\text{-}\mathrm{Top}_{/I})\) whose objects are the \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi fibred over \(I\) with fibre categories elements of \(\mathcal{V}\), and whose morphisms are the morphisms of \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi fibred over \(I\). Moreover, as in IV 3.3.2, the composition map \[ \mathrm{Homtop}_{/I}(F,G) \times \mathrm{Homtop}_{/I}(G,H) \to \mathrm{Homtop}_{/I}(F,H) \] is the map induced on the objects by a "functor of composition of morphisms": \[ \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{/I}(F,G) \times \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{/I}(G,H) \to \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{/I}(F,H) \] and the considerations of IV 3.3 and IV 3.4 extend without change to the case of fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi. The reader will moreover have noticed that when \(I\) is a punctual category (one object, one identity morphism) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over \(I\) "is nothing other than" a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos, and a morphism of fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi "is nothing other than" a morphism of \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi, and the preceding constructions reduce to those of IV 3.

Let \(p : F \to I\) be a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos and \(\varphi : J \to I\) a functor. The fibred category \(p_J : F_J \to J\) deduced from \((F,p)\) by the base change \(\varphi : J \to I\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over \(J\). Let \(p' : F' \to I^\circ\) and \((p_J)' : (F_J)' \to J^\circ\) be the fibred categories deduced respectively from \((F,p)\) and \((F_J,p_J)\) by the construction of 7.1.3. One immediately verifies that the category \(((F_J)', (p_J)')\) is canonically isomorphic to the category \((p')_J : (F')_J \to J^\circ\) deduced from \(p' : F' \to I^\circ\) by the base change \(\varphi^\circ : J^\circ \to I^\circ\). These two fibred categories over \(J^\circ\) will henceforth be identified and denoted \(p'_J : F'_J \to J^\circ\). The operation of base change is functorial, and even 2-functorial, with respect to its argument: for every pair \(p : F \to I\) and \(G \to I\) of \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi fibred over \(I\), one has two commutative diagrams of categories and functors: \[ \text{(7.1.9.1)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(F,G) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_I(G,F)^\circ \ar[d] \\ \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_J(F_J,G_J) \ar[r] & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_J(G_J,F_J)^\circ } \] \[ \text{(7.1.9.2)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(F,G) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(F',G') \ar[d] \\ \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_J(F_J,G_J) \ar[r] & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{J^\circ}(F'_{J^\circ},G'_{J^\circ}) } \] where the vertical functors are base-change functors and where the horizontal functors are respectively, in (7.1.9.1), the functors "morphism \(\mapsto\) inverse image" (7.1.7.1), and in (7.1.9.2) the functors "morphism \(\mapsto\) direct image" (7.1.7.2).
7.2. Fibred sites

A \(\mathcal{U}\)-site fibred \(C\) over a category \(I\) is a fibred category \(p : C \to I\) whose fibres are equipped with topologies making them \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites (IV 3.0.2) such that for every morphism \(f : i \to j\) of \(I\), the inverse-image functor \(f^* : C_j \to C_i\) is a morphism of the site \(C_i\) into the site \(C_j\) (IV 4.9.1).

Let \(p : C \to I\) and \(q : D \to I\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites fibred over \(I\). A morphism of fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites from \(C\) to \(D\) is an \(I\)-functor (6.0.) \(m : D \to C\) such that for every object \(i\) of \(I\), the functor \(m_i : D_i \to C_i\) is a morphism of the site \(C_i\) into the site \(D_i\). One denotes by \(\mathrm{Morsite}_I(C,D)\) the set of morphisms of fibred sites from \(C\) to \(D\). A continuous functor from the fibred site \(D\) into the fibred site \(C\) is an \(I\)-functor from \(D\) into \(C\) that induces on the fibres continuous functors (III 1). One denotes by \(\mathrm{Cont}_I(D,C)\) the set of continuous functors from the fibred site \(D\) into the fibred site \(C\). One denotes by \(\underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_I(C,D)\) the full subcategory of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_I(D,C)^\circ\) defined by the set of objects \(\mathrm{Morsite}_I(C,D) \subset \mathrm{Hom}_I(D,C)\). One denotes likewise by \(\underline{\mathrm{Cont}}_I(D,C)\) the full subcategory of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_I(D,C)\) defined by the subset of objects \(\mathrm{Cont}_I(D,C) \subset \mathrm{Hom}_I(D,C)\). One thus has two fully faithful functors, injective on objects, \[ \text{(7.2.2.1)} \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_I(C,D) \to \underline{\mathrm{Cont}}_I(D,C)^\circ \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_I(D,C)^\circ \] One defines, as in 7.1.7, the cartesian morphisms of the fibred site \(C\) into the fibred site \(D\). One has a diagram of full subcategories \[ \text{(7.2.2.2)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/I}(C,D) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/I}(D,C)^\circ \ar[d] \\ \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_I(C,D) \ar[r] & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_I(D,C)^\circ } \]

Morphisms of fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites compose. This makes it possible to define the category \((\mathcal{V}\text{-}\mathcal{U}\text{-}\mathrm{Site}/I)\) whose objects are the \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites whose fibres belong to a universe \(\mathcal{V}\) (of which \(\mathcal{U}\) is an element). The category \(\mathcal{V}\text{-}\mathcal{U}\)-site is moreover equipped with a structure of 2-category, and in particular the composition of morphisms of fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites is functorial with respect to the morphisms between morphisms. For every functor \(\varphi : J \to I\) and every fibred site \(p : C \to I\), the category \(p_J : C_J \to J\) deduced from \((C,p)\) by the base change \(\varphi : J \to I\), is canonically equipped with a structure of \(\mathcal{U}\)-site fibred over \(J\). The operation of base change is 2-functorial.

Let \(p : C \to I\) be a fibred category whose fibres are equipped with topologies making them \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites. Suppose that projective limits are representable in the fibre categories. For \(p : C \to I\) to be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site fibred, it suffices that the inverse-image functors be left exact and transform covering families into covering families, and this condition is also sufficient when the topologies of the fibres are coarser than the canonical topology (IV 4.9.2). All the fibred sites used in this seminar will be of the type described above. Likewise, let \(p : C \to I\) and \(q : D \to I\) be two fibred sites such that finite projective limits in the fibre categories are representable. A cartesian functor \(m : D \to C\) that induces on the fibre categories left exact functors and that transforms the covering families of the fibre categories into covering families is a morphism of fibred sites from \(C\) to \(D\), the converse being true if the fibre topologies of \(C\) are coarser than the canonical topology (IV 4.9.2). All the morphisms of fibred sites used in this seminar will be of the type described above.

A fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(p : F \to I\) is a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-site when one equips the fibres with the canonical topology, which we shall always do henceforth. Let \(m : F \to G\) be a morphism of fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi. The inverse-image functor \(m^* : G \to F\) (7.1.7) is a morphism of the fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-site \(F\) into the fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-site \(G\). One thus has a functor \((\mathcal{V}\text{-}\mathcal{U}\text{-}\mathrm{Top}_{/I}) \to (\mathcal{V}\text{-}\mathcal{U}\text{-}\mathrm{Site}_{/I})\), a functor which is not faithful in general. But this functor in fact extends naturally to a 2-functor which induces, for two fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi \(F\) and \(G\) over \(I\), a functor: \[ \text{(7.2.5.1)} \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(F,G) \to \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_I(F,G) \] which is an equivalence of categories, as follows immediately from the definitions. Moreover, the functor (7.2.5.1) composed with the canonical inclusion \(\underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_I(F,G) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_I(G,F)^\circ\) is nothing other than the functor (7.1.7.1) which, to a morphism of fibred topoi, associates its inverse image.

Let \(p : C \to I\) be a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-site. Let us choose for every morphism \(f : i \to j\) of \(I\) a base-change functor \(f^* : C_j \to C_i\). Passing to the categories of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaves, the functor \(f^*\) extends to a functor \(\mathrm{Top}(f)^* : \widetilde{C}_j \to \widetilde{C}_i\), where \(\mathrm{Top}(f) : \widetilde{C}_i \to \widetilde{C}_j\) is a morphism of topoi (IV 4.9.1.1), making the following diagram commutative up to isomorphism: \[ \text{(7.2.6.1)} \qquad \xymatrix{ C_j \ar[r]^-{f^*} \ar[d]_-{\varepsilon_j} & C_i \ar[d]^-{\varepsilon_i} \\ \widetilde{C}_j \ar[r]_-{\mathrm{Top}(f)^*} & \widetilde{C}_i } \] Let

be the canonical isomorphisms (6.1.2.1) and \[ \text{(7.2.6.3)} \qquad b_f : \mathrm{Top}(f)^* \varepsilon_j \to \varepsilon_i f^* \] the isomorphisms that "make commutative" the diagrams (7.2.6.1). Using the fact that the functors \(\mathrm{Top}(f)^*\) commute with inductive limits, one immediately verifies that for every pair of composable morphisms \(i \xrightarrow{f} j \xrightarrow{g} k\), there exists one and only one isomorphism: \[ \text{(7.2.6.4)} \qquad \mathrm{Top}(c_{f,g}) : \mathrm{Top}(f)^* \mathrm{Top}(g)^* \to \mathrm{Top}(gf)^* \] such that one has \[ \text{(7.2.6.5)} \qquad \varepsilon_i(c_{f,g})\, b_f\, \mathrm{Top}(f)^*(b_g) = b_{gf}\, \mathrm{Top}(c_{f,g}) . \] Moreover, the isomorphisms (7.2.6.4) automatically satisfy the cocycle condition of 6.2.2.2. One can therefore construct a fibred category \[ \text{(7.2.6.6)} \qquad \widetilde{p} : C^{\sim/I} \to I \] whose fibres are canonically isomorphic to the \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi \(\widetilde{C}_i\) (6.1.3), and a cartesian functor \[ \text{(7.2.6.7)} \qquad \varepsilon_{C/I} : C \to C^{\sim/I} \] which induces on the fibres the functors \(\varepsilon_i : C_i \to \widetilde{C}_i\). It follows immediately from the definitions that \(\widetilde{p} : C^{\sim/I} \to I\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over \(I\), that \(\varepsilon_{C/I}\) is a cartesian morphism of fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites from \(C^{\sim/I}\) to \(C\), and that the fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(C^{\sim/I} \to I\) and the cartesian functor \(\varepsilon_{C/I}\) do not depend, up to canonical isomorphism, on the various choices used to construct them (choice of the base-change functors \(f^*\) and choice of the extensions \(\mathrm{Top}(f)^*\)). The fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(C^{\sim/I}\) is called the fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos associated to the fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-site.
One verifies that the formation of the fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos associated to a fibred site "commutes" with the operations of change of base category.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.2.7

Let \(E\) be a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos over \(I\) and \(C\) a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-site over \(I\). The functor \(m \mapsto m^* \varepsilon_{C/I}\), associating to every morphism of fibred topoi \(m : E \to C^{\sim/I}\) the composite with \(\varepsilon_{C/I}\) of the associated inverse-image functor \(m^* : C^{\sim/I} \to E\), induces an equivalence of categories preserving cartesian objects \[ \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(E,C^{\sim/I}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_I(E,C) . \] When finite projective limits are representable in the fibre categories of \(C\), the corresponding fully faithful functor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(E,C^{\sim/I}) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_I(C,E)^\circ \] has as essential image the set of \(I\)-functors \(g : C \to E\) that are left exact fibre by fibre and that transform the covering families of the fibre categories into epimorphic families of the corresponding fibre categories.
This proposition merely generalizes to the fibred context proposition IV 4.9.4, and the proof given in IV 4.9.4 generalizes immediately.
7.3. Example

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 7.3.1 (the fibred topos of morphisms of a topos)

Let \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos, \(\mathrm{Fl}(E)\) the category of morphisms of \(E\) and \(p : \mathrm{Fl}(E) \to E\) the functor that associates to a morphism its target. The category \((\mathrm{Fl}(E),p)\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over \(E\). (7.1.1 and IV 5.1). The fibre at any object \(X\) of \(E\) is the topos \(E_{/X}\). The inverse-image functor \(f^* : E_{/Y} \to E_{/X}\) by a morphism \(f : X \to Y\) is the fibre-product functor. To any functor \(\varphi : I \to E\), one can therefore associate the \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over \(I\) \[ \text{(7.3.1.1)} \qquad p_I : \mathrm{Fl}(E)_I \to I , \] obtained by the base change \(\varphi : I \to E\), whose fibre at any object \(i\) of \(I\) is \(E_{/\varphi(i)}\) (7.1.9). If \(\mathcal{V}\) is a universe of which \(E\) is an element, one has, with the notations of 7.1.8, a map \[ \text{(7.3.1.2)} \qquad \mathrm{Hom}(I,E) \to \mathrm{ob}(\mathcal{V}\text{-}\mathcal{U}\text{-}\mathrm{top}_{/I}) , \] which associates to every functor \(\varphi \in \mathrm{Hom}(I,E)\) the \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over \(I\) deduced from \((\mathrm{Fl}(E),p)\) by the base change \(\varphi : I \to E\). Let \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) be two functors from \(I\) into \(E\) and \(m : \varphi_1 \to \varphi_2\) a morphism of functors. Denote by \(p_1 : \mathrm{Fl}(E)_1 \to I\) and \(p_2 : \mathrm{Fl}(E)_2 \to I\) the \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi fibred over \(I\) deduced from \(p : \mathrm{Fl}(E) \to E\) by the base changes \(\varphi_1 : I \to E\) and \(\varphi_2 : I \to E\) respectively. Let us choose, for every object \(i\) of \(I\), a morphism of topoi (IV 5.5.2) \[ \text{(7.3.1.3)} \qquad \mathrm{loc}(m(i)) : E_{/\varphi_1(i)} \to E_{/\varphi_2(i)} \] One then easily verifies that there exists one and only one(∗) cartesian morphism of topoi fibred over \(I\): \[ \text{(7.3.1.4)} \qquad \mathrm{loc}(m) : \mathrm{Fl}(E)_1 \to \mathrm{Fl}(E)_2 , \] which induces on the fibred topoi the morphisms \(\mathrm{loc}(m(i))\). The morphism \(\mathrm{loc}(m) : \mathrm{Fl}(E)_1 \to \mathrm{Fl}(E)_2\) is determined up to canonical isomorphism by the morphism of functors \(m : \varphi_1 \to \varphi_2\). If \(n : \varphi_2 \to \varphi_3\) is a morphism of functors, one has an isomorphism \[ \text{(7.3.1.5)} \qquad c(m,n) : \mathrm{loc}(n)\mathrm{loc}(m) \simeq \mathrm{loc}(nm) , \] and the isomorphisms \(c(m,n)\) have a cocycle property analogous to 6.1.2.2.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 7.3.2 (The fibred site of morphisms of a site)

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site in which fibre products are representable, \(\mathrm{Fl}(C)\) the category of morphisms of \(C\) and \(p : \mathrm{Fl}(C) \to C\) the functor that associates to a morphism its target. The fibred category \((\mathrm{Fl}(C),p)\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site fibred over \(C\) when one equips the fibre categories with the induced topologies (II 5.2). Let \(\varepsilon_C : C \to \widetilde{C}\) be the canonical functor from \(C\) into the category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaves on \(C\). Denoting by \(\mathrm{Fl}(\varepsilon_C)\) the natural extension of the latter functor to the categories of morphisms, one has a commutative diagram of categories and functors: \[ \text{(7.3.2.1)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \mathrm{Fl}(C) \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{Fl}(\varepsilon_C)} \ar[d]_-{p} & \mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C}) \ar[d]^-{p} \\ C \ar[r]_-{\varepsilon_C} & \widetilde{C} } \] whence a cartesian functor between fibred categories over \(C\): \[ \text{(7.3.2.2)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \mathrm{Fl}(C) \ar[rr] \ar[dr]_-{p} & & \mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_C \ar[dl]^-{p_{/C}} \\ & C & } \] where \(p_{/C} : \mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_C \to C\) is deduced from \(\mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C}) \to \widetilde{C}\) by the base change \(\varepsilon_C : C \to \widetilde{C}\). The functor \(\mathrm{Fl}(C) \to \mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_C\) of 7.3.2.2 is a morphism of the fibred site \(\mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_C\) into the fibred site \(\mathrm{Fl}(C)\) (7.2.2), whence by 7.2.7 a morphism of topoi fibred over \(C\): \[ \text{(7.3.2.3)} \qquad \mathrm{can} : \mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_C \to \mathrm{Fl}(C)^{\sim/C} , \] where \(\mathrm{Fl}(C)^{\sim/C}\) is the fibred topos over \(C\) associated to the fibred site \(\mathrm{Fl}(C) \to C\) (7.2.6). It follows from the definition of the associated fibred topos (7.2.6) and from II 5.5 that the morphism \(\mathrm{can}\) of 7.3.2.3 is a \(C\)-equivalence of \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi fibred over \(C\), i.e. there exists a morphism \(\theta : \mathrm{Fl}(C)^{\sim/C} \to \mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_C\) of \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi fibred over \(C\) such that the composites \(\theta \circ \mathrm{can}\) and \(\mathrm{can} \circ \theta\) are \(C\)-isomorphic to the identity.

Let \(\varphi : I \to C\) be a functor. One deduces from it by base change a fibred site over \(I\): \[ \text{(7.3.2.4)} \qquad p_I : \mathrm{Fl}(C)_I \to I \] and since the formation of the associated fibred topos commutes with base change (7.2.6), one has an \(I\)-equivalence of fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi \[ \text{(7.3.2.5)} \qquad \mathrm{can}_I : \mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_I \to \mathrm{Fl}(C)^{\sim/I} \] where \(\mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_I \to I\) is the fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos obtained by the base change \(\varepsilon_C \circ \varphi : I \to \widetilde{C}\).

Finally, let \(\varphi_1 : I \to C\) and \(\varphi_2 : I \to C\) be two functors and \(m : \varphi_1 \to \varphi_2\) a morphism of functors. Denote by \(\mathrm{Fl}(C)_1\) and \(\mathrm{Fl}(C)_2\) the fibred sites over \(I\) deduced from \(p : \mathrm{Fl}(C) \to C\) by the base changes \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) respectively. One constructs, as in 7.3.1, a morphism of fibred sites over \(I\): \[ \text{(7.3.2.6)} \qquad \mathrm{loc}(m) : \mathrm{Fl}(C)_1 \to \mathrm{Fl}(C)_2 . \] Denote by \(\mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_1 \to I\) and \(\mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_2 \to I\) the \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi fibred over \(I\) obtained by the base changes \(\varepsilon_C \circ \varphi_1\) and \(\varepsilon_C \circ \varphi_2\) respectively. One has a diagram commutative up to isomorphism of morphisms over \(I\): \[ \text{(7.3.2.7)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_1 \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{loc}(\varepsilon_C * m)} \ar[d] & \mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{C})_2 \ar[d] \\ \mathrm{Fl}(C)_1 \ar[r]_-{\mathrm{loc}(m)} & \mathrm{Fl}(C)_2 } \] where the vertical morphisms are deduced by base change from the morphisms of 7.3.2.2.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 7.3.3 (Small and big fibred sites)

This exercise is a continuation of exercise IV 4.10.6, whose hypotheses and notations we use. One denotes by \(\underline{M}\) the full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Fl}(S)\) defined by the morphisms of \(\underline{M}\), and \(p : \underline{M} \to S\) the functor that associates to a morphism its target.

  1. 6°)

    Show that \((\underline{M},p)\) is a fibred site over \(S\) and that, when in \(S\) fibre products are representable, the inclusion functor \(\underline{M} \to \mathrm{Fl}(S)\) is a cartesian morphism of the fibred site \(\mathrm{Fl}(S) \to S\) into the fibred site \(\underline{M} \to S\).

  2. 7°)

    Let \(\underline{M}^{\sim/S} \to S\) be the fibred topos associated to \(\underline{M} \to S\). Show that one has, with the notations of 7.3.2, a canonical morphism \(g : \mathrm{Fl}(\widetilde{S})_{/S} \to \underline{M}^{\sim/S}\) of topoi fibred over \(S\) which induces on each fibre at \(X \in \mathrm{ob}(S)\) the morphism \((\mathrm{Prol}_X,\mathrm{Res}_X)\) (IV 4.10.6 4°)). Show that, although for every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}(S)\) the morphism \(g_X : \widetilde{S}_{/X} \to S(X)^\sim\) admits a section (loc. cit.), the morphism \(g\) does not admit a section in general.
7.4. The total topology of a fibred topos or site

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.4.1

Let \(p : C \to I\) be a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and for every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\), denote by \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to C\) the inclusion functor of the fibre category \(C_i\) into \(C\). One calls total topology on \(C\) the coarsest topology on \(C\) that makes continuous the functors \(\alpha_{i!}\) for \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\) (III 3.6). One calls total site the category \(C\) equipped with the total topology.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.4.2

Let \(p : C \to I\) be a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(T\) the total topology on \(C\) and for every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\), \(T_i\) the topology of the fibre \(C_i\).

  1. 1)

    Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\) over an object \(i\) of \(I\). A family \((X_\beta \to X)_{\beta \in B}\) is covering for \(T\) if and only if it is refined by a covering family for \(T_i\) \((Y_\gamma \to X)_{\gamma \in \Gamma}\) of \(C_i\).

  2. 2)

    The topology \(T\) induces on the categories \(C_i\) the topologies \(T_i\).

  3. 3)

    For every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\), the functor \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to C\) is cocontinuous.

Property 3) follows from 1) and from III 2.1. Let us prove 1). Let, for every object \(X\) of \(C\), \(J(X)\) be the set of sieves of \(C/X\) described in 1). One verifies that the \(J(X)\) have the properties T 1), T 2) and T 3) of II 1.1, and that they consequently define a topology \(T'\) on \(C\). The topology \(T'\) is the coarsest of the topologies on \(C\) for which the covering families for the topologies \(T_i\) are covering. The topology \(T'\) is therefore coarser than \(T\) (III 1.6). To show that \(T' = T\), it therefore suffices to show that for every object \(i\) of \(I\), the functor \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to C\) is continuous when one equips \(C\) with the topology \(T'\); or again, it suffices to show that the topology induced by \(T'\) on the category \(C_i\) is the topology \(T_i\), which will demonstrate at the same time property 2). Let \(T'_i\) be the topology on \(C_i\) induced by \(T'\), and \(u : R \hookrightarrow X\) a covering sieve for \(T'_i\). By III 3.2 the morphism \(\alpha_{i!}(u) : \alpha_{i!}(R) \to \alpha_{i!}(X)\) is bicovering and in particular covering, which amounts to saying, by the definition of \(T'\), that the sieve \(R \hookrightarrow X\) is covering for \(T_i\). The topology \(T'_i\) is therefore coarser than \(T_i\), and to demonstrate that \(T'_i\) is finer than \(T_i\), it suffices, by the definition of the induced topology (III 3.1), to show that the functor \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to C\) is continuous when one equips the categories \(C_i\) and \(C\) with the topologies \(T_i\) and \(T'\) respectively. In summary, to demonstrate properties 1) and 2), it suffices, via III 1.2 and 1.5, to demonstrate the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.4.2.2

With the hypotheses and notations of 7.4.2 and 7.4.2.1, let \(X\) be an object of \(C\) over \(i\) and \(R \xrightarrow{u} X\) a morphism of \(\widehat{C}_i\). The following properties are equivalent:

  1. i)

    The morphism \(R \to X\) is bicovering for \(T_i\).

  2. ii)

    The morphism \(\alpha_{i!}(u) : \alpha_{i!}(R) \to \alpha_{i!}(X)\) is bicovering for \(T'\).

i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii): It is clear that if \(R \xrightarrow{u} X\) is bicovering for \(T_i\), the morphism \(\alpha_{i!}(u)\) is covering for \(T'\). It remains to show that it is bicovering (II 5.2). Let \(Y\) be an object of \(C\) over an object \(j\) of \(I\), and let \(m\) and \(n\), \(n : Y \rightrightarrows \alpha_{i!}(R)\) be two morphisms of \(\widehat{C}\) such that \(\alpha_{i!}(u)m = \alpha_{i!}(u)n\), and set \(f = p(\alpha_{i!}(u)m)\). Since the functor \(\alpha_{i!}\) commutes with inductive limits (I 5.4.3)), we have (I 3.4): \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(Y,\alpha_{i!}(R)) \simeq \varinjlim_{C_i/R} \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(Y, \alpha_{i!}(\,\cdot\,)) . \] Since for every object \(Z\) of \(C_i\) we have, with the notation of 6.1.1: \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(Y,Z) \simeq \coprod_{w \in \mathrm{Hom}(j,i)} \mathrm{Hom}_w(Y,Z) , \] we deduce \[ \varinjlim_{C_i/R} \mathrm{Hom}(Y,\alpha_{i!}(\,\cdot\,)) \simeq \coprod_{w \in \mathrm{Hom}(j,i)} \varinjlim_{C_i/R} \mathrm{Hom}_w(Y,\alpha_{i!}(\,\cdot\,)) . \] But for every \(w \in \mathrm{Hom}(j,i)\), we have an inverse image functor \(w^* : C_i \to C_j\), and we have \(\mathrm{Hom}_w(Y,\alpha_{i!}(\,\cdot\,)) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}_{C_j}(Y,w^*(\,\cdot\,))\). Hence, denoting again by \(w^* : \widehat{C}_i \to \widehat{C}_j\) the extension of \(w^*\) to presheaves (which, according to I 5.4, ought to be denoted \((w^*)_!\)) and observing that the functor \(w^* : \widehat{C}_i \to \widehat{C}_j\) commutes with inductive limits (I 5.4.3)), we obtain an isomorphism: \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(Y,\alpha_{i!}(R)) = \coprod_{w \in \mathrm{Hom}(j,i)} \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}_j}(Y,w^*(R)) . \] In this isomorphism, the morphisms \(m\) and \(n : Y \rightrightarrows \alpha_{i!}(R)\) correspond to two morphisms \(m'\) and \(n' : Y \rightrightarrows f^*(R)\) such that \(f^*(u)m' = f^*(u)n'\). Since the inverse image functor is a morphism of topoi, it is in particular continuous, and consequently \(f^*(u)\) is bicovering (III 3.2). There therefore exists a covering family of \(C_j\) \((Y_\delta \xrightarrow{v_\delta} Y)_\delta\) such that for every \(\delta\) we have \(m' v_\delta = n' v_\delta\). We deduce that \(m v_\delta = n v_\delta\) for every \(\delta\), and consequently that \(\alpha_{i!}(u)\) is bicovering for \(T'\).

ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i): Suppose that \(\alpha_{i!}(R) \xrightarrow{\alpha_{i!}(u)} \alpha_{i!}(X)\) is bicovering. The functor \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to C\) is cocontinuous (III 2.1). Consequently \(\alpha_i^* \alpha_{i!}(u)\) is bicovering (III 2.3.2) and (II 5.3 ii)). The functor \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to C\) possesses property (PPF) of I 5.14. Consequently we have a cartesian diagram in \(\widehat{C}_i\) (I 5.14 3)): \[ \xymatrix{ R \ar[r] \ar[d]_-{u} & \alpha_i^* \alpha_{i!}(R) \ar[d]^-{\alpha_i^* \alpha_{i!}(u)} \\ X \ar[r] & \alpha_i^* \alpha_{i!}(X) } \] Consequently \(u\) is bicovering (II 5.2).

1. 1)

    Proposition 7.4.2 can be stated and proved in a somewhat more general framework than that of fibred sites, but apparently with no interest: instead of a fibred site \(p : C \to I\), one considers a fibred category \(p : C \to I\) whose fibres are equipped with topologies and whose inverse image functors are continuous for these topologies (whereas in the case of fibred sites one further requires that these inverse image functors be morphisms of sites (IV 4.9)).

  2. 2)

    One can prove that the total topology of a fibred site is the finest topology making the functors \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to C\) cocontinuous (III 2).

  3. 3)

    Let \(p : C \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred site over a category equivalent to a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category. Then the total site \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site (II 3.0.2). Indeed, if for every object \(i\) of \(I\) \((X_\beta)_{\beta \in B_i}\) is a small topologically generating family of \(C_i\), the family \((X_\beta)_{\beta \in \coprod B_i}\) is topologically generating for \(C\) and is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small. We call Total topos, and denote by \(\mathrm{Top}(C)\), the topos of sheaves on the total site.

  4. 4)

    Let \(p : C \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred site on a small category. Since the functor \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to C\) is cocontinuous, it gives rise to a morphism of topoi \(\alpha_i = (\alpha_i^*, \alpha_{i*})\) from \(\widehat{C}_i\) to \(\mathrm{Top}(C)\) (IV 4.7). Since moreover the functor \(\alpha_{i!} :\) \(C_i \to C\) is continuous, the functor \(\alpha_i^* : \mathrm{Top}(C) \to \widehat{C}_i\) admits a left adjoint, again denoted \(\alpha_{i!} : \widehat{C}_i \to \mathrm{Top}(C)\), which extends the functor \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to C\) (III 1.2 iv)).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.4.4

Let \(p : C \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred site on a small category \(I\).

  1. 1)

    A presheaf \(F\) on \(C\) is a sheaf for the total topology if and only if for every object \(i\) of \(I\), the presheaf \(F \circ \alpha_{i!} = F|C_i\) is a sheaf on \(C_i\).

  2. 2)

    A functor \(m\) from \(C\) to a site \(D\) is a continuous functor from the total site \(C\) to the site \(D\) if and only if for every object \(i\) of \(I\) the functor \(m|C_i = m \circ \alpha_{i!} : C_i \to D\) is continuous.

If \(F\) is a sheaf for the total topology, the presheaf \(F \circ \alpha_{i!}\) is a sheaf on \(C_i\) because \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to C\) is continuous. Suppose that for every \(i\), \(F \circ \alpha_{i!}\) is a sheaf on \(C_i\). Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\) over an object \(i\) of \(I\). For every covering sieve \(R\) of \(C_i/X\), we have \(F(X) \simeq F \circ \alpha_{i!}(R)\) and consequently \(F(X) \simeq F(\alpha_{i!}(R))\). Let \(R' \hookrightarrow X\) be the sieve of \(C/X\) that is the image of the canonical morphism \(\alpha_{i!}(R) \to X\). The morphism \(\alpha_{i!}(R) \to R'\) is an epimorphism of presheaves and consequently \(F(R') \to F(\alpha_{i!}(R))\) is injective. Since \(F(R') \to F(\alpha_{i!}(R))\) is also surjective, the map \(F(R') \to F(\alpha_{i!}(R))\) is bijective, and consequently the map \(F(X) \to F(R')\) is bijective. Since the covering sieves \(R' \hookrightarrow X\) obtained in this way are cofinal in the set of covering sieves of \(X\) (7.4.2. 1)), the presheaf \(F\) is a sheaf; for, going back to the construction of the associated sheaf (II 3), we see that \(F\) is isomorphic to its associated sheaf (II 3.3). The second assertion follows immediately from the first and from the definition of continuity (III 1.1).

Let \(p : C \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred site on a category \(I\) equivalent to a small category, and let \[ f : i \to j \] be an arrow of the index category \(I\). Denoting again by \(f : \widehat{C}_i \to \widehat{C}_j\) the morphism of topoi determined by the fibred site structure, we have (with the notation of 7.4.3 4)) a diagram of morphisms of \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi \[ \text{(7.4.5.1)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \widehat{C}_i \ar[r]^-{\alpha_i} \ar[d]_-{f} & \mathrm{Top}(C) \\ \widehat{C}_j \ar[ur]_-{\alpha_j} & } \] where \(\mathrm{Top}(C)\) is the total topos (7.4.3.3). The diagram (7.4.5.1) is not commutative in general. We are going to define a canonical morphism of morphisms of topoi: \[ \text{(7.4.5.2)} \qquad \rho_f : \alpha_i \to \alpha_j \circ f . \] It suffices to define such a morphism at the level of inverse images, i.e. to define a morphism of functors: \[ \text{(7.4.5.3)} \qquad \beta_f^* : f^* \circ \alpha_j^* \to \alpha_i^* , \] or again, using the adjunction between the functors \(f^*\) and \(f_*\), it suffices to define a morphism of functors: \[ \text{(7.4.5.4)} \qquad \gamma_f : \alpha_j^* \to f_* \alpha_i^* . \] So let \(Y\) be an object of \(C_j\) and \(F\) a sheaf on the total site \(C\). We have, by definition, \(\alpha_j^* F(Y) = F(\alpha_{j!}(Y))\) and \(f_* \alpha_i^* F(Y) = F(\alpha_{i!}(f^*(Y)))\), where in the second member \(f^* : C_j \to C_i\) denotes the inverse image functor for the fibred structure. But, by definition of this inverse image functor, we have a canonical cartesian morphism: \[ \text{(7.4.5.5)} \qquad m_Y : \alpha_{i!} f^* \to \alpha_{j!} ; \] hence, applying the functor \(F\), a map functorial in \(Y\): \[ \text{(7.4.5.6)} \qquad \gamma_f(F)(Y) = F(m_Y) : \alpha_j^* F(Y) \to f_* \alpha_i^* F(Y) , \] a map defining a morphism of sheaves on \(C_j\): \[ \text{(7.4.5.7)} \qquad \gamma_f(F) : \alpha_j^* F \to f_* \alpha_i^* F ; \] hence the morphism of functors \(\gamma_f\) of (7.4.5.4).

Now let \(f : i \to j\) and \(g : j \to k\) be two composable morphisms of \(I\). We have a canonical isomorphism \[ c'_{g,f} : g_* f_* \to (gf)_* \] and one immediately verifies the compatibility formula: \[ \text{(7.4.5.8)} \qquad c'_{g,f} \circ g_*(\gamma_f) \circ \gamma_g = \gamma_{gf} . \]

Let us now introduce the \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topos \(p^{\sim/I} : C^{\sim/I} \to I\) associated with \(p : C \to I\) (7.2.6) and the corresponding fibred category over \(I^\circ\) \((p^{\sim/I})' : (C^{\sim/I})' \to I^\circ\) (7.1.3.2). The foregoing considerations allow us to associate, to every object \(F\) of \(\mathrm{Top}(C)\), a family \(F_i = (\alpha_i^* F)_{i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)}\) of objects of the \(\widehat{C}_i\) and a family of morphisms \[ \gamma_f F : F_j \to f_* F_i , \quad f \in \mathrm{Fl}(I) , \quad f : i \to j , \] this family of morphisms being subject to the compatibility conditions of (7.4.5.8). We have thus associated to \(F\) an \(I^\circ\)-functor from the category \(I^\circ\) to the category \((C^{\sim/I})'\), i.e. an object \(\theta_C(F)\) of the category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})')\). Since this construction is functorial in \(F\), we have in the end a functor: \[ \text{(7.4.6.1)} \qquad \theta_C : \mathrm{Top}(C) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})') . \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.4.7

Let \(C \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred site with \(I\) equivalent to a small category. The functor \(\theta_C\) (7.4.6.1) is an equivalence of categories.

We shall content ourselves with describing a functor quasi-inverse to \(\theta_C\). Let \(\sigma \in \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})')\), i.e. an \(I^\circ\)-functor \(i \mapsto \sigma(i)\) from \(I^\circ\) to \((C^{\sim/I})'\). For every object \(X\) of \(C\) above \(p(X) = i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\), we have at our disposal a sheaf \(\sigma(p(X)) \in \mathrm{ob}\, \widehat{C}_i\); hence a set \(\sigma(p(X))(X)\). Let \(m : X \to Y\) be a morphism of \(C\) above the morphism \(f : i \to j\) of \(I\). The morphism \(m\) factors in a unique way as a morphism \(m' : X \to f^*Y\) of \(C_i\) followed by the canonical cartesian morphism \(f^*(Y) \to Y\). Likewise the morphism \(\sigma(f)\) factors in a unique way as a morphism \(\gamma_f(\sigma) : \sigma(p(Y)) \to f_* \sigma(p(X))\) followed by the canonical \(I^\circ\)-cartesian morphism \(f_* \sigma(p(X)) \to \sigma(p(X))\). We thus have a map from \(\sigma(p(Y))(Y)\) to \(\sigma(p(X))(X)\), obtained by composing the maps: \[ \sigma(p(Y))(Y) \xrightarrow{\gamma_f(\sigma)(Y)} f_* \sigma(p(X))(Y) = \sigma(p(X))(f^*Y) \xrightarrow{\sigma(p(X))(m')} \sigma(p(X))(X) . \] We have thus associated to every object \(X\) of \(C\) a set \(\sigma(p(X))(X)\), and to every morphism \(m : X \to Y\) a map \(\sigma(p(Y))(Y) \to \sigma(p(X))(X)\). One checks that one has indeed determined in this way a presheaf on \(C\), a presheaf which does not depend on the choice of inverse image functors used to construct it. It follows from 7.4.4 that the presheaf \(X \mapsto \sigma(p(X))(X)\) is a sheaf on the total site \(C\), and it is clear that this sheaf depends functorially on the object \(\sigma\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})')\). It is also clear, returning to the definition of the functor \(\theta_C\), that the functor from \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})')\) to \(\mathrm{Top}(C)\) that we have just constructed is a functor quasi-inverse to \(\theta_C\).

It follows in particular from 7.4.7 that the category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})')\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos. This last fact can be seen directly. One sees immediately, using I 9.21.10, that conditions a), b) and c) of IV 1.1.2 are satisfied, and the existence of a small generating category follows from I 9.25.

Let \(p : C \to I\) and \(q : D \to I\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred sites on a small category, and let \(m\) be a morphism from the fibred site \(C\) to the fibred site \(D\) (7.2.2). Denote by \(m^{\sim/I} : C^{\sim/I} \to D^{\sim/I}\) the corresponding morphism between the associated \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi. The morphism of fibred topoi \(m^{\sim/I}\) is defined up to canonical isomorphism (7.2.7). To it corresponds a direct image functor \(m^{\sim/I}_* : (C^{\sim/I})' \to (D^{\sim/I})'\) (7.1.7) which yields, on passing to sections over \(I^\circ\), a functor: \[ \text{(7.4.9.1)} \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,m^{\sim/I}_*) : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})') \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(D^{\sim/I})') . \] Moreover, the functor \(m\) is a continuous functor between the total sites (7.4.4) and consequently yields, by composition, a functor \(m_* : \mathrm{Top}(C) \to \mathrm{Top}(D)\).

In summary, we have a diagram of functors: \[ \text{(7.4.9.2)} \qquad \xymatrix@C=5em{ \mathrm{Top}(C) \ar[r]^-{\theta_C} \ar[d]_-{m_*} & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})') \ar[d]^-{\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,m^{\sim/I}_*)} \\ \mathrm{Top}(D) \ar[r]_-{\theta_D} & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(D^{\sim/I})') } \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.4.10

The diagram 7.4.9.2 is commutative up to isomorphism. When \(m\) is cartesian, \(m_*\) is a morphism from the total site \(C\) to the total site \(D\).

We leave to the reader the task of verifying the commutativity up to isomorphism of the diagram (7.4.9.2). To show that \(m_*\) is a morphism between the total sites, it suffices, in view of 7.4.7, to show that the functor left adjoint to the functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,m^{\sim/I}_*)\) is left exact. We shall first describe the functor left adjoint to \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,m^{\sim/I}_*)\). Denote by \((m^{\sim/I})^* : D^{\sim/I} \to C^{\sim/I}\) the inverse image functor of the morphism \(m^{\sim/I}\) (7.2.7), and for every object \(i\) of \(I\), denote by \(m_i^* : \widetilde{D}_i \to \widetilde{C}_i\) the functor induced by \((m^{\sim/I})^*\) on the fibres over \(i\). Choose, for every morphism \(f : i \to j\) of \(I\), morphisms of topoi, denoted in both cases \((f^*,f_*) : \widetilde{C}_i \to \widetilde{C}_j\) and \((f^*,f_*) : \widetilde{D}_i \to \widetilde{D}_j\). Since \((m^{\sim/I})^*\) is a cartesian \(I^\circ\)-functor, we have, for every \(f : i \to j\), a canonical isomorphism \[ \text{(7.4.10.1)} \qquad m_i^* f^* \to f^* m_j^* , \] and since the functors \(f^*\) and \(f_*\) are adjoint, we have canonical morphisms (adjunction morphisms) \[ \text{(7.4.10.2)} \qquad \varphi : \mathrm{id} \to f_* f^* , \qquad \psi : f^* f_* \to \mathrm{id} . \] Consider then the sequence of functorial morphisms: \[ \text{(7.4.10.3)} \qquad m_j^* f_* \xrightarrow{(1)} f_* f^* m_j^* f_* \xrightarrow{(2)} f_* m_i^* f^* f_* \xrightarrow{(3)} f_* m_i^* , \] where the morphism (1) is derived from \(\varphi\), the morphism (2) is derived from the isomorphism (7.4.10.1) and the morphism (3) is derived from \(\psi\). Composing the various morphisms of the sequence (7.4.10.3), we obtain a functorial morphism: \[ \text{(7.4.10.4)} \qquad \mathrm{can}_f : m_j^* f_* \to f_* m_i^* . \] Now let \(\tau\) be an object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(D^{\sim/I})')\). We thus have, for every object \(i\) of \(I\), an object \(\tau(i)\) of \(\widetilde{D}_i\) and, for every morphism \(f : i \to j\), a morphism \[ \text{(7.4.10.5)} \qquad \gamma_f(\tau) : \tau(j) \to f_* \tau(i) , \] where the family of the \(\gamma_f(\tau)\) possesses a compatibility property analogous to (7.4.5.8). Set then \(\sigma(i) = m_i^*(\tau(i))\) and denote by \[ \text{(7.4.10.6)} \qquad \gamma_f(\sigma) : \sigma(j) \to f_* \sigma(i) \] the composed morphism \(m_j^* \tau(j) \xrightarrow{m_j^* \gamma_f(\tau)} m_j^* f_* \tau(i) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{can}_f(\tau(i))} f_* m_i^* \tau(i)\). One verifies that the \(\gamma_f(\sigma)\) possess the compatibility property of (7.4.5.8) and consequently that one has defined in this way an object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})')\). An "adjoint functor chasing" then shows that the functor from \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(D^{\sim/I})')\) to \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})')\) that we have just constructed is left adjoint to the functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,m^{\sim/I}_*)\). It remains to show that this left adjoint commutes with finite projective limits, which follows immediately from the fact that in the categories of sections the projective limits are computed fibre by fibre and that all the functors used to construct this left adjoint commute with finite projective limits.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.4.11

Let \(p : C \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred site on a small category, \(p^{\sim/I} : C^{\sim/I} \to I\) the associated \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topos (7.2.6), \(\varepsilon_I : C \to C^{\sim/I}\) the canonical morphism from the \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred site \(C^{\sim/I}\) to the \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred site \(C\). The morphism \(\varepsilon_I\) induces an equivalence \(\mathrm{Top}(\varepsilon_I) : \mathrm{Top}(C) \to \mathrm{Top}(C^{\sim/I})\) between the corresponding total topoi.
This follows from the commutativity of the diagram (7.4.9.2) and from the fact that the morphism \(\varepsilon_I\) yields an equivalence between the associated \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi.
It follows from 7.4.11 that in questions concerning the total topos one may replace fibred sites by the corresponding fibred topoi.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.4.12

Let \(p : C \to I\) be a fibred site on a small category \(I\) and \(i\) a final object of \(I\) (I 10). The functor \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to \mathrm{Top}(C)\) (7.4.3.4) is exact and fully faithful. The pairs of functors \(\beta_i = (\alpha_{i!}, \alpha_i^*) : \mathrm{Top}(C) \to \widetilde{C}_i\) and \(\alpha_i = (\alpha_i^*, \alpha_{i*}) : \widetilde{C}_i \to \mathrm{Top}(C)\) are morphisms of topoi. The composed morphism \(\beta_i \alpha_i : \widetilde{C}_i \to \widetilde{C}_i\) is isomorphic to the identity morphism.

For every object \(j\) of \(I\), denote by \(f_j : j \to i\) the unique morphism from \(j\) to \(i\). Using the equivalence \(\theta_C : \mathrm{Top}(C) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})')\) (7.4.7) one sees that for every object \(X\) of \(C_i\), \(\alpha_{i!}(X)\) is the section \(j \mapsto f_j^*(X)\) and that for every section \(j \mapsto \sigma(j) \in \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,(C^{\sim/I})')\), \(\alpha_i^*(j \mapsto \sigma(j))\) is the object \(\sigma(i)\). Consequently \(\alpha_i^* \alpha_{i!}\) is isomorphic to the identity. Hence \(\alpha_{i!}\) is fully faithful. Since the functors \(f_j^*\) are left exact, the functor \(\alpha_{i!}\) is left exact. Hence \(\beta_i\) is a morphism of topoi, and since \(\alpha_i^* \alpha_{i!}\) is isomorphic to the identity, the morphism \(\beta_i \alpha_i\) is isomorphic to the identity morphism.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 7.4.13.1

Let \(p : C \to I\) and \(q : D \to I\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred sites on a small category \(I\) and \(m : D \to C\) an \(I\)-functor. For \(m\) to be a morphism from the fibred site \(C\) to the fibred site \(D\) (7.2.2), it suffices that \(m\) be a morphism from the total site \(C\) to the total site \(D\).

We must show that if an \(I\)-functor \(m : D \to C\) is a morphism from the total site \(C\) to the total site \(D\), the functor \(m\) is a morphism from the fibred site \(C\) to the fibred site \(D\), i.e. that for every object \(i\) of \(I\), the functor \(m_i : D_i \to C_i\) induced by \(m\) on the fibres over \(i\) is a morphism from the site \(C_i\) to the site \(D_i\). The proof of this last assertion occupies subsections 7.4.13.3 to 7.4.13.7.

Let us show that for every object \(i\) of \(I\), the functor \(m_i : D_i \to C_i\) is continuous. Indeed we have a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ D_i \ar[r]^-{m_i} \ar[d]_-{\alpha_{i!}} & C_i \ar[d]^-{\alpha_{i!}} \\ D \ar[r]_-{m} & C } \] and it suffices to show that for every covering sieve \(R \hookrightarrow X\) of \(C_i/X\), the morphism \(m_i(R) \to m_i(X)\) is bicovering (III 1.2 and 1.5). But, by virtue of the commutativity of the diagram on page 133 and of the fact that the functors \(\alpha_{i!}\) and \(m\) are continuous, the morphism \(\alpha_{i!}m_i(R) \to \alpha_{i!}m_i(X)\) is bicovering. The assertion follows therefore from 7.4.2.2.
7.4.13.4. Reduction to the case where \(C\) and \(D\) are \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi

Since the functors \(m_i\) are continuous, they admit natural extensions to the categories of sheaves, which we shall denote \(m_i^* : \widetilde{D}_i \to \widetilde{C}_i\) (III 1.2 iv)). Let \(D^{\sim/I}\) and \(C^{\sim/I}\) be the \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi associated with the fibred sites \(D\) and \(C\) respectively, and for every morphism \(f\) of \(I\), denote by \(f^*\) the inverse image functors for the four fibred categories \(C\), \(D\), \(C^{\sim/I}\) and \(D^{\sim/I}\). Since the functor \(m\) is an \(I\)-functor, we have, for every \(f : i \to j\), a canonical morphism \[ f^* m_j \to m_i f^* . \] Since the functors \(f^*\), \(m_i\) and \(m_j\) are continuous, we deduce, on passing to the categories of sheaves, canonical isomorphisms \[ f^* m_j^* \to m_i^* f^* . \] These isomorphisms possess compatibility properties, allowing one to construct a cartesian functor \(m^* : D^{\sim/I} \to C^{\sim/I}\) which induces on the fibre topoi the functors \(m_i^*\). Moreover, the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ D \ar[r]^-{m} \ar[d]_-{\varepsilon_I} & C \ar[d]^-{\varepsilon_I} \\ D^{\sim/I} \ar[r]_-{m^*} & C^{\sim/I} } \] is commutative up to isomorphism. Since the functors \(\varepsilon_I\) induce equivalences on the total topoi (7.4.11) and since \(m\) is a morphism between the total sites, the functor \(m^* : D^{\sim/I} \to C^{\sim/I}\) is a morphism between the total sites. We are thus reduced to proving the assertion of 7.4.13.2 when \(D\) and \(C\) are \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi, which we shall henceforth assume.

For every object \(i\) of \(I\), the functor \(m_i : D_i \to C_i\) transforms the final object of \(D_i\) into the final object of \(C_i\). Denote by \(m : \widetilde{D} \to \widetilde{C}\) the natural extension of \(m\) to the total topoi (III 1.2). Using the equivalences \(\theta_D : \widetilde{D} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,D')\) (7.4.7), one verifies immediately that \(m\) associates to every section \(\sigma \in \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,D')\) the section \((i \mapsto m_i \sigma(i)) \in \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,C')\). Since \(m\) is a morphism of sites, the functor \(m\) is left exact and in particular transforms the final object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,D')\) into the final object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,C')\). For every object \(i\) of \(I\), denote by \(e_i\) a final object of \(D_i\). A final object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,D')\) is the section \(i \mapsto e_i\). Hence the section \(i \mapsto m_i(e_i)\) is a final object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,C')\) and consequently, for every object \(i\) of \(I\), \(m_i(e_i)\) is a final object of \(C_i\).
7.4.13.6. Reduction to the case where \(i\) is a final object of \(I\)

Let \(i\) be an object of \(I\). The functor \(\alpha_{i!} : D_i \to D\) factors as \[ D_i \xrightarrow{\ \bar{\alpha}_{i!}\ } D_{/e_i} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{loc}(e_i)\ } D , \] where \(\bar{\alpha}_i\) is the obvious functor and \(\mathrm{loc}(e_i)\) the forgetful functor. Denote by \(m/i : D_{/e_i} \to C_{/m(e_i)}\) the functor which associates to every object \(u : X \to e_i\) of \(D_{/e_i}\) the object \(m(u) : m(X) \to m(e_i)\) of \(C_{/m(e_i)}\). We have a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ D_i \ar[r]^-{m_i} \ar[d]_-{\bar{\alpha}_{i!}} & C_i \ar[d]^-{\bar{\alpha}_{i!}} \\ D_{/e_i} \ar[r]_-{m/i} & C_{/m(e_i)} } \] Since \(e_i\) and \(m(e_i)\) are final objects of \(D_i\) and \(C_i\) respectively (7.4.13.5), the categories \(D_{/e_i}\) and \(C_{/m(e_i)}\) are \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi over \(I/i\) and the functor \(m_{/i}\) is an \(I_{/i}\)-functor. Since the property for a functor to be a morphism of sites is local (IV 4.9), the functor \(m_{/i}\) is a morphism from the total site \(C_{/m(e_i)}\) to the total site \(D_{/(e_i)}\). We are thus reduced to proving that \(m_i\) is a morphism of topoi when \(i\) is a final object of \(I\), which we shall henceforth assume.
7.4.13.7. End of the proof

Denote by \(\alpha_{i!} : D_i \to \widetilde{D}\), \(m^\sim : \widetilde{D} \to \widetilde{C}\), \(\alpha_{i!} : C_i \to \widetilde{C}\), the natural extensions to the categories of sheaves of the functors \(\alpha_{i!}\) and \(m\). We have a diagram commutative up to isomorphism: \[ \xymatrix{ D_i \ar[r]^-{m_i} \ar[d]_-{\alpha_{i!}} & C_i \ar[d]^-{\alpha_{i!}} \\ \widetilde{D} \ar[r]_-{m^\sim} & \widetilde{C} } \] Since \(i\) is a final object, the functor \(\alpha_i^* \alpha_{i!} : C_i \to C_i\) is isomorphic to the identity (7.4.12) and consequently \(m_i\) is isomorphic to \(\alpha_i^* m^\sim \alpha_{i!}\). Moreover the functors \(\alpha_i^*\), \(m^\sim\) and \(\alpha_i^*\) are left exact (7.4.12). Consequently \(m_i\) is left exact and is therefore a morphism from the site \(C_i\) to the site \(D_i\).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 7.4.14

Let \(X = (X_i)_{i \in I}\) be a fibred topos over \(I\) and \(T\) a topos. Show that the categories \(\underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}(X_i,T)\) are the fibres of a fibred category, which we shall denote \(\underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(X,T \times I)\). Show that the category of sections over \(I\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(X,T \times I)\) is canonically equivalent to \(\underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}(\mathrm{Top}(X),T)\), where \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) is the total topos of \(X\).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 7.4.15

Let \(X = (X_i)_{i \in I}\) be a fibred topos over \(I\). Define a cartesian morphism \(m\) from \(X\) to the constant fibred topos with fibre \((\mathrm{Ens})\). Show that the total topos of the constant fibred topos with fibre \((\mathrm{Ens})\) is canonically equivalent to \(\widehat{I}\). Deduce from this a morphism of topoi \[ \mathrm{Top}(m) : \mathrm{Top}(X) \to \widehat{I} . \] Let \(F = (F_i)_{i \in I}\) (where \(F_i = F|X_i\)) be an object of \(\mathrm{Top}(X)\) (7.4.7). Show that \[ \mathrm{Top}(m)(F) = (i \mapsto \Gamma(X_i,F_i)) . \] Deduce from 7.4.12 that if \(F\) is abelian injective, \(F_i\) is abelian injective for every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\). Deduce from this that \[ R^q \mathrm{Top}(m)(F) = (i \mapsto H^q(X_i,F_i)) . \] Show that the Cartan-Leray spectral sequence of the morphism \(m\) (V 5) is: \[ H^{p+q}(\mathrm{Top}(X),F) \Longleftarrow \varprojlim^{(p)}_I H^q(X_i,F|X_i) . \]

(∗) see the footnote at the bottom of page 112.
(∗) uniqueness comes from the fact that one requires, with the notation of (IV 5.5.3), the formula: \((gf)_1 = g_1 f_1\).

blocks.html: 8. Projective limits of fibred topoi
8.1. Generalities

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 8.1.1

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe and \(p : F \to I\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topos.
