A pair \((C,m)\) consisting of a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(C\) and a cartesian morphism \(m : C \times I \to F\) of \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi over \(I\) is called a projective limit of the fibred topos \(F\) if for every \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(D\), the functor \[ \text{(8.1.1.1)} \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}(D,C) \to \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(D \times I,F) \] obtained by composing the base change functor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}(D,C) \to \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_I(D \times I,C \times I) \] and the functor of composition with \(m\) (7.1.8), is an equivalence of categories. (cf. 8.1.3.3 for a more "geometric" formulation).

We use the notation of 8.1.1. Let \(D\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos and \(m_1 : D \times I \to F\) a morphism of \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi. Translating the definition 8.1.1, one sees at once that there exists a morphism of topoi \(n : D \to C\), and an isomorphism of morphisms of fibred topoi over \(I\), \(\gamma : m_1 \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } m \circ (n \times \mathrm{id}_I)\), making the diagram commutative: \[ \text{(8.1.2.1)} \qquad \xymatrix{ D \times I \ar[rr]^-{m_1} \ar[dr]_-{n \times \mathrm{id}_I} & & F \\ & C \times I \ar[ur]_-{m} & } \] Moreover, if \((n',\gamma')\) is another pair possessing the above property, there exists a unique isomorphism \(\eta : n \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } n'\) such that \[ \text{(8.1.2.2)} \qquad \gamma \circ m(\eta \times \mathrm{id}) = \gamma' . \] It results from this that, if \((D,m_1)\) is a projective limit of \(F\), \(n\) is an equivalence of \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi (IV 3.4) and that the additional datum of the isomorphism \(\gamma\) making the diagram (8.1.2.1) commute determines the pair \((n,\gamma)\) up to canonical isomorphism. The existence of the projective limit will be proved in 8.2.3 when \(I\) is cofiltered.

One denotes by \[ \operatorname*{Limtop}_I F \quad \text{or} \quad \operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i \quad \text{or else} \quad \underline{F} \] a projective limit of the fibred topos \(F\), by \(\mu : (\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F) \times I \to F\) the canonical morphism, and for every object \(i\) of \(I\) one denotes by \[ \mu_i : \underline{F} \simeq \underline{F} \times \{i\} \to F_i \] the morphism of topoi induced by \(\mu\) on the fibres over \(i\).

Let us choose a bisplitting of \(F\) (7.1.4), i.e. for every \(f : i \to j\) a morphism of topoi \(f_\cdot = (f^*,f_*) : F_i \to F_j\) such that \(f^*\) is an inverse image functor for the fibred structure. We then have, for every pair \(i \xrightarrow{f} j \xrightarrow{g} k\) of composable morphisms of \(I\), an isomorphism of morphisms of topoi (7.1.3) \[ c_{f,g} : g_\cdot f_\cdot \simeq (gf)_\cdot . \] Since \(\mu\) is a cartesian morphism of fibred topoi, we have, for every morphism \(f : i \to j\) of \(I\), an isomorphism of morphisms of topoi (7.1.6) \[ \text{(8.1.3.1)} \qquad b_f : f_\cdot \mu_i \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mu_j , \] and the family of the \(b_f\) satisfies relations analogous to the relations (7.1.6.2)

Let \(D\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos, \(m : D \times I \to F\) a morphism of fibred topoi, \(m_i : D \simeq D \times \{i\} \to F_i\) the morphisms induced by \(m\) on the fibres, and for every \(f : i \to j\): \[ b'_f : f_\cdot m_i \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } m_j , \] the transition isomorphism. It follows from 8.1.2 that there exists a morphism of topoi \(n : D \to \underline{F}\) and a family of isomorphisms: \[ \gamma_i : m_i \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mu_i n \qquad i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I , \] such that for every \(f : i \to j\) we have: \[ b_f \circ f_\cdot(\gamma_i) = \gamma_j \circ b'_f . \] Moreover, the morphism \(n\) and the family of the \(\gamma_i\), \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\), are determined up to unique isomorphism (8.1.2).

Conversely, when one is given a topos \(\underline{F}\), morphisms \(\mu_i : \underline{F} \to F_i\) and isomorphisms \(b_f\) (8.1.3.1), satisfying the usual compatibility conditions, and when all these data possess the universal property described above, there exists a unique morphism \(\mu : \underline{F} \times I \to F\) of fibred topoi that gives rise to the \(\mu_i\) and the \(b_f\), and \((\underline{F},\mu)\) is a projective limit of the fibred topos \(F\).

Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a universe such that \(\mathcal{U} \in \mathcal{V}\). The above considerations thus allow one to interpret the projective limits of fibred topoi as "projective limits", in the sense of 2-categories, of the pseudo-functors with values in the 2-category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi that are elements of \(\mathcal{V}\), deduced from the fibred structure by choosing the morphisms \(f_\cdot\). However, the reader should take care not to confuse this notion of "projective limit" in the sense of 2-categories (with commutation isomorphism) with the strict (or naive) notion of projective limit (strict commutation of diagrams). Even when the strict notion makes sense (when the pseudo-functor is a genuine functor) the notions of generalized "projective limit" and of strict projective limit do not in general coincide.

Let \(p : F \to I\) and \(q : G \to I\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi and \(m : F \to G\) a morphism of fibred topoi. Suppose that the fibred topoi \(F\) and \(G\) possess projective limits (8.1.1). It then follows immediately from the definition 8.1.1 that there exists a morphism of topoi: \[ \text{(8.1.4.1)} \qquad \underline{m} : \underline{F} \to \underline{G} , \] and an isomorphism of morphisms of fibred topoi \(\gamma : m \circ \mu \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mu \circ \underline{m} \times \mathrm{id}_I\), making

the diagram commutative \[ \text{(8.1.4.2)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \underline{F} \times I \ar[r]^-{\mu} \ar[d]_-{\underline{m} \times \mathrm{id}_I} & F \ar[d]^-{m} \\ \underline{G} \times I \ar[r]_-{\mu} & G } \] Moreover, if \((\underline{m}',\gamma')\) is another pair possessing the above property, there exists a unique isomorphism \(\eta : \underline{m} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{m}'\) of morphisms of topoi such that \[ \gamma \circ \mu(\eta \times \mathrm{id}) = \gamma' . \]

Let \(p : F \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topos element of \(\mathcal{V}\), \(\varphi : I' \to I\) a functor element of \(\mathcal{V}\), \(p_\varphi : F_\varphi \to I'\) the \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topos deduced from \((F,p)\) by the base change \(\varphi\) (7.1.9). Let \((\underline{F},\mu)\) be a projective limit of \(F\). One obtains by base change a morphism of fibred topoi over \(I'\): \[ \mu' : \underline{F} \times I' \to F_\varphi . \] Let \((\underline{F}_\varphi,\mu_\varphi)\) be a projective limit of \(F_\varphi\). We then have, by the universal property of the projective limit (8.1.2), a morphism of topoi \[ m_\varphi : \underline{F} \to \underline{F}_\varphi , \] and an isomorphism of morphisms of fibred topoi over \(I'\): \[ \gamma : \mu' \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mu_\varphi \circ (m_\varphi \times \mathrm{id}_{I'}) . \] The pair \((m_\varphi, \gamma)\) is determined up to unique isomorphism.

Let \(p : F \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred site on a small category \(I\), \(F^{\sim/I} \to I\) the associated \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topos (7.2.6) and \(D\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos. We have first a functor \[ \text{(8.1.6.1)} \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(D \times I,F^{\sim/I}) \to \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(D \times I,F) , \] which associates to every \(m\) the functor composed of \(m^*\) with \(\varepsilon_{F/I}\) (7.2.7). Moreover, by definition of the category \(\underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(D \times I,F)\) (7.2.2.2), we have a functor \[ \text{(8.1.6.2)} \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(D \times I,F) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(F,D \times I)^\circ . \] Finally, by definition of the Inductive limit (6.3), we have a functor \[ \text{(8.1.6.3)} \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(F,D \times I)^\circ \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} F, D)^\circ . \] Denote by \[ \text{(8.1.6.4)} \qquad \theta : \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(D \times I,F^{\sim/I}) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} F, D)^\circ \] the functor composed of these last three functors, and \[ \text{(8.1.6.5)} \qquad \Pi : F \to \varinjlim_{I^\circ} F , \] the canonical functor.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.1.7

The functor \(\theta\) is fully faithful. Its essential image is the set of functors \(m : \varinjlim_{I^\circ} F \to D\) such that the functor \[ (m \circ \Pi, p) : F \to D \times I \] is a morphism from the total site \(D \times I\) to the total site \(F\).

It follows from 7.2.7 that the functor (8.1.6.1) is an equivalence of categories, from 7.2.2 that the functor (8.1.6.2) is fully faithful and from 6.3 that the functor (8.1.6.4) is an equivalence of categories. Consequently \(\theta\) is fully faithful. A functor \(m : \varinjlim_{I^\circ} F \to D\) is isomorphic to the image under \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(F,D \times I)^\circ \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} F,D)^\circ\) of the functor \((m \circ \Pi, p)\), and such a functor is in the essential image of (8.1.6.2) if and only if it is a morphism from the total site \(D \times I\) to the total site \(F\) (7.4.13.1); hence the proposition.
8.2. Construction of the projective limit when the index category is cofiltered

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.2.1

Let \(I\) and \(I'\) be two cofiltered categories (I 8.1) and \(\varphi : I' \to I\) a functor such that \(\varphi^\circ : I'^\circ \to I^\circ\) is cofinal (I 8.1). Let moreover \(p : F \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topos, \(D\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos, \(m : D \times I \to F\) a cartesian morphism of fibred topos, \(m' : D \times I' \to F'\) the morphism of fibred topoi deduced from \(m\) by the base change \(\varphi\) (7.1.9). The pair \((D,m)\) is a projective limit of \(F\) if and only if \((D,m')\) is a projective limit of \(F'\).
The proof is merely a rather long routine verification. It is left to the patient reader, who may use the point of view of projective limits of pseudo-functors (8.1.3.3).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.2.2

Let \(p : F \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred site on a small cofiltered category, \(F_{\to}\) the Inductive limit of the fibred category \(F\) (6.3.9), \(\pi : F \to F_{\to}\) the canonical functor. Let us equip \(F_{\to}\) with the coarsest topology making the functor \(\pi\) continuous (III 1). Let \(D\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(n : F_{\to} \to D\) a functor. The following properties are equivalent:

  1. i)

    \(n\) is a morphism of sites \(D \to F_{\to}\).

  2. ii)

    \(n \circ \pi\) is a morphism of sites (where \(F\) is equipped with the total topology).

  3. iii)

    \((n \circ \pi, p) : F \to D \times I\) is a morphism from the total site \(D \times I\) to the total site \(F\).

  4. iv)

    For every object \(i\) of \(I\), the composed functor \(F_i \xrightarrow{\alpha_{i!}} F \xrightarrow{n \circ \pi} D\) is a morphism of sites.

We have i) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) ii) by (6.6) and iii) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) iv) by (7.4.13). Let us show that iii) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) ii). For this it suffices to show that the first projection functor \(\mathrm{pr}_1 : D \times I \to D\) is a morphism of sites. Denote by \(\widetilde{D}\) the topos of sheaves on \(D\). It follows from (7.4.7) that \(\widetilde{(D \times I)}\) is equivalent to the topos \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ, \widetilde{D} \times I^\circ) = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(I^\circ,\widetilde{D})\). Moreover, one sees immediately that the natural extension of \(\mathrm{pr}_1 : D \times I \to D\) to sheaves (III 1.2) is the functor from \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(I^\circ,\widetilde{D})\) to \(\widetilde{D}\) which associates to the functor \(i \mapsto \sigma(i)\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(I^\circ,\widetilde{D})\) the object \(\varinjlim_I \sigma(i)\). Since \(I^\circ\) is filtered, the inductive limits along \(I^\circ\) are exact (II 4) and consequently \(\mathrm{pr}_1\) is a morphism of sites (IV 4.9). It remains to prove that ii) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) iv). Let us first treat the case where \(D\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos and \(F\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topos over \(I\). Let \(i\) be an object of \(I\). Reasoning as in 7.4.13.6, one sees that the functor \(\alpha_{i!} : F_i \to F\) factors as a morphism \(\bar{\alpha}_{i!} : F_i \to F/\alpha_{i!}(e_i)\) and the localization functor \(F/\alpha_{i!}(e_i) \to F\), where \(e_i\) is a final object of \(F_i\). It thus suffices to show that the composed functor \(F/\alpha_{i!}(e_i) \xrightarrow{n \circ \pi} D\) is a morphism of sites. But we have a diagram commutative up to isomorphism: \[ \xymatrix{ F/\alpha_{i!}(e_i) \ar[r]^-{n \circ \pi/\alpha_{i!}(e_i)} \ar[d] & D/n \circ \pi \, \alpha_{i!}(e_i) \ar[d] \\ F \ar[r]_-{n \circ \pi} & D } \] Since the property of being a morphism is local (IV 5.10), it suffices to show that \(n \circ \pi \circ \alpha_{i!}(e_i)\) is a final object of \(D\). For every morphism \(f : j \to k\) of \(I\), there exists one and only one morphism \(e_f : \alpha_{j!}(e_j) \to \alpha_{k!}(e_k)\) above \(f\), and this morphism is cartesian. We thus have a cartesian section \(j \mapsto \alpha_{j!}(e_j)\) of \(F\) over \(I\). Consequently the canonical morphism \(n \circ \pi \circ \alpha_{i!}(e_i) \to \varinjlim_I n \circ \pi \circ \alpha_{j!}(e_j)\) is an isomorphism, because \(\pi\) transforms cartesian morphisms into isomorphisms. On the other hand \(\varinjlim_I \alpha_{j!}(e_j)\), where the inductive limit is taken in \(\widehat{F}\), is a final object of \(\widehat{F}\). Since \(n \circ \pi\) is a morphism, it transforms the final object of \(\widehat{F}\) into a final object of \(D\). Consequently \(\varinjlim_I n \circ \pi \circ \alpha_{j!}(e_j)\) is a final object of \(D\), which completes the proof in this case. In the general case, the functor \((n\pi, p) : F \to D \times I\) is cartesian and continuous (7.4.4). Moreover, the functor \(n \circ \pi\) is the composed functor \[ F \xrightarrow{(n\pi,p)} D \times I \xrightarrow{\mathrm{pr}_1} D . \] Passing to the associated \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi, we obtain a diagram commutative up to isomorphism: \[ \xymatrix{ F \ar[r]^-{(n\pi,p)} \ar[d]_-{\varepsilon_{F/I}} & D \times I \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{pr}_1} \ar[d]^-{\varepsilon_D \times \mathrm{id}} & D \ar[d]^-{\varepsilon_D} \\ F^{\sim/I} \ar[r]_-{(n\pi,p)^{\sim/I}} & \widetilde{D} \times I \ar[r]_-{\mathrm{pr}_1} & \widetilde{D} } \] Since \((n\pi,p)^{\sim/I}\) is cartesian, it is of the type \((n'\pi',p')\) where \(p' : F^{\sim/I} \to I\) and \(\pi' : F^{\sim/I} \to \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \widetilde{F}_i\) are the canonical functors. We thus have \(\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ (n\pi,p)^{\sim/I} = n'\). Since the functors \(\varepsilon_{F/I}, \varepsilon_D\) induce an equivalence on the topoi of sheaves (7.4.11), the functors \(n\) and \(n'\) give isomorphic functors on passing to the associated sheaves (III 1.2) and consequently \(n'\) is a morphism of sites. By what precedes, the functor \((n\pi,p)^{\sim/I}\) induces on the fibres morphisms of topoi. It is therefore a morphism from the total site \(F\) to the total site \(\widetilde{D} \times I\) (7.4.13). Since the functors \(\varepsilon_{F/I}, \varepsilon_D \times \mathrm{id}\) induce equivalences on the total topoi (7.4.11), the functor \((n\pi,p)\) is a morphism of fibred sites (7.4.13), whence the assertion.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 8.2.3

Let \(p : F \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred site on an essentially small cofiltered category (I 8.1).

  1. 1)

    Denote by \(F_{\to}\) the site whose underlying category is the inductive limit of the fibred category \(F \to I\) (6.3) and whose topology is the coarsest topology making the canonical functor \(\pi : F \to F_{\to}\) continuous. Then \(F_{\to}\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \[ (\pi,p) : F \to F_{\to} \times I \] is a morphism from the fibred site \(F_{\to} \times I\) to the fibred site \(F\).

  2. 2)

    Let \(\mu : (F_{\to})^\sim \times I \to F^{\sim/I}\) be the morphism of \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi deduced from \((\pi,p)\) on passing to the associated \(\mathcal{U}\)-fibred topoi. The pair \(((F_{\to})^\sim, \mu)\) is a projective limit of \(F^{\sim/I}\).

1. 1)

    In view of the notation introduced in 8.1.3, one may set \[ \operatorname*{Limtop}_I F^\sim = (F_{\to})^\sim \]

  2. 2)

    It follows from 7.4.4 that the topology on \(F_{\to}\) is also the coarsest topology making continuous the family of functors \(\pi_j : F_j \to F \xrightarrow{\pi} F_{\to}\), \(j \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 8.2.5

The site \(F_{\to}\) introduced in 8.2.3 is called the projective limit site of the fibred site \(F\).

As an exercise, the reader may, as in 8.2.1, define the notion of projective limit of a fibred site and verify that the site \(F_{\to}\) is indeed a projective limit of the site \(F\). The second assertion of the theorem can therefore be paraphrased thus: The topos of sheaves on the projective limit site is equivalent to the projective limit of the associated fibred topos.
8.2.6. Proof of the theorem: Reduction to the case of a small index category

We shall confine ourselves to giving some indications. Let \(I'\) be a full subcategory of \(I\) such that \(I'^\circ\) is cofinal in \(I^\circ\). Let \(F' \to I'\) denote the fibred category deduced from \(F\) by the base change \(I' \to I\), and \(\pi' : F' \to F'_{\to}\) the canonical functor. One observes first of all that the categories \(F_{\to}\) and \(F'_{\to}\) are equivalent and that the topology on \(F'_{\to}\) deduced from the topology of \(F_{\to}\) by this equivalence is the coarsest topology making the functor \(\pi' : F' \to F'_{\to}\) continuous. Assertion 1) of the theorem then follows once it is proved in the case where \(I\) is small. Assertion 2) in the general case then follows from assertion 2) in the case where \(I\) is small by lemma 8.2.1.
8.2.7. End of the proof of the theorem

The first assertion follows from lemma 8.2.2 applied to the case where \(D = F_{\to}\) and \(n = \mathrm{id}\). Let \(D\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos. We have a diagram commutative up to isomorphism: \[ \xymatrix@C=2.2em@R=3em{ \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}(D,(F_{\to})^\sim) \ar[r]^-{(1)} \ar[d]_-{(3)} & \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}(D,F_{\to}) \ar[d]^-{(3)} & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(F_{\to},D)^\circ \ar[l]_-{(2)} \ar[dd]^-{(5)} \\ \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/I}(D \times I,(F_{\to})^\sim \times I) \ar[r]^-{(1)} \ar[d]_-{(4)} & \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/I}(D \times I,(F_{\to}) \times I) \ar[d]^-{(4)} & \\ \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/I}(D \times I,F^{\sim/I}) \ar[r]^-{(1)} & \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_{\mathrm{Cart}/I}(D \times I,F) & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(F,D \times I)^\circ \ar[l]_-{(2)} } \] where the functors of type (1) are equivalences (IV 4.9.4 and 7.2.7), the functors of type (2) are fully faithful (IV 4.9.1 and 7.2.2), the functors of type (3) are base-change functors, the functors of type (4) are composition functors (with \(\mu\), resp. \((\pi,p)\)), and the functor (5) is the equivalence deduced from the universal property of the inductive limit (6.3). To show that the functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}(D,(F_{\to})^\sim) \xrightarrow{(4) \circ (3)} \underline{\mathrm{Homtop}}_{/I}(D \times I,F^{\sim/I})\) is an equivalence, it suffices to show that the functor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}(D,F_{\to}) \xrightarrow{(4) \circ (3)} \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_{/I}(D \times I,F) \] is an equivalence of categories, or again it suffices to show that the two fully faithful functors \[ \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}(D,F_{\to}) \xrightarrow{(5) \circ (2)} \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(F,D \times I)^\circ \] \[ \underline{\mathrm{Morsite}}_{/I}(D \times I,F) \xrightarrow{(2)} \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I}(F,D \times I)^\circ \] have the same essential images, which follows immediately from lemma 8.2.2.

Let \(p : F \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over a category \(I\), and \((\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i, \mu)\) a projective limit of \(F\). We thus have a cartesian morphism of \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over \(I\): \[ \mu : \operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i \times I \to F , \] whence, on passing to the categories fibred over \(I^\circ\) via the direct-image functors (7.1.3), a cartesian functor: \[ \mu_* : \operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i \times I^\circ \to F' \] which is the direct-image functor by \(\mu\) (7.1.7). We thus have, by the definition of the projective limit of a fibred category (6.10), a canonical functor \[ \text{(8.2.8.1)} \qquad \theta : \operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i \to \varprojlim_{I,f_*} F_i = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I^\circ}(I^\circ,F') . \]

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 8.2.9

We use the notation of 8.2.8, and we assume that \(I\) is an essentially small cofiltered category. Then the functor \(\theta\) is an equivalence of categories. Suppose \(I\) small. Set \(\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i = (F_{\to})^\sim\) (which is permissible by 8.2.3 and 8.2.4) and interpret the category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\) as the category of sheaves on the total site \(F\) (7.4.7). Then the composite functor \[ (F_{\to})^\sim = \operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i \xrightarrow{\theta} \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I^\circ}(I^\circ,F') \hookrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F') \simeq \widetilde{F} , \] is none other than the direct-image functor by the morphism of sites defined by the functor \[ \pi : F \to F_{\to} \]

A few comments before the proof of theorem 8.2.9. Apart from the solution of the existence problem for projective limits in the case where the index category is cofiltered — a solution which, curiously, is not trivial in this theory — theorems 8.2.3 and 8.2.9 provide two further pieces of information essential for handling projective-limit topoi in practice. First, the theorem 8.2.3 interprets the projective-limit topos as the topos of sheaves on a site whose underlying category is the inductive-limit category of the categories \(F_i\) along the system of inverse-image functors. In applications, one will be able to interpret this category and its topology concretely. On the other hand, the theorem 8.2.9 asserts that a sheaf of the projective limit is known once one knows the system of its direct images in the topoi \(F_i\) (which furnishes a cartesian section over \(I^\circ\) of the category \((F^{\sim/I})')\). This theorem asserts moreover that, conversely, when one is given for every object \(i\) of \(I\) a sheaf \(X_i\) on \(F_i\) and for every morphism \(f : i \to j\) of \(I\) an isomorphism \(X_j \simeq f_* X_i\), these isomorphisms being subject to compatibility conditions, there exists essentially a single sheaf of the projective limit which gives rise, by direct images, to the system of the \(X_i\).

Assertion 2) of 8.2.3 and the first assertion of 8.2.9 can be summarized in the striking formula: \[ \text{(8.2.11.1)} \qquad \varprojlim_{I,f_*} \widetilde{F}_i \simeq \operatorname*{Limtop}_{I,f_\cdot} \widetilde{F}_i \simeq (\varinjlim_{I^\circ,f^*} F_i)^\sim . \]
8.2.12. Proof of theorem 8.2.9

To prove the first assertion, one reduces to the case where the category \(I\) is small by using 8.2.1 and an analogous lemma on the projective limits of fibred categories. We leave the details to the reader. Suppose henceforth that \(I\) is a small category. We know that the functor \[ \pi : F \to \varinjlim_{I^\circ} F_i \] is a morphism of sites (8.2.2). The direct-image functor \[ \pi_* : (\varinjlim_{I^\circ} F_i)^\sim \to \widetilde{F} \] which it defines on the topoi is then fully faithful, and its essential image is the set of sheaves on \(F\) which transform the cartesian morphisms of \(F\) into isomorphisms (6.6). Now it is immediate that these sheaves correspond, under the equivalence \(\widetilde{F} \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\), to the cartesian sections of \(F'\) over \(I^\circ\) (7.4.7). Moreover, for every \(j \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\), let \(\alpha_{j!} : F_j \to F\) denote the inclusion functor which gives rise to the three functors \((\alpha_{j!}, \alpha_j^*, \alpha_{j*}) : F_j \rightrightarrows F\) (7.4.3). It follows from the definition of the equivalence \(\widetilde{F} \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\) (7.4.7) that to a sheaf \(X\) on \(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} F_i\) there corresponds, under the functor \((\varinjlim_{I^\circ} F_i)^\sim \xrightarrow{\pi_*} \widetilde{F} \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\), the cartesian section \(j \mapsto \alpha_j^* \pi_*(X)\). Now it follows from the description of the functor \(\mu : (\varinjlim_{I^\circ} F_i)^\sim \times I \to F\) given in 8.2.3 that for every object \(j\) of \(I\), the functor \(\mu_{j*} : (\varinjlim_{I^\circ} F_i)^\sim \to F_j\), the direct image by the morphism \(\mu_j : (\varinjlim_{I^\circ} F_i)^\sim \to F_j\) deduced from \(\mu\) by passing to the fibres at \(j\), is none other than the functor \(\alpha_j^* \pi_*\). Consequently the functor \((\varinjlim_{I^\circ} F_i)^\sim \xrightarrow{\pi_*} \widetilde{F} \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\) is none other than the functor \((\varinjlim_{I^\circ} F_i)^\sim \xrightarrow{\theta} \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I^\circ}(I^\circ,F') \hookrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\), whence the theorem.
8.3. Topology of the projective-limit site: the case of coherent topoi

In this section, \(p : F \to I\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site fibred over an essentially small cofiltered category, whose inverse-image functors \(f^* : F_j \to F_i\) commute with fibre products. One is moreover given, for every object \(X\) of a fibre category \(F_i\), a set \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\) of covering families for the topology of \(F_i\) which possess the properties (PT0) and (PT1) of II 1.3 and which generate the topology of \(F_i\). Finally one supposes that for every \(f : i \to j\), every \(Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, F_j\), and every family \((Y_\alpha \to Y)_{\alpha \in A}\) of \(\mathrm{Cov}(Y)\), the family \((f^*(Y_\alpha) \to f^*(Y))_{\alpha \in A}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{Cov}(f^*(Y))\). These conditions on \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\) are satisfied for example if one takes \(\mathrm{Cov}(X) = \{\text{all covering families of } X \text{ in } F_i \}\).
We propose to study in this section the projective-limit site of \(F\) under suitable finiteness hypotheses (8.3.13).

Let \(\pi : F \to F_{\to}\) be the canonical functor and \(Y\) an object of \(F_{\to}\). Denote by \(\mathrm{Cov}(Y)\) the set of families \((Y_\alpha \xrightarrow{n_\alpha} Y)_{\alpha \in A}\) of the following type:

There exist an \(i \in I\), an object \(X\) of \(F_i\), a family \((X_\alpha \xrightarrow{n'_\alpha} X)_{\alpha \in A}\) \(\in \mathrm{Cov}(X)\), an isomorphism \(\varphi : \pi(X) \simeq Y\) and a family of isomorphisms \(\varphi_\alpha : \pi(X_\alpha) \simeq Y_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in A\), such that for every \(\alpha \in A\) one has a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ \pi(X_\alpha) \ar[r]^-{\varphi_\alpha} \ar[d]_-{\pi(n'_\alpha)} & Y_\alpha \ar[d]^-{n_\alpha} \\ \pi(X) \ar[r]_-{\varphi} & Y } \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.3.3
  1. 1)

    The set of families \(\in \mathrm{Cov}(Y)\), \(Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, F_{\to}\), generates the topology of the projective-limit site (8.2.5).

  2. 2)

    The family \(Y \mapsto \mathrm{Cov}(Y)\), \(Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, F_{\to}\), possesses the properties (PT0) and (PT1) of II 1.3.
We shall need the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.3.4

Let \(i\) be an object of \(I\), and \(n : X' \to X\) a squarable morphism of \(F_i\) such that for every \(f : j \to i\), \(f^*(n)\) is squarable. Then \(\pi(n)\) is squarable. The functors: \[ \pi_j : F_j \hookrightarrow F \xrightarrow{\pi} F_{\to} , \quad j \in \mathrm{ob}\, I , \] commute with fibre products.

Recall that every object \(Y\) of \(F_{\to}\) is equal to an object \(\pi(Z)\), \(Z \in \mathrm{ob}\, F\), and that every morphism \(m : Y \to \pi(X)\) is of the form: \[ \pi(Z) \xrightarrow{\pi(s)^{-1}} \pi(Z') \xrightarrow{\pi(m')} \pi(X) , \] where \(s\) is a cartesian morphism of \(F\). Consequently, to show that \(\pi(n)\) is squarable, it suffices to show that the fibre product of every diagram \[ \xymatrix{ & \pi(X') \ar[d]^-{\pi(u)} \\ \pi(Z') \ar[r]_-{\pi(m')} & \pi(X) } \] is representable. But the morphism \(m' : Z' \to X\) factors as \(Z' \xrightarrow{m''} X'' \xrightarrow{s'} X\), where \(p(m'')\) is the identity of \(p(Z') = j\) and where \(s'\) is cartesian above \(p(s') = f\). Set \(X''' = f^*(X')\), \(n' = f^*(n)\). One then has a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ X''' \ar[r]^-{s''} \ar[d]_-{n'} & X' \ar[d]^-{n} \\ X'' \ar[r]_-{s'} & X } \] whence a commutative diagram in \(F_{\to}\): \[ \xymatrix{ \pi(X''') \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_-{\pi(u')} & \pi(X') \ar[d]^-{\pi(n)} \\ \pi(Z') \ar[r]_-{\pi(m')} & \pi(X'') \ar[r]_-{\sim} & \pi(X) } \] where \(n'\) is a squarable morphism of \(F_j\). To show that \(\pi(n)\) is squarable, it therefore suffices to show that the product \(\pi(Z') \times_{\pi(X'')} \pi(X''')\) is representable, and consequently it suffices to show that \(\pi_j : F_j \hookrightarrow F \to F_{\to}\) commutes with fibre products.

Let \[ \xymatrix{ Y' \ar[r] \ar[d] & X' \ar[d] \\ Y \ar[r] & X } \] be a cartesian diagram of \(F_j\) and \(W\) an object of \(F\) above \(k \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\). One has (6.5): \[ \mathrm{Hom}(\pi(W),\pi(Y')) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:\ell\to j,\ g:\ell\to k} \mathrm{Hom}_{F_\ell}(g^*(W),f^*(Y')) . \] But since \(f^* : F_j \to F_\ell\) commutes with fibre products, one has \[ \mathrm{Hom}(g^*(W),f^*(Y')) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(g^*(W),f^*(Y)) \times_{\mathrm{Hom}(g^*(W),f^*(X))} \mathrm{Hom}(g^*(W),f^*(X')) . \] Then, using the commutation of filtered limits with fibre products (I 2) and the formula (6.5), one obtains an isomorphism: \[ \mathrm{Hom}(\pi(W),\pi(Y')) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(\pi(W),\pi(Y)) \times_{\mathrm{Hom}(\pi(W),\pi(X))} \mathrm{Hom}(\pi(W),\pi(X')) , \] which shows that the diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ \pi(Y') \ar[r] \ar[d] & \pi(X') \ar[d] \\ \pi(Y) \ar[r] & \pi(X) } \] is cartesian in \(F_{\to}\).

Let us first prove the second assertion. It follows from 8.3.4 that the families of \(\mathrm{Cov}(Y)\), \(Y \in F_{\to}\), are composed of squarable morphisms, whence the property (PT0). To show that these families possess the property (PT1) (stability under base change), one is reduced, by carrying out a sequence of reductions as in the proof of 8.3.3, to proving the following assertion:

For every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\), every \(Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, F_i\), every \((Y_\alpha \to Y)_{\alpha \in A} \in \mathrm{Cov}(Y)\), and every morphism \(u : Z \to Y\) of \(F_i\), the family \((\pi(Z) \times_{\pi(Y)} \pi(Y_\alpha) \to \pi(Z))_{\alpha \in A}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{Cov}(\pi(Z))\).

This last assertion follows from the fact that the \(\pi_i : F_i \hookrightarrow F \xrightarrow{\pi} F_{\to}\) commute with fibre products (8.3.3) and that the families \(X \mapsto \mathrm{Cov}(X)\) of \(F_i\) are stable under base change. Let us prove the first assertion. It is clear that the families belonging to the \(\mathrm{Cov}(Y)\), \(Y \in F_{\to}\), are covering for the topology \(T\) the coarsest making the functor \(\pi\) continuous (III 1). Hence the topology \(T'\) generated by these families is coarser than \(T\). To show that it is finer than \(T\) (and consequently equal to \(T\)), it suffices to show that every sheaf \(M\) for \(T'\) is such that \(M \circ \pi\) is a sheaf on \(F\), or again (8.2.4) that \(M \circ \pi_i\) is a sheaf on \(F_i\) for every \(i\) ob \(I\). Now, since the functors \(\pi_i : F_i \to F_{\to}\) commute with fibre products (8.3.4), \(M\) is a sheaf for \(T'\) if and only if (II 2.3 and I 2.12) for every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\), for every \(Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, F_i\), for every \((Y_\alpha \to Y)_{\alpha \in A} \in \mathrm{Cov}(Y)\), the sequence of sets \[ M(\pi_i(Y)) \to \prod_{\alpha \in A} M(\pi_i(Y_\alpha)) \rightrightarrows \prod_{(\alpha,\beta) \in A \times A} M(\pi_i(Y_\alpha \times_Y Y_\beta)) \] is exact, i.e. (loc. cit.) if and only if for \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\), \(M \circ \pi_i\) is a sheaf on \(F_i\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.3.6

We use the notation and hypotheses of 8.3.1 and 8.3.2. If for every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\), \(X \mapsto \mathrm{Cov}(X)\) is a pretopology on \(F_i\) (II 1.3) and if for every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, F_i\), the covering families of \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\) are finite, then for every \(Y \in F_{\to}\), the covering families of \(\mathrm{Cov}(Y)\) are finite and \(Y \mapsto \mathrm{Cov}(Y)\) is a pretopology on \(F_{\to}\).

The only thing to prove is that the families \(Y \mapsto \mathrm{Cov}(Y)\) possess the property (PT2) of (II 1.3) (stability under composition). Let \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\), \(Y\) an object of \(F_i\), \((Y_\alpha \to Y)_{\alpha \in A} \in \mathrm{Cov}(Y)\). Let moreover \(i_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in A\), be a family of objects of \(I\), for every \(\alpha\), \(Z_\alpha\) an object of \(F_{i_\alpha}\) and \((Z_{\alpha\beta} \xrightarrow{n_{\alpha\beta}} Z_\alpha)_{\beta \in B_\alpha}\) a family of \(\mathrm{Cov}(Z_\alpha)\). Finally let us give ourselves, for every \(\alpha \in A\), an isomorphism \(\varphi_\alpha : \pi(Z_\alpha) \simeq \pi(Y_\alpha)\). Returning to the definition of the families of \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\), \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, F_{\to}\) (8.3.2), one sees that it is a matter of proving that the family \[ (\pi(Z_{\alpha\beta}) \xrightarrow{\pi(n_\alpha) \circ \varphi_\alpha \circ \pi(n_{\alpha\beta})} \pi(Y))_{\alpha\beta \in \coprod_A B_\alpha} \] belongs to \(\mathrm{Cov}(\pi(Y))\), which we shall do after five reductions.
8.3.8. Reduction to the case where for every \(\alpha \in A\), one has \(\varphi_\alpha = \pi(m_\alpha)\), \(m_\alpha : Z_\alpha \to Y_\alpha\)

For every \(\alpha \in A\), one has \(\varphi_\alpha = \pi(m_\alpha) \pi(s_\alpha)^{-1}\) (6.5) where \(s_\alpha\) is a cartesian morphism above \(f_\alpha : i'_\alpha \to i_\alpha\). One thus has commutative diagrams

\[ \xymatrix{ Z_{\alpha\beta} \ar[d]_-{n_{\alpha\beta}} & f_\alpha^*(Z_{\alpha\beta}) \ar[l]_-{s_{\alpha\beta}} \ar[d]^-{f_\alpha^*(n_{\alpha\beta})} \\ Z_\alpha & f_\alpha^*(Z_\alpha) \ar[l]^-{s_\alpha} } \qquad \alpha\beta \in \coprod_A B_\alpha , \]

which furnish commutative diagrams \[ \xymatrix{ \pi(Z_{\alpha\beta}) \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar[d]_-{\pi(n_{\alpha\beta})} & \pi(f_\alpha^*(Z_{\alpha\beta})) \ar[d]^-{\pi(f_\alpha^*(n_{\alpha\beta}))} \\ \pi(Z_\alpha) \ar[r]_-{\pi(s_\alpha)^{-1}}^-{\sim} & \pi(f_\alpha^*(Z_\alpha)) \ar[r]^-{\pi(m_\alpha)} & \pi(Y_\alpha) } \qquad \alpha\beta \in \coprod_A B_\alpha . \] Since the families \((f_\alpha^*(Z_{\alpha\beta}) \xrightarrow{f_\alpha^*(n_{\alpha\beta})} f_\alpha^*(Z_\alpha))\) belong to \(\mathrm{Cov}(f_\alpha^*(Z_\alpha))\), one may reduce to the case where for every \(\alpha\), one has \(\varphi_\alpha = \pi(m_\alpha)\).
8.3.9. Reduction to the case where, for every \(\alpha \in A\), \(i_\alpha = j\) and \(p(m_\alpha) = k : j \to i\)

Set \(g_\alpha = p(m_\alpha)\). Since \(I\) is cofiltered and since \(A\) is finite, there exists an object \(j\) of \(I\) and morphisms \(h_\alpha : j \to i_\alpha\) such that for every pair \((\alpha,\alpha')\) one has \(g_\alpha h_\alpha = g_{\alpha'} h_{\alpha'} = k\). Using the inverse-image functors \(h_\alpha^*\) as in 8.3.8, one reduces to the case described.
8.3.10. Reduction to the case where \(i = j\) and \(k : j \to i\) is the identity

One has, for every \(\alpha\), a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ Z_\alpha \ar[r]^-{m'_\alpha} & k^*(Y_\alpha) \ar[r]^-{t_\alpha} \ar[d]_-{k^*(n_\alpha)} & Y_\alpha \ar[d]^-{n_\alpha} \\ & k^*(Y) \ar[r]_-{t} & Y } \] where the morphisms \(t\) and \(t_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in A\), are cartesian, where \(m'_\alpha\) is above the identity of \(j\) and where \(t_\alpha \circ m'_\alpha = m_\alpha\). On replacing the family \((Y_\alpha \to Y)_{\alpha \in A}\) by the family \((k^*(Y_\alpha) \to k^*(Y))_{\alpha \in A} \in \mathrm{Cov}(k^*(Y))\), and the morphisms \(m_\alpha\) by the morphisms \(m'_\alpha\), one reduces to the case described.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.3.11

Let \(j\) be an object of \(I\) and \(m : X' \to X\) a morphism of \(F_j\) such that \(\pi(m)\) is an isomorphism. There exists a morphism \(\ell : j' \to j\) such that \(\ell^*(m)\) is an isomorphism.

Let us show that there exist a morphism \(f : i \to j\) and a morphism \(q : f^*(X) \to f^*(X')\) such that \(f^*(m) q = \mathrm{id}_{f^*(X)}\) and such that \(\pi(q)\) is an isomorphism. Indeed, there exists an isomorphism \(n : \pi(X) \to \pi(X')\) such that \(\pi(m) \circ n = \mathrm{id}_{\pi(X)}\). There exist therefore (6.5) two morphisms \(X \xleftarrow{s_1} Y_1 \xrightarrow{q_1} X'\), where \(s_1\) is cartesian, such that \(n = \pi(q_1) \pi(s_1)^{-1}\). One thus has \(\pi(m) \circ \pi(q_1) = \pi(s_1)\). The morphisms \(mq_1\) and \(s_1\) from \(Y_1\) to \(X\) have the same image in \(F_{\to}\). Consequently (cf. the description of the morphisms in the inductive limit (6.5)), there exists a cartesian morphism \(s_2 : Y_2 \to Y_1\) such that \(mq_1 s_2 = s_1 s_2\). Set \(q_1 s_2 = q_2\) and denote by \(s_3\) the cartesian morphism \(s_1 s_2\). One thus has \(mq_2 = s_3\). The morphism \(q_2 : Y_2 \to X'\) factors in an essentially unique manner as \(Y_2 \xrightarrow{q} Y_3 \xrightarrow{s_4} X'\) where \(s_4\) is cartesian and where \(q\) is above the identity of \(p(Y_2)\). One thus has a commutative diagram \[ \text{(8.3.11.1)} \qquad \xymatrix{ Y_3 \ar[d]_-{s_4} & Y_2 \ar[l]_-{q} \ar[d]^-{s_3} \\ X' \ar[r]_-{m} & X } \] Set \(p(s_4) = p(s_3) = f : i \to j\). One has \(f^*(X') \simeq Y_3\), \(f^*(X) \simeq Y_2\), and \(f^*(m) : Y_2 \to Y_3\) makes commutative the diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ Y_3 \ar[d]_-{s_4} & Y_2 \ar[l]_-{f^*(m)} \ar[d]^-{s_3} \\ X' \ar[r]_-{m} & X } \] One thus has \(s_3 = s_3(f^*(m) \circ q)\); since \(s_3\) is cartesian and since \(f^*(m) \circ q\) is above the identity of \(p(Y_2)\), one has \(f^*(m) \circ q = \mathrm{id}_{Y_2}\). Moreover, it follows from the commutativity of the diagram (8.3.11.1) that \(\pi(q)\) is an isomorphism.

Let us then apply the preceding result to the morphism \(q : f^*(X) \to f^*(X')\): there exist a morphism \(f' : j' \to i\) and a morphism \(q' : f'^*(X') \to f'^*(X)\), such that \(f'^*(q)q' = \mathrm{id}_{f'^*(X')}\). But on setting \(\ell = ff'\); one has an isomorphism \(f'^* f^* \simeq \ell^*\). One thus has a morphism \(f'^*(q) : \ell^*(X) \to \ell^*(X')\) and a morphism \(q' : \ell^*(X') \to \ell^*(X)\), such that \(\ell^*(m) f'^*(q) = \mathrm{id}_{\ell^*(X)}\) and \(f'^*(q)q' = \mathrm{id}_{\ell^*(X')}\). Consequently \(\ell^*(m)\) is an isomorphism.
8.3.12. End of the proof

Since \(I\) is cofiltered and \(A\) finite, it follows from 8.3.11 that there exists an inverse-image functor \(\ell^*\) which transforms all the morphisms \(m_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in A\), into isomorphisms. One therefore reduces to the case where the \(m_\alpha\) are isomorphisms. But then the covering families \((Z_{\alpha\beta} \to Z_\alpha)_{\beta \in B_\alpha}\) are deduced by the base change \(m_\alpha : Z_\alpha \to Y_\alpha\) from covering families \((Y_{\alpha\beta} \to Y_\alpha)_{\beta \in B_\alpha} \in \mathrm{Cov}(Y_\alpha)\). One is therefore reduced to the case where \(Z_\alpha = Y_\alpha\) and \(\varphi_\alpha = \mathrm{id}_{\pi(Y_\alpha)}\). But in this case the family \((Y_{\alpha\beta} \xrightarrow{n_\alpha \circ n_{\alpha\beta}} Y)_{\alpha\beta \in \coprod_A B_\alpha}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{Cov}(Y)\) (property (PT2)). Hence its image by \(\pi\) belongs to \(\mathrm{Cov}(\pi(Y))\) (8.3.2).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 8.3.13

Let \(p : F \to I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over an essentially small cofiltered category. If for every object \(i\) of \(I\) the fibre topos \(F_i\) is coherent (2.3) and if for every morphism \(f : i \to j\), the morphism of topoi \(f_\cdot = (f^*,f_*) : F_i \to F_j\) is coherent (3.1), then the topos \(\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i\) is coherent and for every object \(i\) of \(I\), the canonical morphism of topoi \[ \mu_i : \operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i \to F_i \] is coherent.

Moreover, denoting by \(F_{\mathrm{coh}}\) the full subcategory of \(F\) defined by the objects of \(F\) that are coherent in their fibre (1.13), the category \(F_{\mathrm{coh}}\) is fibred over \(I\) and \((F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}}\) is canonically equivalent to the category of coherent objects of \(\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i\).

For every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\), denote by \((F_i)_{\mathrm{coh}}\) the \(\mathcal{U}\)-site (endowed with the induced topology) of coherent objects of \(F_i\) (1.13). Since \(F_i\) is coherent, \(F_i\) is the topos of sheaves on \((F_i)_{\mathrm{coh}}\). For every morphism \(f : i \to j\), the morphisms \(f_\cdot = (f^*,f_*)\) are coherent and consequently \(f^*(F_j)_{\mathrm{coh}} \subset (F_i)_{\mathrm{coh}}\). One thus has a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site fibred \(p_{\mathrm{coh}} : F_{\mathrm{coh}} \to I\), whose fibre sites are the sites \((F_i)_{\mathrm{coh}}\) and whose associated fibred topos is equivalent to \(p : F \to I\). Consequently one has (8.2.3): \[ \text{(8.3.13.1)} \qquad \operatorname*{Limtop}_{I,f_\cdot} F_i \simeq ((F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}})^\sim . \] Since the topoi \(F_i\) are coherent, the finite products and the fibre products are representable in \((F_i)_{\mathrm{coh}}\) (2.2). Moreover the functors \(f^* : (F_j)_{\mathrm{coh}} \to (F_i)_{\mathrm{coh}}\) are left exact. Finally, since the objects of \((F_i)_{\mathrm{coh}}\) are quasi-compact, the finite covering families form a pretopology. It then follows from (8.3.4) that the finite products and the fibre products are representable in \(\varinjlim_{I^\circ,t} (F_i)_{\mathrm{coh}}\) (addendum to lemma 8.3.4.: Show that the canonical functors \((F_i)_{\mathrm{coh}} \to (F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}}\) transform the final object into the final object) and from (8.3.6) that the objects of \((F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}}\) are quasi-compact. Consequently (2.4.5), \(\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i\) is coherent. Finally the canonical morphisms \(\mu_i : \operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i \to F_i\) are deduced, by passing to the topoi of sheaves, from the morphisms of sites (8.2.3): \[ (F_i)_{\mathrm{coh}} \to (F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}} \] hence (3.3) the morphisms \(\mu_i\) are coherent.

Let us prove the last assertion. One has (8.3.13.1) \[ \operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i \simeq ((F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}})^\sim . \] Let \(X\) be a coherent object of \(((F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}})^\sim\). Since \(X\) is quasi-compact, there exists a finite covering family \((Y_\alpha \to X)\) where \(Y_\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, (F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}}\) (1.1). Up to taking an index \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\) small enough, one may suppose that the \(Y_\alpha\) are the images by \(\mu_i : F_{i,\mathrm{coh}} \to (F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}}\) of a family \(Y'_\alpha\) whence, on taking the direct sum of the \(Y'_\alpha\) (1.15), one sees that there exist an index \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\), a \(Y' \in F_{i,\mathrm{coh}}\) and a surjective morphism \(\mu_i(Y') \to X\). The equivalence relation \(R = \mu_i(Y') \times_X \mu_i(Y')\) is then a coherent object since \(((F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}})^\sim\) is a coherent topos (2.2). Let us first show that \(R\) is an object of \((F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}}\). By definition \(R\) is a subobject of \(\mu_i(Y' \times Y')\) and since \(R\) is coherent, one may, up to changing the index \(i\), find an arrow \(m : Z \to (Y' \times Y')\) of \(F_{i\,\mathrm{coh}}\) such that \(\operatorname{Im}(\mu_i(m)) = R\). It follows that, \(F_i\) being coherent, \(\operatorname{Im}(m)\) is coherent in \(F_i\) (1.17.1) and consequently belongs to \(F_{i\,\mathrm{coh}}\). There exist therefore an index \(i\) and a diagram \(R \underset{p_2}{\overset{p_1}{\rightrightarrows}} Y'\) of \(F_{i\,\mathrm{coh}}\) such that \(\mu_i(R) \underset{\mu_i(p_2)}{\overset{\mu_i(p_1)}{\rightrightarrows}} \mu_i(Y')\) is an equivalence relation and such that \(X = \mu_i(Y')/\mu_i(R)\). Set \(X_i = \operatorname{coker}(p_1,p_2)\) and \(R' = Y' \times Y'\). One has a canonical morphism in \(F_i\): \(u : R \to R'\). Moreover \(\mu_i^*(u)\) is an isomorphism. Hence, up to changing the index \(i\), one may suppose that \(R = R'\), i.e. that \(R\) is an equivalence relation. But then \(X_i\) belongs to \(F_{i\,\mathrm{coh}}\) (1.17.1) and consequently \(X = \mu_i(X_i)\) belongs to \((F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}}\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.3.14

Let \(I\) be an essentially small cofiltered category, \(p : F \to I\) and \(q : G \to I\) two \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over \(I\) such that for every object \(i\) of \(I\) the topoi \(F_i\) and \(G_i\) are coherent and such that for every morphism \(f : i \to j\) the morphisms \(f_\cdot : F_i \to F_j\) and \(G_i \to G_j\) are coherent. Let moreover \(m : F \to G\) be a cartesian morphism of \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred such that for every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\), \(m_i : F_i \to G_i\) is coherent. Then the morphism \(\underline{m}\) deduced from \(m\) by passing to the projective limit is coherent.

For every object \(i\) of \(I\), the morphism \(m_i\) induces a functor \(m_{i,\mathrm{coh}}^* : G_{i,\mathrm{coh}} \to F_{i,\mathrm{coh}}\), whence a cartesian functor \(m_{\mathrm{coh}}^* : G_{\mathrm{coh}} \to F_{\mathrm{coh}}\) which is a morphism from the fibred site \(F_{\mathrm{coh}}\) into the fibred site \(G_{\mathrm{coh}}\) (7.4.13). The functor \(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} m_{\mathrm{coh}}^* : \varinjlim_{I^\circ} G_{\mathrm{coh}} \to \varinjlim_{I^\circ} F_{\mathrm{coh}}\) is a morphism of sites which furnishes, on passing to the corresponding topoi, the morphism \(\underline{m}\). The assertion then follows from 8.3.13 and from 3.3.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.3.15

With the notation of 8.3.13, show that if the \(F_i\), \(i \in I\), are algebraic (2.3) and if the morphisms \(f_\cdot : F_i \to F_j\), \(f \in \mathrm{Fl}(I)\), are coherent, \(\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i\) is algebraic and that \((\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i)_{\mathrm{coh}} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (F_{\to})_{\mathrm{coh}}\).
8.4. Example: Local topoi

Let \(X = (X_i)_{i \in I}\) be a topos fibred over a category \(I\). One deduces from it a topos fibred over the category \(\mathrm{Pro}(I)\) (I 8.10) by the formula \[ \text{(8.4.1.1)} \qquad X_{\underline{a}} = \operatorname*{Limtop}_{i_\alpha} X_{i_\alpha} \] for every pro-object \(\underline{a} = (i_\alpha)\) of \(I\) (to see this one may generalize to pseudo-functors exercise I 8.2.8).

Let \(E\) be a topos and \(p : \mathrm{Fl}(E) \to E\) the topos fibred considered in 7.3.1. On extending as in 8.4.1, one obtains a topos fibred \(\overline{\mathrm{Fl}(E)} \to \mathrm{Pro}(E)\). The category \(\mathrm{Point}(E)\) is sent by a fully faithful functor into \(\mathrm{Pro}(E)\) (IV 6.8.5), whence, by base change (7.1.9), a topos fibred \(\mathrm{Loc}(E) \to \mathrm{Point}(E)\). The fibre \(\mathrm{Loc}_p(E)\) at a point \(p\) of \(E\) is called the localized topos of \(E\) at the point \(p\). This topos depends, by what precedes, covariantly on the point \(p\). One has, by definition, \[ \text{(8.4.2.1)} \qquad \mathrm{Loc}_p(E) = \operatorname*{Limtop}_{X \in \mathrm{Vois}(p)} E_{/X} , \] where \(\mathrm{Vois}(p)\) is the category of neighbourhoods of \(p\) (IV 6.8).

Let \(m : p' \to p\) be a morphism of \(\mathrm{Point}(E)\) (IV 6). One deduces from it, for every \(X \in \mathrm{Vois}(p)\), a point \(p'_X\) of \(E_{/X}\), whence, by the universal property of \(\operatorname*{Limtop}\) (8.1), a point \(\theta_p(m)\) of \(\mathrm{Loc}_p(E)\). One thus defines a functor \[ \text{(8.4.3.1)} \qquad \theta_p : \mathrm{Point}(E)_{/p} \to \mathrm{Point}(\mathrm{Loc}_p(E)) , \] which one immediately observes to be an equivalence of categories. Consequently \(\mathrm{Point}(\mathrm{Loc}_p(E))\) is canonically equivalent to the category of generizations of \(p\) (IV 7.1.8). One has moreover a canonical equivalence of topoi: \[ \mathrm{can} : \mathrm{Loc}_{\theta(m)}(\mathrm{Loc}_p(E)) \to \mathrm{Loc}_{p'}(E) , \] which fits into a diagram commutative up to isomorphism \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{Loc}_{\theta(m)}(\mathrm{Loc}_p(E)) \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{can}} \ar[dr]_-{\varphi} & & \mathrm{Loc}_{p'}(E) \ar[dl]^-{m} \\ & \mathrm{Loc}_p(E) & } \] where \(\varphi\) is the canonical morphism (8.4.2.1).

The localized topoi seem to present an interest only in the case of the topoi coming from algebraic geometry, or at least only in the case of the topoi possessing suitable finiteness properties. Thus, when \(E\) is the topos of sheaves on a separated topological space, one observes immediately (with the help for example of 8.2.9) that the localized topoi are punctual topoi. Moreover in this case, the category \(\mathrm{Point}(E)\) is discrete and the situation described in 8.4.2 is trivial. On the other hand, let \(E = \mathrm{Top}(X)\) be the topos of sheaves for the Zariski topology on a scheme \(X\), \(x\) a point of \(X\), \(O_x\) the local ring of \(X\) at \(x\), \(Y = \mathrm{spec}(O_x)\). One observes that \[ \mathrm{Loc}_x(E) = \mathrm{Top}(Y) . \] For other examples coming from the étale topology, we refer to Exposé VIII of the present seminar.

When \(E\) is locally coherent (2.3), the localized topoi \(\mathrm{Loc}_p(E)\) are coherent (one may in 8.4.2.1 confine oneself to the \(X \in \mathrm{Vois}(p)\) that are algebraic and coherent, and then apply 8.3.13). For every morphism of points \(m : p' \to p\), the morphism of topoi \(m_\cdot : \mathrm{Loc}_{p'}(E) \to \mathrm{Loc}_p(E)\) is coherent (8.3.14).

One calls a local topos a topos \(X\) such that the functor \(\Gamma(X,-)\) = "section on \(X\)" (IV 4.3) is a fibre functor (IV 6). The point corresponding to this fibre functor is called the centre of the local topos. When \(E\) is locally coherent, the localized topoi are local topoi (1.2.3, 8.5.2 and 8.5.7). The centre of \(\mathrm{Loc}_p(E)\) is canonically isomorphic to \(\theta_p(\mathrm{id}_p)\) (8.4.3.1). The image of the centre of \(\mathrm{Loc}_p(E)\) in \(E\) is isomorphic to \(p\). The localized topos \(\mathrm{Loc}_p(E)\) endowed with the morphism
canonical \(\mathrm{Loc}_p(E) \to E\) is the solution of the universal problem (2-universal!) which consists in sending local topoi into \(E\) so as to send the centre "onto" \(p\).

Concerning local topoi, there arise a certain number of problems that the authors have not addressed. Thus, if \(X\) is a local topos, the final object \(e\) of \(X\) possesses a maximal open \(U \neq e\). The complement \(Y\) of \(U\) is a local topos which possesses no non-trivial open. Is such a topos punctual? Let \(U\) be a topos and \(X = (U, \Phi: U \to (\mathrm{Ens}))\) a topos obtained by gluing. What are the conditions on the gluing functor \(\Phi\) for \(X\) to be a local topos?
8.5. Structure of the sheaves of a filtered projective limit of topoi

In this section, \(F = (F_i)_{i \in I}\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over a small cofiltered category \(I\). One chooses a bisplitting (7.1.4) of \(F\), i.e., for every \(f \in \mathrm{Fl}(I) : i \to j\) one chooses morphisms of topoi \(f_\cdot : F_i \to F_j\) such that \(f^* : F_j \to F_i\) is the inverse-image functor for the fibred structure. One then has canonical isomorphisms \(c_{f,g}\) possessing a cocycle property (7.1.3). One denotes by \(\underline{F}\) the projective limit of the topos fibred \(F\) (8.2.3) and for every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\), one denotes by \[ \text{(8.5.1.1)} \qquad \mu_i : \underline{F} \to F_i , \] the canonical morphism (8.1.3). One denotes by \(\mathrm{Top}(F)\) the total topos of \(F\) (7.4.3.3). By 8.2.9, the canonical functor \(F \to \underline{F}\) defines a morphism of topoi \[ \text{(8.5.1.2)} \qquad Q : \underline{F} \to \mathrm{Top}(F) . \] The topos \(\underline{F}\) is identified with \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\) (8.2.9) and the topos \(\mathrm{Top}(F)\) is identified with \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\) (7.4.7). These identifications made, the morphism \(Q\) is none other than the embedding morphism of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cart}/I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\) into \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\) (8.2.9), and for every object \(M\) of \(\underline{F}\), one has \[ \text{(8.5.1.3)} \qquad Q_*(M) = (i \mapsto \mu_{i*}(M)) . \] By 7.4.3.4, one has for every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\), a morphism of topoi \[ \text{(8.5.1.4)} \qquad \alpha_i : F_i \to \mathrm{Top}(F) . \] The diagram \[ \text{(8.5.1.5)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \underline{F} \ar[rr]^-{\mu_i} \ar[dr]_-{Q} & & F_i \\ & \mathrm{Top}(F) \ar[ur]_-{\alpha_i} & } \] is not commutative in general (even up to isomorphism). But one has, by the definition of the morphisms involved, a canonical isomorphism \[ \text{(8.5.1.6)} \qquad \alpha_i^* Q_* \simeq \mu_{i*} . \] When \(i\) is a final object of \(I\), \(\alpha_i\) is an embedding admitting a retraction \(\beta_i : \mathrm{Top}(F) \to F_i\) (7.4.12) and the diagram \[ \text{(8.5.1.7)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \underline{F} \ar[rr]^-{\mu_i} \ar[dr]_-{Q} & & F_i \\ & \mathrm{Top}(F) \ar[ur]_-{\beta_i} & } \] is commutative up to canonical isomorphism.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.5.2

Let \(j \mapsto M_j\) be an object of \(\mathrm{Top}(F)\). There exists a functorial isomorphism \[ \text{(8.5.2.1)} \qquad Q^*(j \mapsto M_j) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_j^* M_j . \]

An object of \(\mathrm{Top}(F)\) (7.1.3) consists of the datum of a map \(j \mapsto M_j\), \(M_j\) \(\in \mathrm{ob}\, F_j\), and of the datum, for every morphism \(f : i \to j\), of a morphism \[ \text{(8.5.2.2)} \qquad \beta_f : M_j \to f_* M_i \] or equivalently by adjunction, of a morphism \[ \text{(8.5.2.3)} \qquad \beta'_f : f^* M_j \to M_i , \] the morphisms \(\beta'_f\) being subject to the condition that for every pair of composable morphisms \(i \xrightarrow{f} j \xrightarrow{g} k\), the diagram below is commutative: \[ \text{(8.5.2.4)} \qquad \xymatrix{ f^* g^* M_k \ar[r]^-{f^* \beta'_g} \ar[d]_-{c^*_{g,f}} & f^* M_j \ar[d]^-{\beta'_f} \\ (gf)^* M_k \ar[r]_-{\beta'_{gf}} & M_i } \] Recall moreover (8.1.3.1) that for every morphism \(f : i \to j\), one has an isomorphism \(b_f : f_\cdot \mu_i \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mu_j\), and that for every pair of composable morphisms \(i \xrightarrow{f} j \xrightarrow{g} k\), one has a commutative diagram: \[ \text{(8.5.2.5)} \qquad \xymatrix{ g_\cdot f_\cdot \mu_i \ar[r]^-{c_{g,f}} \ar[d]_-{g_\cdot(b_f)} & (gf)_\cdot \mu_i \ar[d]^-{b_{gf}} \\ g_\cdot \mu_j \ar[r]_-{b_g} & \mu_k } \] Let then \(f : i \to j\) be a morphism of \(I\). Denote by \[ \text{(8.5.2.6)} \qquad t_f : \mu_j^*(M_j) \to \mu_i^*(M_i) \] the composite morphism \(\mu_j^*(M_j) \xrightarrow{b_f^*} \mu_i^*(f^*(M_j)) \xrightarrow{\mu_i^*(\beta'_f)} \mu_i^*(M_i)\). We leave to the reader the task of verifying that the commutativity of the diagrams (8.5.2.4) and (8.5.2.5) entails that for every pair of composable morphisms \(i \to j \to k\), one has \[ \text{(8.5.2.7)} \qquad t_f t_g = t_{gf} . \] Consequently one has defined a functor \(I^\circ \to \underline{F}\) whose inductive limit \(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^*(M_i)\) one may consider. Let then \(N\) be an object of \(\underline{F}\). One has \[ \text{(8.5.2.8)} \qquad \mathrm{Hom}(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^*(M_i),N) \simeq \varprojlim_{I^\circ} \mathrm{Hom}(\mu_i^*(M_i),N) , \] whence, by adjunction, an isomorphism \[ \text{(8.5.2.9)} \qquad \mathrm{Hom}(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^*(M_i),N) \simeq \varprojlim_{I^\circ} \mathrm{Hom}_{F_i}(M_i, \mu_{i*}(N)) . \]

We propose to interpret the second member of 8.5.2.9. For this, denote, for every morphism \(f : i \to j\), by \[ d_f : \mathrm{Hom}_{F_i}(M_i,\mu_{i*}(N)) \to \mathrm{Hom}_{F_j}(M_j, \mu_{j*}(N)) . \] the transition morphism of the projective system appearing in (8.5.2.9). It follows from the definition of the morphisms \(t_f\) (8.5.2.6) that the map \(d_f\) associates to a morphism \[ u_i : M_i \to \mu_{i*}(N) \] the morphism \[ d_f(u_i) : M_j \to \mu_{j*}(N) , \] obtained by composing the morphisms \[ M_j \xrightarrow{\beta_f} f_*(M_i) \xrightarrow{f_*(u_i)} f_* \mu_{i*}(N) \xrightarrow{b_f} \mu_{j*}(N) . \] Consequently an element of the second member of (8.5.2.9) is interpreted as a family of morphisms \(u_i : M_i \to \mu_{i*}(N)\), \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\), such that for every \(f : i \to j\), the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ M_j \ar[r] \ar[d]_-{u_j} & f_*(M_i) \ar[d]^-{f_*(u_i)} \\ \mu_{j*}(N) \ar[r]^-{\sim} & f_* \mu_{i*}(N) } \] is commutative, that is to say as a morphism from the section \((i \mapsto M_i) \in\) \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\) into the section \(Q_*(N)\). One thus has a functorial isomorphism \[ \mathrm{Hom}(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^*(M_i),N) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}((i \mapsto M_i),Q_*(N)) ; \] whence the proposition by adjunction.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.5.3

If for every \(f : i \to j \in \mathrm{Fl}(I)\) the functors \(f_* : F_i \to F_j\) commute with small filtered inductive limits, one has, for every section \((i \mapsto M_i) \in \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\): \[ \text{(8.5.3.1)} \qquad Q_* Q^*(i \mapsto M_i) \simeq i \mapsto \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_* M_j . \]

We leave to the reader the task of making explicit, in terms of the \(\beta_f\) (8.5.2.2) and the \(c_{f,g}\) (8.5.1), the transition morphisms of the inductive systems \((f : j \to i) \mapsto f_*(M_j)\) and the transition morphisms of the section \(i \mapsto \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_* M_j\). Since the functors \(f_*\) commute with filtered inductive limits, the section \(i \mapsto \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_* M_j\) is cartesian. Moreover one has a natural morphism \(u\) from \((i \mapsto M_i)\) into the section \((i \mapsto \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_* M_j)\), and it is clear that every morphism from \((i \mapsto M_i)\) into a cartesian section factors in a unique manner through \(u\), whence the isomorphism (8.5.3.1).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.5.4

Under the hypotheses of 8.5.3 the functor \(Q_*\) commutes with small filtered inductive limits.

Let \(\alpha \mapsto N^\alpha\) be a small filtered inductive system of \(\underline{F}\). Set \(M^\alpha = Q_*(N^\alpha)\), so that \(M^\alpha\) is a section \(i \mapsto M_i^\alpha\). One has \(N^\alpha \simeq Q^* Q_*(N^\alpha)\) and since \(Q^*\) commutes with inductive limits, one has \(\varinjlim_\alpha N^\alpha \simeq Q^*(\varinjlim_\alpha M^\alpha)\). The inductive limits in \(\mathrm{Top}(F) = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F')\) are computed fibre by fibre. One thus has \(\varinjlim_\alpha M \simeq (i \mapsto \varinjlim_\alpha M_i^\alpha)\). By virtue of (8.5.3.1), one has \[ Q_*(\varinjlim_\alpha N^\alpha) \simeq Q_* Q^*(\varinjlim_\alpha M^\alpha) \simeq i \mapsto \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_*(\varinjlim_\alpha M_j^\alpha) . \] Since the functors \(f_*\) commute with filtered inductive limits, it comes: \[ Q_*(\varinjlim_\alpha N^\alpha) \simeq i \mapsto \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} \varinjlim_\alpha f_*(M_j^\alpha) \simeq i \mapsto \varinjlim_\alpha \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_*(M_j^\alpha) \simeq \varinjlim_\alpha Q_*(N^\alpha) . \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.5.5

If the functors \(f_* : F_i \to F_j\) commute with small filtered inductive limits, one has, for every object \(i\) of \(I\) and for every \(M_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, F_i\) \[ \text{(8.5.5.1)} \qquad \mu_{i*} \mu_i^*(M_i) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_* f^*(M_i) . \]

Up to making the base change \(I/i \to I\), one may suppose that \(i\) is a final object of \(I\) (8.2.1). The morphism \(\mu_i : \underline{F} \to F_i\) is then the morphism composite of the morphisms (8.2.9) and (7.4.12): \[ Q : \underline{F} \to \widetilde{F} , \] \[ \beta_i : (\alpha_{i!},\alpha_i^*) : \widetilde{F} \to F_i . \] One thus has \(\mu_i^*(M_i) \simeq Q^* \beta_i^*(M_i)\), where \(\beta_i^*(M_i)\) is the section \((f : i \to j) \mapsto f^*(M_i)\) whose transition morphisms are deduced from the \(c_{f,g}\). The assertion then follows from 8.5.3.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.5.6

Under the hypotheses of 8.5.5, the functors \[ \mu_{i*} : \underline{F} \to F_i \] commute with filtered inductive limits.
The functor \(\mu_{i*}\) is composed of the functor \(Q_*\) which commutes with filtered inductive limits, and the functor "restriction to the fibre at \(i\)", which commutes with inductive limits.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.5.7

Under the hypotheses of 8.5.3, let \(i\) be an object of \(I\) and \(X\) an object of \(F_i\) such that the functor \(\mathrm{Hom}(X,-)\) on \(F_i\) commutes with filtered inductive limits. Then the functor \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mu_i^*(X),-)\) commutes with filtered inductive limits and for every object \(M_i\) of \(F_i\) one has \[ \text{(8.5.7.1)} \qquad \mathrm{Hom}(\mu_i^*(X), \mu_i^*(M_i)) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} \mathrm{Hom}(f^*(X),f^*(M_i)) . \] For every object \((j \mapsto M_j)\) of \(\mathrm{Top}(F)\) one has \[ \text{(8.5.7.2)} \qquad \mathrm{Hom}(\mu_i^*(X), Q^*(j \mapsto M_j)) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} \mathrm{Hom}(f^*(X),M_j) . \]

The functor \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mu_i^*(X),-)\) is isomorphic to the functor \(\mathrm{Hom}(X,\mu_{i*}(-))\) and the latter commutes with filtered inductive limits (8.5.4). By (8.5.5.1), one has \[ \mathrm{Hom}(\mu_i^*(X), \mu_i^*(M_i)) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(X,\mu_{i*}\mu_i^*(M_i)) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(X, \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_* f^*(M_i)) , \] whence the formula (8.5.7.1). Likewise, by (8.5.3.1), one has
\[ \mathrm{Hom}(\mu_i^*(X),Q^*(j \mapsto M_j)) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(X,\mu_{i*}Q^*(j \mapsto M_j)) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}(X, \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_*(M_j)) , \]
whence the formula (8.5.7.2).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.5.8

Let \(G \to I\) be a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos and \(m : F \to G\) a cartesian morphism of fibred topoi (7.1.15). One uses for \(G\) the notation introduced in 8.1.1. Let \(\underline{m} : \underline{F} \to \underline{G}\) be the morphism deduced from \(m\) by passing to the projective limit (8.1.4). The diagram of topoi and of morphisms of topoi: \[ \text{(8.5.8.1)} \qquad \xymatrix{ \underline{F} \ar[r]^-{Q} \ar[d]_-{\underline{m}} & \mathrm{Top}(F) \ar[d]^-{m^\sim} \\ \underline{G} \ar[r]_-{Q} & \mathrm{Top}(G) } \] is commutative up to isomorphism. For every object \(N\) of \(\underline{F}\), one has \[ \text{(8.5.8.2)} \qquad \underline{m}_*(N) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_j^* m_{j*} \mu_{j*}(N) . \]

The commutativity of the diagram (8.5.8.1) follows immediately from the definitions (8.2.8 and 8.5.1). One has \(\underline{m}_*(N) \simeq Q^* Q_* \underline{m}_*(N)\) and, by virtue of the commutativity of (8.5.8.1), \(\underline{m}_*(N) \simeq Q^* m^\sim_* Q_*(N)\). Consequently, one has an isomorphism \(\underline{m}_*(N) \simeq Q^* m^\sim_*(j \mapsto \mu_{j*}(N))\). The functor \(m^\sim_*\) is none other than the functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,\underline{m})\) (7.4.10), and consequently one has a canonical isomorphism \(\underline{m}_*(N) \simeq Q^*(j \mapsto m_{j*} \mu_{j*}(N))\). The formula (8.5.8.2) then follows from 8.5.2.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.5.9

With the hypotheses and notation of 8.5.8, one supposes moreover that for every object \(i\) of \(I\), the functor \(m_{i*} : F_i \to G_i\) commutes with filtered inductive limits and that for every morphism \(f : i \to j\) of \(I\) the functor \(f_* : F_i \to F_j\) commutes with filtered inductive limits. Then the functor \(\underline{m}_* : \underline{F} \to \underline{G}\) commutes with filtered inductive limits, and for every object \((i \mapsto M_i)\) of \(\mathrm{Top}(F)\) one has a canonical isomorphism: \[ \text{(8.5.9.1)} \qquad \underline{m}_* Q^*(i \mapsto M_i) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_j^* m_{j*}(M_j) . \]

The first assertion follows from (8.5.8.2) and from (8.5.6). By (8.5.8.2) and (8.5.3.1), one has a functorial isomorphism \[ \underline{m}_* Q^*(i \mapsto M_i) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^* m_{i*} (\varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_*(M_j)) . \] Using the commutation of the \(m_{i*}\) with filtered inductive limits and the isomorphisms \(m_{i*} f_* \simeq f_* m_{j*}\) (7.1.6), one obtains: \[ \underline{m}_* Q^*(i \mapsto M_i) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^* (\varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_* m_{j*}(M_j)) . \] Since the functors \(\mu_i^*\) commute with inductive limits, it comes: \[ \underline{m}_* Q^*(i \mapsto M_i) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} \mu_i^* f_* m_{j*}(M_j) . \] This last object may be interpreted as an inductive limit over the category \(\mathrm{Fl}(I)^\circ\) where \(\mathrm{Fl}(I)\) is the category of morphisms of \(I\). Let then \(\varphi : I \to \mathrm{Fl}(I)\) be the functor which associates to every object \(i\) of \(I\) the identity morphism of \(I\). The functor \(\varphi^\circ : I^\circ \to \mathrm{Fl}(I)^\circ\) is cofinal and consequently (I 8.1) one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \underline{m}_* Q^*(i \mapsto M_i) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_j^* m_{j*}(M_j) . \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.5.10

Under the conditions of 8.5.9, for every object \(i\) of \(I\) and every object \(M_i\) of \(F_i\), one has a canonical isomorphism: \[ \text{(8.5.10.1)} \qquad \underline{m}_* \mu_i^*(M_i) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} \mu_j^* m_{j*} f^*(M_i) . \]
The proof is analogous to that of corollary 8.5.5.

Recall that the direct-image functor by a coherent morphism between coherent topoi commutes with filtered inductive limits (5.1). Consequently the propositions 8.5.3 to 8.5.7 and 8.5.9, 8.5.10 apply when the fibred topoi under consideration are coherent and the morphisms of fibred topoi under consideration are coherent.
8.6. Ringed fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi

One says that a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos is ringed if it is endowed with a sheaf of rings on the total site (7.4.1). Let \(p : F \to I\) be a fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos. Let us choose a bisplitting (7.1.4). It follows from 7.4.7 that giving a sheaf of rings on \(F\) amounts to giving, for every object \(i\) of \(I\), a ring \(A_i\) of \(F_i\), and for every morphism \(f : i \to j\), a morphism \(\varphi_f : A_j \to f_* A_i\), the family of the \(\varphi_f\) being subject to compatibility conditions made explicit in loc. cit. The morphisms of topoi \(f_\cdot : F_i \to F_j\) are therefore morphisms of ringed topoi (respectively by \(A_i\) and \(A_j\)) (IV 11), and the ringed structure on \(F\) together with the choice of the morphisms \(f_\cdot\) furnishes a pseudo-functor from \(I\) into the 2-category of ringed topoi. Conversely, when one is given such a pseudo-functor, one may reconstruct a ringed fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos giving rise to it.

One may, as in 8.1, define the notion of projective limit of a ringed \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \((F_i,A_i,\ i \in I)\). We shall suppose that this immediate generalization has been made and we shall apply freely to this situation the language introduced in 8.1. When it exists, this projective limit is a ringed \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \((H,B)\), and one has for every object \(i\) of \(I\) morphisms of ringed topoi \(\mu_i : (H,B) \to (F_i,A_i)\). If the fibred topos \(F\) (non-ringed) admits a projective limit \(\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i\), and if the inductive system of rings \(i \mapsto \mu_i^*(A_i)\) admits an inductive limit \(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^* A_i\) in the category of rings of \(\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i\) (which is always the case if \(I\) is small) then the ringed topos \((\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i, \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^* A_i)\) is evidently a projective limit of the ringed fibred topos considered.

The formulas of section 8.5. established for sheaves of sets are valid for abelian sheaves. They are also valid for sheaves of modules, provided one interprets the inverse-image functors appearing in them as inverse-image functors in the sense of sheaves of modules (IV 11.1). We leave the verification of this to the reader.

Let \((p : F \to I, A)\) be a ringed \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred over a cofiltered category. One says that \((p : F \to I, A)\) is a right-flat ringed fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos (resp. left-) if for every morphism \(f : i \to j\), the morphism \(f_\cdot : (F_i,A_i) \to (F_j,A_j)\) is a right-flat (resp. left-flat) morphism of ringed topoi (V 1.8). Suppose \(I\) essentially small. Then the ringed-topos morphism \[ Q : (\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i, \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^*(A_i)) \to (\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{I^\circ}(I^\circ,F'),A) \quad \text{(8.5.1)} \] is right-flat (resp. left-flat), as follows from the definition and from 8.5.2, and this holds without flatness hypotheses on the transition morphisms \(f_\cdot\). If one supposes moreover that \((p : F \to I, A)\) is a right-flat (resp. left-flat) ringed fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos, the morphisms \(\mu_i : (\operatorname*{Limtop}_I F_i, \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^* A_i) \to (F_i,A_i)\) are right-flat (resp. left-flat). This follows from the fact that the inverse image of a flat module is flat (V 1.7.1), and from the fact that a filtered inductive limit of flat Modules is a flat Module. One proves by the same arguments the following fact: If \(m : (F_i,A_i,\ i \in I) \to (G_i,A_i,\ i \in I)\) is a cartesian morphism of ringed fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos over an essentially small cofiltered category and if for every object \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\), the morphism \(m_i\) is right-flat (resp. left-flat), then the morphism \(\underline{m}\) deduced from \(m\) by passing to the projective limit is right-flat (resp. left-flat).
8.7. Cohomology of the sheaves of a projective limit of topoi

In this section, \(I\) denotes a small cofiltered category, \((p : F \to I,A)\) and \((q : G \to I, B)\) two ringed fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos, \(m : (p : F \to I,A) \to (q : G \to I,B)\) a morphism of ringed fibred \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos. One supposes that for every morphism \(f : i \to j\) of \(I\), the derived functors \(R^n f_*\), \(n \in \mathbf{N}\), of the functor \(f_* : \mathrm{Mod}(F_i,A_i) \to \mathrm{Mod}(F_j,A_j)\) for modules, commute with filtered inductive limits, and that for every object \(i \in I\), the derived functors \(R^n m_{i*}\) of the functor \(m_{i*} : (F_i,A_i) \to (G_i,B_i)\) for modules(1) commute with filtered inductive limits. Recall that these hypotheses are satisfied when the categories \(F_i\), \(G_i\) (\(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\)) are coherent and when the morphisms \(f_\cdot : F_i \to F_j\), (\(f : i \to j \in \mathrm{Fl}(I)\)) and \(m_i : F_i \to G_i\), (\(i \in I\)) are coherent (5.2). One uses the notation of 8.5.1. Moreover one denotes by \(\underline{A}\) (resp. \(\underline{B}\)) the sheaf \(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^*(A_i)\) (resp. \(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_i^*(B_i)\)). Finally for the Modules, one uses the notation \(\mu_i^{-1}\) to denote the inverse image in the sense of abelian sheaves, reserving the notation \(\mu_i^*\) for the inverse image in the sense of Modules (IV 11).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.7.2

Let \(j \mapsto M_j\) be an injective \(A\)-Module of \(\mathrm{Top}(F)\). Then \(Q^*(j \mapsto M_j)\) is an \(\underline{A}\)-Module acyclic for \(\underline{m}_*\) and for every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\), \(M_i\) is flasque.

Let \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\) and \(e_i\) a final object of \(F_i\). The \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos fibred \(F/e_i \to I/i\) is deduced from \(F \to I\) by the base change \(I/i \to I\). The sheaf \(j \mapsto M_j\), being injective, is flasque (V 4.6). Its restriction to the topos localized \(F/e_i\) is flasque (V 4.12). The restriction functor from \(F/e_i\) to \(F_i\) is a direct-image functor by a morphism of topoi (7.4.12). Consequently, it transforms flasque Modules into flasque Modules (V 5.2). Hence \(M_i\) is flasque.

Let us prove the first assertion of the lemma. Set \(N' = Q^*(j \mapsto M_j)\). By (8.5.3.1), one has, for every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\) \[ \mu_{i*}(N') = \mu_{i*} Q^*(j \mapsto M_j) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} f_*(M_j) . \] Using the hypothesis (8.7.1), one sees that the sheaf \(N'\) possesses the following property:
(P) For every object \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\), \(\mu_{i*}(N')\) is \(m_{i*}\)-acyclic, and for every morphism \(f : i \to j\) of \(I\), \(\mu_{i*}(N')\) is \(f_*\)-acyclic.

It suffices to show that every object \(N'\) which possesses the property (P) is \(\underline{m}_*\)-acyclic. Since the injectives possess the property (P), it suffices to verify the following two properties (V 0.4): For every exact sequence \(0 \to N' \to N \to N''\) \(\to 0\), where \(N'\) and \(N\) possess the property (P), (a) \(N''\) possesses the property (P) and (b) \(\underline{m}_*(N) \to \underline{m}_*(N'')\) is an epimorphism. The verification of (a) is trivial. Let us verify (b). Set \(K = \operatorname{coker}(Q_*(N') \to Q_*(N))\) so that \(K\) is the section \((i \mapsto K_i = \operatorname{coker}(\mu_{i*}(N') \to \mu_{i*}(N)))\). For every \(f : i \to j\), one has a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & f_* \mu_{i*}(N') \ar[r] & f_* \mu_{i*}(N) \ar[r] & f_*(K_i) \ar[r] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & \mu_{j*}(N') \ar[r] \ar[u] & \mu_{j*}(N) \ar[r] \ar[u] & K_j \ar[r] \ar[u] & 0 } \] Since \(\mu_{i*}(N')\) is \(f_*\)-acyclic, the top horizontal sequence is exact. Since \(i \mapsto \mu_{i*}(N')\) and \(i \mapsto \mu_{i*}(N)\) are cartesian sections, the first two vertical morphisms are isomorphisms. Consequently the canonical morphism \(K_j \to f_*(K_i)\) is an isomorphism and \(i \mapsto K_i\) is a cartesian section. Hence \(K\) is of the form \(Q_*(K')\), and the canonical morphisms \(Q_*(N) \to K\) and \(K \to Q_*(N'')\) are of the form \(Q_*(u)\) and \(Q_*(v)\) respectively, since \(Q_*\) is fully faithful. Since \(Q^*\) is exact and since \(Q^* Q_*\) is isomorphic to the identity, \(v\) is an isomorphism and consequently \(Q_*(v)\) is an isomorphism. The sequence \(0 \to Q_*(N') \to Q_*(N) \to Q_*(N'') \to 0\) is therefore exact and consequently, for every object \(i\) of \(I\), the sequence \(0 \to \mu_{i*}(N') \to \mu_{i*}(N) \to \mu_{i*}(N'') \to 0\) is exact. Since \(\mu_{i*}(N')\) is \(m_{i*}\)-acyclic, the sequence \(0 \to m_{i*} \mu_{i*}(N') \to m_{i*} \mu_{i*}(N)\) \(\to m_{i*} \mu_{i*}(N'') \to 0\) is exact. Moreover one has an isomorphism \(\underline{m}_* \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_j^* m_{j*} \mu_{j*}\) (8.5.8.2). The functor \(\mu_j^{-1}\) is exact and filtered inductive limits are exact. Hence the sequence \(0 \to \underline{m}_*(N') \to \underline{m}_*(N) \to\) \(\underline{m}_*(N'') \to 0\) is exact.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 8.7.3

The notation and hypotheses are those of 8.7.1. For every integer \(n \in \mathbf{N}\), the derived functor \(R^n \underline{m}_*\) commutes with filtered inductive limits, and one has a functorial isomorphism for every \(A\)-Module \(j \mapsto M_j\): \[ \text{(8.7.3.1)} \qquad R^n \underline{m}_* Q^*(j \mapsto M_j) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_j^* R^n m_{j*}(M_j) . \]

One has \(Q^{-1}(A) = \underline{A}\), and consequently the inverse image for the Modules is isomorphic to the inverse image for the abelian sheaves. One deduces from this by 8.5.8.2 that for every section \(j \mapsto M_j\), one has a canonical isomorphism \(\varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_j^{-1}(M_j) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_j^*(M_j)\). Moreover, under the hypotheses of 8.7.1, one has a canonical isomorphism (8.5.9.1) \(\underline{m}_* Q^*(j \mapsto M_j) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_j^{-1} m_{j*}(M_j)\). Since for every injective \(j \mapsto M_j\), the \(M_j\) are flasque and \(Q^*(j \mapsto M_j)\) is acyclic for \(\underline{m}_*\) (8.7.2), one has an isomorphism \(R^n \underline{m}_* Q^*(j \mapsto M_j) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_j^{-1} R^n m_{j*}(M_j)\), whence the formula (8.7.3.1) using what precedes. The first assertion follows immediately from formula 8.7.3.1.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.7.4

One has functorial isomorphisms for \(n \in \mathbf{Z}\): \[ \text{(8.7.4.1)} \qquad R^n \underline{m}_*(N) \simeq \varinjlim_{I^\circ} \mu_j^* R^n m_{j*} \mu_{j*}(N) . \]
Indeed \(N\) is isomorphic to \(Q^*(j \mapsto \mu_{j*}(N))\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.7.5

For every object \(i\) of \(I\), every integer \(n\) and every \(A_i\)-Module \(M_i\), one has a functorial isomorphism \[ \text{(8.7.5.1)} \qquad R^n \underline{m}_* \mu_i^*(M_i) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} \mu_j^* R^n m_{j*} f^*(M_i) . \]

Up to making the base change \(I_{/i} \to I\), one may suppose that \(i\) is a final object of \(I\) (8.2.1). The object \(\mu_i^*(M_i)\) is then isomorphic to \(Q^*((f : j \to i) \mapsto f^*(M_i))\) (cf. 8.5.5).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.7.6

Let \(i\) be an object of \(I\) and \(n\) an integer. One has a functorial isomorphism in the section \(j \mapsto M_j\): \[ \text{(8.7.6.1)} \qquad R^n \mu_{i*} Q^*(j \mapsto M_j) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} R^n f_*(M_j) \] One has an isomorphism in the \(A\)-Module \(N\): \[ \text{(8.7.6.2)} \qquad R^n \mu_{i*}(N) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} R^n f_* \mu_{j*}(N) . \] One has a functorial isomorphism in the \(A_i\)-Module \(M_i\): \[ \text{(8.7.6.3)} \qquad R^n \mu_{i*} \mu_i^*(M_i) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} R^n f_* f^*(M_i) . \] The functors \(R^n \mu_{i*}\) commute with filtered inductive limits.

By making the base change \(I_{/i} \to I\) one reduces to the case where \(i\) is a final object of \(I\). The formulas (8.7.6.1) and (8.7.6.2) are then special cases of the formulas (8.7.3.1), (8.7.4.1) and (8.7.5.1), respectively obtained by taking for \(G\) the constant fibred topos of fibre \(F_i\) and for morphism \(m\) the morphism \((f_\cdot,\ f \in \mathrm{ob}(I_{/i}))\). The last assertion follows from 8.7.6.2 taking (8.5.4) into account.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.7.7

Let \(i\) be an object of \(I\), \(X\) an object of \(F_i\) such that the functors \(H^n(X,-)\), \(n \in \mathbf{N}\), commute with filtered inductive limits. One has for every \(n\) a canonical isomorphism functorial in the \(A_i\)-Module \(M_i\): \[ \text{(8.7.7.1)} \qquad H^n(\mu_i^*(X), \mu_i^*(M_i)) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} H^n(f^*(X),f^*(M_i)) \] and the functors \(H^n(\mu_i^*(X),-)\) commute with filtered inductive limits. In particular if the functors \(H^n(F_i,-)\) commute with filtered inductive limits, the functors \(H^n(\underline{F},-)\) commute with filtered inductive limits, and one has canonical isomorphisms, functorial in the \(A_i\)-Modules \(M_i\) \[ \text{(8.7.7.2)} \qquad H^n(\underline{F}, \mu_i^*(M_i)) \simeq \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} H^n(F_j,f^*(M_i)) . \]

It follows from (V 5.3) that one has two spectral sequences \[ \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {}'E_2^{pq} = \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} H^p(X,R^q f_* f^*(M_i)) \Longrightarrow \varinjlim_{f:j\to i} H^{p+q}(f^*(X),f^*(M_i)) \\[1.2ex] {}''E_2^{pq} = H^p(X,R^q \mu_{i*} \mu_i^*(M_i)) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(\mu_i^*(X), \mu_i^*(M_i)) , \end{array} \right. \] and from (8.5.7.1) that one has a morphism between these two spectral sequences.
